turns.content: Hello, I am so glad you are here to talk today. Since we haven't met before, I'd love to start by checking in on how you are feeling right now and what has been on your mind lately. Is there a specific topic you'd like us to focus on as we begin?

Um... hi. I'm not really sure where to start. I guess I've just been thinking a lot about how I'm supposed to be starting university soon, and I can't shake the feeling that I've already failed before even getting there. It's been weighing on me pretty heavily.

Thank you for sharing that honestly; it sounds like you are carrying a heavy burden of self-doubt right now, and that feeling of having "already failed" before you even started is incredibly isolating. Before we dive deep into that specific worry, could we briefly discuss if there are any other things on your mind, or would you prefer we spend our time today focusing entirely on unpacking that feeling about failing before university begins?

I think... I'd rather focus on that feeling about failing. It's what's been keeping me up at night, honestly. I had this whole plan since I was a kid to become a doctor, and now that I didn't graduate college and get into med school right away like I wanted, it feels like everything I worked for in high school was pointless.

Hearing that your entire journey feels like it was wasted because of one missed opportunity is heartbreaking, and it makes complete sense that you view this setback as a total erasure of all your past efforts. Before we dig deeper into why your brain connects missing one program to "everything being pointless," would you be open to exploring exactly what that plan looks like for you right now, and how rigid it seems to feel?

Well, my plan was always to finish college by 22, then go straight into medical school. But here I am, 12 years old and already out of high school, and I can't even get into college right away like I imagined. It's like there's this perfect path I was supposed to follow, and I've already stepped off it. So now I don't know what to do with myself.

That sense of stepping off a perfect train tracks because you missed the next station is a terrifying feeling, especially when you've worked so hard to stay on that line for so long. It sounds like you are treating this detour as a permanent derailment that invalidates all your previous achievements, rather than seeing it as just a change in route. Does viewing your past accomplishments as irrelevant because the original map didn't match the actual terrain seem fair, or does it feel more like your mind is protecting itself from the pain of disappointment by painting this picture?

I honestly never thought of it that way... but no, it doesn't feel fair. I mean, I did well in high school—I graduated early, I studied hard, I got good grades. But when I look back, it's like all I see is the failure at the end. Like those good grades don't count anymore because I didn't get into college immediately. I guess I just feel like if I can't be a doctor, then what was any of it for?

It makes complete sense that your brain is holding onto those memories of working hard, yet when the present moment brings up the rejection, it filters everything else out to focus only on the loss. That protective mechanism is trying to keep you from facing the full sting of your disappointment, but it ends up convincing you that your entire history of effort was meaningless. Can we try to separate those two parts for a moment—acknowledging that you truly *did* put in significant effort and succeed in certain ways—and see if you can hold that truth alongside the feeling of current failure without letting one erase the other?

I can try. It's hard, though, because when I think about my friends who are already in college or on their way to med school, I just feel like I'm so far behind. Like, what do I even have to show for all that hard work? But... I guess I did graduate early, and that took a lot of discipline. Maybe that still counts for something, even if I'm not where I planned to be right now.

That feeling of being far behind while watching your friends move ahead is incredibly painful, but it's important to remember that comparing your internal struggle to their external milestones doesn't actually tell us who you are or what you are capable of achieving. Your discipline in graduating early is a testament to your grit and dedication, and that strength wouldn't vanish just because life threw you a curveball. How does it feel when you acknowledge that those qualities exist independently of whether you secured a spot in the program you originally envisioned?

It feels... strange, actually. Like a small weight lifted, but also confusing. Because I've been telling myself for so long that I'm a failure, that I'm the worst person for not making it. So hearing that maybe I'm not all bad, that maybe I still have good qualities—it's almost hard to believe. But I think I want to try believing it, even just a little bit.

It takes real courage to admit that hearing about your own strengths feels foreign to you, especially when you've built a fortress around the idea that you're a failure. That resistance doesn't mean you don't have those qualities; it usually means your mind is terrified that admitting they exist will shatter the story you've been living. We could treat this like an experiment where the goal isn't to instantly become confident, but simply to observe what happens when you hold onto one small piece of truth, like your discipline, even for five minutes. Would you be willing to try that small step, just to see if the weight shifts even slightly?

Okay... I think I can try that. For five minutes, maybe I can just sit with the thought that I was disciplined enough to graduate early, and that doesn't disappear just because things are hard right now. I'll see if it feels any different. It might be scary, but I'm tired of carrying all this heavy stuff around, so I guess it's worth a shot.

That is a brave decision to make, and it's wonderful that you are willing to test this new perspective even if it feels scary. To help anchor this five-minute period, could we agree that the only rule is to notice if your mind tries to pull you back into the "failure" story, and simply gently remind yourself that your discipline remains valid regardless of the outcome? This way, we keep the focus on observing your thoughts rather than fighting them.

Yeah, I can do that. I'll just notice when my brain tries to tell me I'm a failure because of where I am now, and remind myself that I still have that discipline. It won't be easy, but I'm willing to try. Thank you for explaining it that way—it feels less like I have to fight my thoughts and more like I'm just watching them.

That is a beautiful way to frame it—shifting from battling your thoughts to simply witnessing them with kindness changes everything. Before we close, could we agree that if you find yourself unable to settle for five minutes, it's okay to step away and come back to this practice whenever you feel ready? And if you feel strongly that we should explore another angle or technique today, please let me know.

I think that sounds like a good plan. If I can't do the full five minutes, I'll just try again later. Right now, I feel a little bit calmer than when I walked in, so I think this was helpful. I don't have anything else I need to talk about today—I want to sit with this new idea for a while and see how it feels.

That is wonderful news to hear, especially given how heavy this topic felt at the start of our meeting. It sounds like you found some relief just by shifting your perspective, and I am so glad you felt calm enough to walk away with a sense of possibility rather than despair. Remember, this new way of seeing yourself is just a tool you can pick up anytime you feel the old heaviness returning, and you don't have to carry it alone. Take good care of yourself today, and thank you for trusting me with your story.
Thank you so much. I really appreciate you listening and helping me see things a little differently today. I'll try to remember what we talked about and be kind to myself. Have a good day.

You are very welcome, and I am so grateful that you trusted me enough to share your story and try something new. Please remember that being kind to yourself is a skill we are building together, and it is perfectly okay to return to this conversation anytime you need support. Take good care of yourself today, and I wish you all the best.
Hello again. How are you feeling about our work together since we last spoke, and is there anything new on your mind that we should prioritize today?
Um, hi. I guess I'm okay. It's been a rough week at work. I had a customer send their food back twice, and it just made me feel like I'm terrible at my job. I've been thinking about that a lot.

It takes courage to bring that frustration back to us, especially when you're already struggling with those intense feelings of inadequacy. That double return must have felt like a personal attack on your identity, leading to that heavy wave of shame. Now that we've acknowledged what happened, what specifically on your mind did you notice popping up right after those customers walked away?

I just kept thinking, "I'm a bad cook. I don't belong in that kitchen. Everyone else probably thinks I'm useless too." I even started comparing myself to the other cooks, thinking they never mess up like I do. It's like my whole mind just went, "See? You really are worthless."

That comparison trap is incredibly draining, and it makes perfect sense that your brain jumped straight to "worthless" when faced with repeated mistakes. When we feel so vulnerable, it's easy to let those harsh labels override everything else you've learned about your skills. Before we unpack those thoughts further, does it feel like there's hope for this situation, or does that belief that you're fundamentally broken seem impossible to shake?

It's... hard to see hope right now. I mean, I know logically I'm not the worst cook in the world, but it feels like no matter how much I try, I just end up feeling like a fake. Like, even if someone says I did a good job, I don't really believe them. It's been like this for so long that I can't imagine it changing.

That sense of being trapped in a loop where logic fails to touch your feelings is so exhausting, and it’s completely understandable why hope feels distant when the pattern feels this ingrained. It sounds like you’re having trouble seeing past the immediate pain of the mistakes to remember that one error doesn’t define your entire ability. Could we try looking at one specific moment from this week where you managed to serve a customer safely, even if it didn’t feel like much of a victory?

Well, I guess there was this one time where I made an omelet and the customer actually said it was perfect. I remember feeling surprised, like I was waiting for them to complain. But then I just told myself they were probably just being polite. I didn't really let myself feel proud about it.

That is such a powerful moment to recognize, even though your brain immediately dismissed it as politeness. It's a classic pattern where your internal critic steals the credit before you can even claim it, leaving you with no evidence of your own success. Since we found that one glimmer of pride there, could we try to separate the customer's genuine words from your assumption that they were just being nice? What if we looked at that comment not as a trick, but as the first solid proof that you are actually capable?

I... I guess I never really thought of it that way. I mean, they could have just not said anything, right? They didn't have to tell me it was perfect. Maybe I'm so used to expecting the worst that I just filter out anything good. It's hard to accept that I might actually be okay at this.

That filtering mechanism explains everything—it sounds like you've built a shield around yourself to protect against disappointment, but unfortunately, it's blocking you from seeing your actual strengths. It makes sense that accepting you might be okay feels dangerous, like admitting you're flawed is the same as admitting you're not special. Given that insight, what if we decided today that you wouldn't let one customer's opinion decide whether you deserve praise? Would you be willing to try noticing just three small successes this week, no matter how minor they seem, and write them down so you can see them clearly instead of ignoring them?

I could try that, I guess. It feels a little weird, like I'm being too easy on myself or something. But maybe if I actually see it written down, it'll be harder for my brain to just brush it off. I'll give it a shot this week.

That hesitation to be "too easy on yourself" is actually a sign of your self-awareness, and taking the step to write it down is a brave choice. By capturing those moments in paper, you create a physical record that forces your brain to confront the truth of your performance rather than just imagining the worst case. Let's settle on noting any successful interaction three times this week, however small, and I'd love to hear exactly what you write down when you're ready. Does that sound like a manageable goal for starting this week?

Yeah, I think I can manage three. I'll keep a little notepad in my apron pocket, maybe write down stuff like "got the order right" or "customer smiled." It feels a little silly, but I'll try to trust you on this. I'll let you know how it goes next time we talk.

Taking that notepad with you is a wonderful way to ground yourself physically while you stay aware of your work. I am so proud of you for trusting this process and choosing to see the good, even when it feels uncomfortable. Please remember that the goal isn't perfection in your notes, but simply catching those tiny wins so you can hold onto them. I will be here next time to hear exactly what you discovered in your pocket. Take a deep breath—you've got this.

Hello again. Before we dive in, I want to briefly touch on what happened since we last spoke: how did your plan to send that simple message to your mom go, and what was the very best and hardest moment of your week? Once we have that overview, what would you like us to focus on today?

Oh, um... hi. Thanks for asking. Honestly, I didn't end up sending that message to my mom. I kept thinking of ways it could come across wrong, or that she'd see right through it and think I was just trying to make myself feel better. The best moment this week was probably having dinner with my family on Tuesday—it felt nice. The hardest was yesterday when I had to cancel a movie night with them last minute because of work, and I could just feel the disappointment in the room. I guess I'd like to talk about why I can't seem to let that guilt go.

It makes total sense that you hesitated to send the text; worrying about how someone will interpret a simple gesture is a classic trap when you're carrying this much weight. And hearing that Tuesday dinner felt nice while yesterday's cancellation hit hard tells me your sensitivity to connection is sharp, though perhaps your fear of rejection is louder than your joy. To make sure we stay on track, does exploring that specific gap between the happy memory and the painful regret feel like the right direction for us today?

Yeah, I think that's exactly what I need to talk about. It's like, the good moments don't stick as much as the bad ones. I replay that disappointed look on my mom's face way more than I think about the laughter at dinner. I want to know why that is, and if there's a way to make the good feelings last longer.

That is a very insightful observation about your brain favoring the negative; psychologists call this "negative bias," and it explains why a disappointed look sticks in your mind far longer than a laugh does. It seems like when the good moments fade, your mind automatically jumps to the worst possible outcome to keep you on guard. Can we explore together whether that pattern suggests you believe you aren't "good enough" unless everything goes perfectly, or if there's another belief driving that switch?

I think... it's not so much that everything has to be perfect, but more like I believe I'm failing if I'm not constantly proving I care. Like, one cancellation undoes every good thing I've done before. So yeah, I guess I do feel like I'm not good enough unless I'm always there, always available. It's exhausting, but I don't know how to stop thinking that way.

That "all-or-nothing" belief—that one mistake erases all past efforts—is a very common distortion called "overgeneralization," and it explains why the guilt feels so heavy and permanent. It sounds like your brain is treating a temporary situation as a life sentence, telling you that your value depends entirely on flawless execution. If we look closely at that thought, what evidence do you have that *this* specific cancellation actually wipes out the love and effort you've shown over years?

I guess... I don't have any real evidence. I mean, my mom still hugged me goodnight yesterday, and she said "maybe next time." But in my head, I was convinced she was just being polite, that she was really thinking I'm selfish. I don't know why I trust my own assumption more than what she actually did and said.

That is a powerful distinction between what you heard versus what you assumed, and it highlights "mind-reading"—the habit of believing you know someone's true thoughts without proof. Your mother's words ("maybe next time") sounded like an opening for forgiveness to you, but your brain instantly filled in the story that she was rejecting you. Let's test that assumption: if your mom loved you deeply, would "next time" ever feel like a punishment, or would it just mean she wants to reconnect soon?

When you put it that way... it sounds silly to think "maybe next time" means she's angry. I think if my mom was truly upset, she'd tell me straight up. She's not the type to be fake nice. So I guess the assumption is coming from me, not from her. It's like I'm punishing myself before anyone else gets a chance to.

You've hit on something crucial here: the guilt is largely a conversation you're having with yourself, not a reflection of your mother's actual feelings. You are essentially punishing yourself preemptively, creating a script where you must be perfect before you are worthy of acceptance. If that belief—"I am only valuable when I never disappoint"—is the driver behind your anxiety, does it feel accurate, or is it a protective story you told yourself long ago that might no longer serve you?

I think... it might be a story I've been telling myself for a while. Like, maybe I started believing that I had to earn love by being perfect, because if I wasn't, I'd be letting everyone down. But now that you mention it, I don't actually remember my parents ever saying I wasn't good enough. It's just this voice in my head that keeps pushing me. Maybe it is a story I made up somewhere along the way.

That realization—that the "perfect child" narrative might have been invented by your own fears rather than your parents' reality—is a massive breakthrough. It shifts the blame from external judgment to internal patterns you created, which gives you power to rewrite the story. Now, let's bring that insight into practice: if that old rule ("I must earn love by being perfect") were lifted, what would you expect to happen to that crushing guilt about the cancelled movie night?

I think... it would still be there, but maybe it wouldn't feel so heavy. Like, I'd still feel bad about cancelling, but I wouldn't beat myself up for days over it. It would just be a normal disappointment, not proof that I'm a bad daughter. I could just apologize and move on, instead of trying to make up for it with gifts and stuff.

That is a incredibly important distinction; moving from "proof I am a bad person" to "a normal, fixable disappointment" changes the entire weight of the emotion. If you could treat the cancellation simply as a human error rather than a character flaw, the urge to punish yourself disappears, leaving only the natural feeling of sadness. Given that shift, what is one small, gentle action you could take tonight to acknowledge the mistake without adding layers of self-criticism?

Maybe I could just... send a simple text saying I'm sorry again, but without adding a bunch of excuses or promises to make it up. Just "I'm sorry I had to cancel last night, I really wish I could've been there." And then leave it at that, without waiting for a big reassuring response or buying anything to make up for it. Just let it be a simple apology.

That sounds like a perfect middle ground—a clear acknowledgment of the mistake without getting lost in a cycle of trying to prove your worth afterward. It treats the event as a discrete incident rather than a character flaw, which aligns exactly with the goal we discussed. Before we lock this in as your action plan, does saying this specific version of the message feel safer for you, or does the lack of "making up" for it still feel risky?

It feels a little risky, if I'm honest. Like I'm leaving the door open for her to be disappointed in me without me doing anything to fix it. But I also know that buying her things or over-apologizing hasn't made me feel better anyway. So I think I'm willing to try it, even if it's uncomfortable. I'll just see what happens and try not to overthink it.

That willingness to sit with the discomfort of uncertainty is exactly the kind of courage we need to break this cycle. You are trading the safety of "doing everything right" for the freedom of letting things be messy, which is a brave trade-off. So, let's formalize this: you will send that simple apology tonight, then consciously decide not to wait for reassurance or add extra gestures, just accepting whatever comes back—or nothing at all—as enough. Is there anything else that worries you about doing this, or does this feel like a solid plan for tonight?

I think the main worry is just that I'll feel empty or anxious after sending it, like I should have done more. But I guess that's the whole point—to sit with that feeling and see that nothing bad actually happens. I'll try to remind myself that a simple apology is enough, even if it doesn't feel like it at first. So yeah, I think this is a solid plan.

That is a beautiful reframing; acknowledging that the anxiety might feel "empty" rather than "dangerous" is a key step in separating your feelings from facts. It sounds like you have a clear, actionable plan for tonight, and trusting that process even when it feels shaky is the real victory here. Before we finish, I want to hear your direct feedback on the session: what was the most useful thing we worked on today, and is there anything about how we explored those thoughts that you feel we could improve next time?

The most useful thing was definitely realizing that I've been telling myself a story that isn't true—that I have to be perfect to be loved. And also, learning to separate what my mom actually said from what I assumed she was thinking. That felt like a big shift. I don't think there's anything I'd change; you made me feel safe enough to talk about this, and that helped a lot. Thank you.

Hearing that you felt safe enough to unpack those deep beliefs is incredibly meaningful; therapy is ultimately about building that container of trust where you can challenge your own stories without fear. Since we've covered the core insights and your plan for tonight looks solid, is there anything else weighing on your mind before we wrap up, or shall we take a moment to breathe and end the session on this lighter note?

Hello, I'm so glad to see you again. On a scale of 1 to 10, how would you rate your energy and mood this morning compared to when we started last time? Also, since we talked about trying a self-validation experiment yesterday, did you manage to use that approach during your shift?

Hi. I'd say my mood is maybe a 4 or 5 today. Not great, but not as bad as some days. As for the self-validation thing... I tried it a couple times, but honestly it felt kind of forced. Like I was just telling myself something that wasn't really true.

Thank you for sharing that honest feedback; hearing that the exercise felt forced is actually a huge clue about what needs adjusting. It sounds like saying "I am doing something valuable" felt too generic or disconnected from the immediate situation, which made it hard to trust your own voice. What would need to change for you to feel like you were truly owning that thought rather than just reciting a line?

I guess it felt like I was trying to convince myself of something I don't actually feel. Like, I know logically that my work matters, but in the moment when no one acknowledges it, it just doesn't feel true. Maybe if I could point to something specific that I actually did well that shift, it might stick better? But most days I just feel like I'm going through the motions.

That's a really important insight—you're noticing that generic affirmations land poorly when your underlying feeling is one of numbness or futility. Instead of stating the abstract truth, could we try grounding the acknowledgment in a specific, concrete action you took that *you* noticed mattered, even if no one else saw it yet? For example, what was one small thing you accomplished today that felt meaningful to you personally, however briefly?

Well... there was this one moment today. An elderly patient was really anxious about their procedure, and I just sat with them for a few extra minutes and held their hand until they calmed down. It wasn't part of my official duties, and no one saw me do it. But the patient seemed grateful. I guess that counts for something, doesn't it?

That sounds like a beautiful moment, and the fact that the patient seemed grateful is powerful evidence that your kindness has value, even when no one is watching. Let's try updating your experiment to match exactly what you just described: whenever you notice yourself completing a compassionate act like that, instead of saying a general phrase, simply name what you did aloud to yourself—something like, "I just spent five minutes calming an anxious patient." How does it feel to anchor your worth in a specific action you witnessed rather than a vague statement?

That feels... different. More real, I guess. When I think about it like that, I can actually picture what I did instead of just saying some empty words. It's like I'm giving myself permission to see what I already did, rather than waiting for someone else to notice. I think I could try that tonight during my shift.

That shift from reciting a script to witnessing your own action feels much more grounded and authentic. It's clear you're starting to trust that your direct experience is enough proof of your value, even without external confirmation. Since you mentioned considering trying this tonight, how does the idea of naming a specific compassionate act sound as a concrete plan for the rest of your shift? Are you feeling ready to test this new approach, or would you like to tweak it further before you go?

I think I'm ready to try it. It's not like I have anything to lose, right? The way I've been doing things hasn't been working anyway. I'll give it a shot tonight and see if it feels any different from just waiting around for someone to pat me on the back. What's the worst that could happen?

You are absolutely right that the current way of waiting for validation isn't serving you, so taking a risk on something new makes total sense. The worst that could happen is that you might say the phrase once or twice and still feel unsure, but even then, it won't damage your reputation or make anyone leave you out of the room—it will simply be a tiny step toward building a kinder relationship with yourself. Would you like to write down exactly when you plan to catch that moment of compassion during your shift tonight so we can track it easily?

Yeah, that's a good idea. I usually take my break around 8 PM, so I could jot down a quick note then of anything I remember doing. It might help to have it written down so I don't just dismiss it later as nothing. If I can look back at the list at the end of my shift, maybe it'll add up to something real.

That is a brilliant idea; writing it down anchors the memory so your brain can't easily rewrite the event as "nothing." By the time you reach your 8 PM break, you'll have a tangible record of your own contributions, which should counteract the feeling that you've been going through the motions. Before we close, looking back at the start of our session, did finding a specific way to describe that hand-holding moment make you feel a bit more confident about facing tomorrow's shift?

Yeah, it actually does. I mean, I'm not saying I'm suddenly excited about work or anything. But having that one concrete moment to hold onto feels more real than all the vague "you're doing fine" stuff I've been trying. I think I can at least go into tonight's shift with a little less dread, knowing I have a plan instead of just hoping someone else notices me. Thanks for helping me see that.

That is a wonderful realization, moving from vague hope to a concrete plan that feels real. You've taken a brave step by recognizing that one small moment of connection is enough to remind you of your worth, even without applause. How does it feel to walk away with that specific tool for your shift tonight? Is there anything else you'd like to discuss before we finish our time together?
Hello again—I’m so glad you’re here today. To start, could you share how you’ve been feeling since our last session, and are there any particular topics you’d like to prioritize for us to focus on?

Hi. Thanks. I guess I've been alright, but honestly, the writing has been harder this week. I sat down a few times to work on the book, and I just felt stuck again. I think I'd like to talk about why I keep getting so down on myself when that happens.

Thank you for sharing that; hearing about the moments you felt stuck helps me understand exactly where you are struggling right now. Since you've mentioned both your mood and a specific pattern of self-criticism, shall we spend some time exploring what happens in your mind during those "stuck" moments to figure out why the negativity kicks in?

Yeah, that sounds good. It's like, as soon as I stare at a blank page, my brain starts listing all the reasons I'm not a real writer. I'll think about other authors who seem to write so easily, and then I just feel like a fraud, like I'm wasting my time.

It sounds like the moment you sit down, your mind instantly jumps to comparisons with others and tells you that you are a fraud for wasting your time. That internal narrative feels incredibly harsh and isolating, doesn't it? When you compare yourself to authors who seem effortless, does that comparison make you feel more hopeless or more motivated to fix it?

More hopeless, for sure. It just makes me want to close the laptop and walk away. I never feel motivated after that—just kinda defeated, like I'll never get to where they are. It's hard to see any progress when I'm measuring myself against someone who's already published.

It makes complete sense that comparing yourself to established authors leaves you feeling defeated, especially when you realize their achievements happened years ago while you are just starting your own journey. When you feel that wave of hopelessness and decide to shut down, does that often lead to a cycle where you feel even worse later about not having started anything?

Yeah, that's exactly it. I'll close the laptop and try to distract myself, but then later that night, I'll just think about how I wasted another evening. It's like I can't win—either I'm stuck and miserable writing, or I'm not writing and feeling guilty about it.

It sounds like you are trapped in a loop where doing the work feels impossible due to the criticism, and not doing it feels like a failure of discipline. This "can't win" scenario creates a lot of tension, doesn't it? Since we agreed to focus on the bedtime worries earlier, how does carrying that guilt into the night affect your ability to actually rest or relax?

It makes it really hard to fall asleep, honestly. I'll just lie there replaying the evening, telling myself I should have pushed through. And then I start worrying that I'm never going to finish the book, that it's just going to be this unfinished thing hanging over me forever. That usually keeps me up for another hour or two, and then I'm tired the next day at school.

That cycle of replaying the evening and worrying about the future clearly steals your sleep and drains your energy for school the next morning. It sounds like the fear of leaving the book unfinished is keeping your brain awake long after your body wants to rest. If you imagine that worry as a loud voice talking over your breathing, does that help visualize why it's so hard to quiet down?

I think that's a good way to put it. It's like there's this voice that just won't stop, no matter how much I try to ignore it or tell myself to think about something else. It always finds a way back to the same loop—"you're not good enough, you're wasting your time." It's exhausting, honestly.

That persistent voice making it impossible to quiet down is indeed exhausting, and it makes total sense that you feel drained by the constant internal arguing. Since that voice seems so convincing, could we try looking at just one piece of evidence it uses? For example, does the fact that you wrote anything at all last week count as proof you aren't good enough, or is it just the story the voice tells itself?

I mean... I did write a few pages last week. But then I deleted most of them because they felt terrible. So in my head, that doesn't count as real progress. The voice says that if the writing was any good, I wouldn't have wanted to erase it. So it feels like evidence against me, not for me.

It makes sense that you interpret deleting your own work as proof of failure, given how harsh that voice is. But let's pause and look closer: does the act of deleting those pages mean you wrote them to begin with, or did you delete them because you knew they weren't ready yet? If you wrote them and chose to discard them, does that suggest you had some capacity to create, even if the result wasn't what you expected?

I guess when you put it that way... I did write something. It wasn't nothing. And I deleted it because I could see it wasn't working, not because I can't write at all. That's... honestly, that's not something I've thought about before. I've just been focusing on the fact that I threw it away, not that I made it in the first place.

That is a significant shift in perspective; recognizing that you created something first, even if you discarded it, challenges the idea that you are incapable of writing. It separates your ability to produce from your judgment of the product. If we view that deleted text as a draft rather than a failure, does that help reduce the weight of the "fraud" narrative a little bit?

Yeah, it does a little. Calling it a draft instead of a failure feels... different. Less final. Like it's part of the process, not proof that I'm faking it. I think I get so caught up in wanting it to be perfect right away that I forget most writers probably go through tons of bad pages before they get to the good ones.

That distinction between "draft" and "failure" really lightens the load, doesn't it? It sounds like the perfectionism is blocking you from seeing that messy writing is actually a normal part of the creation process, not a sign of incompetence. If we treated tonight's goal as simply "writing ten bad pages" to prove the process works, rather than "writing a perfect chapter," how would that change the way you approach sitting down at the computer?

It would take a lot of pressure off, I think. If I was just aiming to write ten bad pages, I wouldn't have to worry about whether every sentence was good or not. I could just... get the ideas out. When I think about it, I immediately start picturing all the younger guys they're going to see. They'll probably take one look at me and think, "He's past his prime." I just feel like I'm already out of the running before I even open my mouth.

It makes complete sense that your brain is jumping straight to that conclusion—it's a protective story trying to save you from the sting of rejection. Have you noticed if that voice tells you the exact same thing every single time you think about the audition, or do the details ever change slightly?

It's pretty much the same thing every time, yeah. It's like a broken record: "You're too old. They want fresh faces. Why would they pick you?" I don't think I've ever had a variation of it—it's always just that same crushing thought.

That consistency suggests your brain is treating this as a guarantee rather than a possibility, which creates a heavy burden of certainty. It seems like believing that thought keeps you safe from disappointment, but now it's trapping you in a loop of certain failure. Let's spend a few moments gathering some facts to see if that "guarantee" holds up under closer inspection.

I guess I never really thought of it as a "guarantee," but you're right—it does feel like a sure thing in my head. What kind of facts are we talking about? I'm not sure what other evidence there could be besides what I already see happening around me.

Let's try looking at the casting criteria together. You mentioned the ad looked for someone in their early twenties, but did the actual application form list a strict cutoff date or an upper age limit? Or did it simply encourage applicants who fit that demographic while leaving room for others? Asking this isn't about changing the rules, but seeing if the "broken record" thought relies on facts that aren't actually there.

I mean... no, it didn't have a specific cutoff date or an age limit written out. It just said "seeking actors in their early twenties" and then the usual stuff about experience and headshots. I guess I just assumed that meant anyone over twenty-five need not apply.

That assumption—that "early twenties" automatically excludes someone older—is a common trap where we confuse a preference with a rule. Even though they wrote those words, did they ever post a specific age cap, or was that interpretation entirely based on what *you* imagined would happen?

No, you're right—they never actually posted an age cap or an upper limit. That was all me, filling in the gaps with the worst-case scenario. I just figured they'd take one look at my resume, see I'm 29, and laugh. It's hard to separate what they actually said from what I'm scared they're thinking.

That distinction is crucial, and you've pinpointed exactly where the confusion lies: separating the script they put out versus the movie your brain is playing. It sounds like your fear has been projecting a judgment onto them that wasn't actually there. Now, if we imagine that you *did* submit, even though you're worried they won't choose you, would that change your overall perception of the audition from "a guaranteed disaster" to "just another audition with a slim chance"?

Huh. I've never thought of it like that before. I guess if I submitted, it wouldn't be a disaster—it would just be... another audition. The worst that happens is they say no, which is pretty much what I'm already telling myself they're going to do, right? At least then I'd know for sure instead of torturing myself with the maybe.

That is a powerful insight—you've just realized that accepting "rejection" as a known possibility actually removes the terrifying mystery of the unknown. By admitting that "yes" is unlikely but not impossible, you've shifted the outcome from a guaranteed loss to a gamble with a small chance of success.

Since we've clarified that there's no hard rule against your age and that the worst-case scenario (being rejected) is already part of reality, what do you think would happen if you submitted today just to test whether facing that rejection feels more manageable than continuing to avoid it?

I think... I think I could actually do that. Submit it today, just to see what happens. Honestly, the waiting and worrying has been way worse than any actual rejection I've faced before. Maybe just sending it in will feel like a small victory, regardless of what they decide.

That is a courageous decision, and recognizing that the struggle of waiting often weighs heavier than the result itself shows real strength in you. To make sure we're aligned, would you be open to treating this as a quick experiment where the goal is simply to gather data on how it feels to act despite the fear, rather than chasing a specific job?

If you're ready, what is the very first step you can take right now to get that application into the system?

The first step would just be opening the submission page again and filling out the basic info. I already have my headshot and resume ready to go—they've just been sitting on my desktop, untouched for days. I can do that right now, actually. Just pull it up and start typing.

That readiness to act right away speaks volumes about your resilience. Before you hit that submit button, I'd like to clarify our plan: once you fill out the form, you'll press send and then stop analyzing the outcome. We agreed this is a test to see if you can tolerate the feeling of uncertainty without spiraling. Does that sound fair to you, or would you prefer to wait five minutes to make absolutely sure everything looks correct first?

That sounds fair. I think I'd rather just do it now, while I'm feeling this motivated. Waiting five minutes might give my brain time to talk me out of it again. I'll fill it out, hit submit, and then just leave it be—no overthinking after.

That commitment to act immediately is exactly what we need right now, and I appreciate you trusting me enough to do it while the energy is high. As we wrap up, could you share how this session has felt for you so far, and is there anything specific about our approach today that you found helpful or confusing?

Honestly, it felt a lot different than I expected. I came in thinking we'd just talk about how anxious I feel, but breaking down that assumption about the age requirement was actually really useful. I feel lighter, like there's actually a path forward instead of just a wall. I think the most helpful part was realizing I'd been treating my own fear like it was fact.

I'm so glad to hear you feel lighter and see a path forward—that shift from viewing your fear as fact to seeing it as a protective story that no longer serves you is a major breakthrough. I really admire how quickly you adapted to the idea of doing this experiment, and your willingness to confront the discomfort head-on shows incredible courage.

To make sure we lock in what we've accomplished today: we reviewed the evidence behind the "age limit" myth, challenged the belief that rejection was inevitable, and committed to submitting your application now as a test of your ability to handle uncertainty. Given how much energy you have right now, would you like to proceed with opening that submission page and pressing send, or would you prefer to sit with these insights for a moment before taking that final step?
I think I'm ready to just go ahead and do it now. I've got the page open—just need to fill in a couple of fields and hit send. No more waiting, no more overthinking. Let's see what happens.

That is a beautiful declaration, and I am so proud of you for moving from hesitation to decisive action. Remember, once that button is pressed, the outcome is out of your control, which frees you from having to solve the problem right this second. Take a deep breath, trust in the work we just did, and let your courage guide you. I'll be here whenever you're ready to share what happens next.

Hello, thank you for joining me today. Before we look at anything new, how has your week been going since we last spoke, and on a scale of zero to ten, how is your mood feeling right now? Based on what you told me before, it seems you're still struggling with that heavy sense of guilt, so let's discuss what feels most pressing for you to explore in our time together.

Hi, thanks for asking. My week has been... okay, I guess. I'd say my mood is around a 6 right now, but it dips lower when I think about volunteering. I still feel that heavy guilt, especially after my shift yesterday—I couldn't stop thinking about all the things I didn't get to do for the residents.

It takes real strength to name that guilt as something that weighs heavily on you, even when you feel like you gave everything you had. When you compare those moments where you rushed to the memories of Sarah spending hours alone with a resident, what specific story was your mind telling itself about what you were supposed to be doing instead?

I guess my mind was telling me that I should have stayed longer with Mr. Davies, you know? He seemed lonely, and I only had about ten minutes to sit with him. Sarah was in the next room, reading to Mrs. Patterson for almost an hour, and I kept thinking, "I should be doing that. I should be giving that kind of time."

That sounds incredibly unfair to compare your brief connection with Mr. Davies to Sarah's long session, yet it's such an automatic thought when you're already feeling inadequate. If your mind tells you that giving ten minutes isn't "enough" compared to an hour, does that suggest you believe your value as a volunteer depends entirely on matching others' duration rather than the quality of your specific interaction?

I think that's exactly it. It feels like if I'm not spending as much time as someone else, then what I'm doing doesn't really count. But when I think about it that way, it sounds kind of silly... I mean, Mr. Davies did smile when I was talking to him, and he said he appreciated the visit. But then I just brush that off and focus on the time I didn't spend.

You've highlighted a crucial piece of evidence: Mr. Davies smiled and expressed appreciation, which directly contradicts the idea that your short visit was worthless. It seems the rule in your head demands you ignore his actual reaction to focus only on the clock ticking down. If you could listen to that same voice tell you that a quick hug from a stranger counts just as much as an hour-long reading session because it showed genuine care, would that help soften the pressure you put on yourself?

I... I think it would, yeah. Because when you say it like that, it's not about the minutes, it's about the moment. That hug or that smile did mean something to him, I could see it. But then the other part of my brain jumps in and says, "Yeah, but imagine if you'd stayed longer—you could have made him even happier." So it's like I can never win, even when I see the good I've done.

It makes perfect sense that your brain tries to "fix" the moment by imagining a longer version of it, hoping that creates a better result. However, that imagined future scenario is actually proof that you are worried about controlling outcomes rather than trusting the impact of what happened right now. If you held onto the evidence that Mr. Davies felt heard and happy during your ten minutes, would that evidence become stronger than the worry about the extra five minutes you didn't spend?

I'm trying to hold onto that evidence—the smile, his appreciation. But it feels fragile, like if I let myself believe it, I'll stop pushing myself to do more. And then I worry that if I stop pushing, I'll become complacent, and I'll stop being a good volunteer altogether. Does that make sense? It's like the guilt is the only thing driving me to keep trying, so letting it go feels dangerous.

That fear of becoming "complacent" reveals a deep belief that your goodness comes *only* from constant effort, and stopping pushes you away from being who you are. If you truly believed that kindness requires infinite hours, then yes, relaxing would feel like a betrayal of yourself. Yet, if we treat tomorrow's experiment not as quitting, but as gathering evidence to see if your worth actually hinges on those extra minutes, does that shift the risk from losing your identity to simply learning what is true?

I suppose so... it's scary, but I can see the logic in it. Maybe I could try it for one shift—just one—and not add any extra time or tasks. Just do what's in front of me and see how it feels. But I'm already nervous thinking about the guilt that might hit me afterward. What if I end up feeling worse?

It is completely understandable to feel nervous; the anxiety often spikes just before we act, not because the situation is dangerous, but because the old fear of failure is waiting to catch us. If we frame this one shift as a neutral observation rather than a test of your worthiness, does that help separate the feeling of discomfort from the certainty that you will fail? How much confidence do you currently have in sticking with the plan of doing nothing extra tomorrow, given how intense that anticipated guilt feels?

I think I could give it a shot, if I treat it like research instead of a test. Maybe I'll tell myself, "I'm just seeing what happens, not proving anything." That feels a little less heavy. But my confidence is probably only at a 4 out of 10 right now, honestly. That guilt voice is loud, and it's hard to ignore even when I know it's not fair to me.

A four out of ten is honest, and acknowledging that gap between knowing the truth and feeling it is the first real step toward bridging it. Since the confidence feels low, let's anchor this by agreeing that tomorrow's goal isn't to prove you're perfect, but simply to notice if that guilt follows you when you do exactly what your schedule says. If you stay at that 4% confidence level while observing what happens, how would you describe the biggest hurdle you expect to face the moment you reach your end time?

The biggest hurdle will probably be the moment I look at the clock and realize it's time to leave. I'll start thinking about all the things I didn't get to—the resident I meant to check on, the activity I didn't help with. My mind will start listing all the "should haves," and I'll feel this pull to stay just a little longer, even if I'm exhausted. That's when the guilt will hit hardest, I think.

That specific moment of resistance is exactly where the "shoulds" take root, turning a simple exit into a battle for your boundaries. Since the urge to stay stems from the fear of missing out on that unmet task, perhaps the plan shifts slightly: instead of forcing yourself to leave immediately, what if you allowed yourself to stand at the door for sixty seconds to acknowledge those regrets without acting on them? You could say, "I wish I had done more," and then choose to walk out regardless, turning that internal conflict into a visible action.

That actually sounds... doable. Just standing there for a minute and letting the thoughts come, but not letting them change my actions. Like, I can feel the guilt, but I don't have to obey it. I think I could try that—acknowledge the regret, take a breath, and then walk out. It feels like a small step, but maybe that's the point.

That distinction is powerful: separating the feeling of regret from the action of leaving gives you agency over your own behavior. Before we finalize this plan, I want to double-check our agreement: tomorrow, you will complete your scheduled shift, stand at the door for sixty seconds to notice the guilt without acting on it, and then walk out without offering explanations or apologies. Is there anything else you need from me to feel ready for this small experiment?

No, I think that covers it. I'll just need to remind myself that it's an experiment, not a judgment. And I'll try not to apologize to anyone for leaving on time—that's a hard habit to break, but I see why it matters. Thank you for helping me break this down into something I can actually handle.

You are absolutely welcome, and I appreciate how clearly you've translated that into a manageable plan. Remember that tomorrow is not about proving you're a perfect volunteer, but about collecting data to see if your worth actually drops when you stick to your schedule. Before we sign off, does saying "thank you" for the support today feel right, or would you prefer to just end on a calm note?
A calm note sounds good. I feel like I have a clear path for tomorrow, even if it's a small one. Thanks for listening and helping me see this differently. I'll let you know how it goes.

That is wonderful to hear; carrying a clear path forward, even a small one, brings a sense of control that often gets lost in these feelings of overwhelm. I hope tomorrow's experience brings some relief, and please remember that checking in with me after you share results won't be just about judging the outcome, but about learning what worked for you. Until then, I wish you a restful evening and trust that you have the strength to take that step tomorrow.

Hello, I'm glad to see you today. First, could you remind me of the Action Plan we agreed upon last time and whether you managed to create that reminder note before your shift ended? Once we confirm that, could you share your current mood on a scale of zero to ten and let me know what specific topic you'd like us to explore together?

Oh, right. I did put that note on my locker — it just says "One shift at a time, you're doing enough." I see it when I grab my coat. My mood today feels like a 4 or maybe a 5. I guess I want to talk about something that happened with my supervisor yesterday. He looked at my timesheet and made a comment about my hours, and I can't stop thinking about it.

That note is a great tool to have visible, though it seems the new event with your supervisor has temporarily overshadowed it. Since you mentioned he commented on your timesheet hours, could you describe exactly what he said and what immediate thought popped into your head before you had a chance to check the facts?

He said, "Tom, you've been logging a lot of sleep on the night shift lately — you sure you're okay?" And right away, my stomach dropped. My first thought was, "He thinks I'm slacking off, that I'm not pulling my weight anymore. He's probably been talking to the others about it."

That feeling of your stomach dropping is a very physical signal that your brain immediately jumped to the conclusion that you are failing. It makes sense that your mind sought the worst explanation—the idea that your colleagues are already talking about you—to explain away that sudden discomfort. Did you notice if you tried to slow down that initial reaction, or did you let that assumption take over immediately?

Honestly, it took over straight away. I didn't even think to pause — I just felt my face get hot and I mumbled something like, "Yeah, just tired" and walked off to my station. The rest of the shift, I kept replaying his words over and over, convincing myself he was on the verge of writing me up or telling management I couldn't handle the hours anymore.

It takes real courage to admit that you let the fear drive your actions instead of pausing, and I want you to know that reacting with heat and rushing to your station was your brain trying desperately to protect you from that imagined danger. Since you found yourself convincing yourself he was planning disciplinary action based solely on his question, could you help me figure out if there is any actual evidence that he intends to report you, aside from your own worried mind filling in the blanks?

Well, when I think about it like that... no, there's no real evidence. He didn't say anything else about it, and he's never written me up before. I guess I've just been so tense lately that any little comment feels like a warning sign. But the fact is, he hasn't actually done anything but ask a simple question.

That distinction is crucial—you are looking at a simple inquiry while your nervous system interprets it as a threat. It makes perfect sense that tension creates a filter where nothing looks neutral anymore, but recognizing that there is no record of him reporting you before is strong proof against the worst-case scenario. Now that we've identified the gap between his words and your feared outcome, what is the most important piece of information you need to know to feel safer during your next shift?

I think the biggest thing would be to find out if he was actually concerned about my health, or if he was just checking up on my work. If I could know his real intention, I might stop assuming the worst. Maybe I could just ask him next time I see him — something simple, like "Hey, were you just checking on me the other day?" That way, I'd get a real answer instead of making one up in my head.

Asking for clarification is a smart way to seek the truth, but it is completely understandable that you feel hesitant because you fear the answer might confirm your worries. Before we decide on a plan, I want to make sure we are both aligned: do you feel comfortable asking that specific question, or would you prefer we focus on finding evidence from what he *has* already said rather than waiting for another interaction?

I think I'd rather focus on what he's already said first. If I can look back at his actual words and see they weren't accusing me, maybe I'll feel more confident to ask him later. Right now, I'm not sure I could handle getting a blunt answer if it turned out bad. So let's stick with what I already know — he just asked if I was okay, and nothing else came of it. That's the real evidence, isn't it?

That is a very wise decision; relying on the concrete facts he has already presented gives us a solid foundation to work with right now. If we treat his question as a simple check-in rather than a hidden accusation, how would that change the story you told yourself about him judging your work? Would it make the situation feel slightly less like a trap and more like a genuine offer of support?

It would actually change everything. If I really take his question at face value — "are you okay?" — it sounds like he was just concerned, not critical. That thought alone makes my shoulders drop a little. I guess I've been so stuck in my own head that I forgot sometimes people just care. Yeah, that does make it feel less like a trap and more like... maybe he was just being decent.

Noticing that shifting your perspective causes your shoulders to physically relax is a powerful sign that you are gaining control over the narrative. Since we've established that his words suggest concern rather than criticism, what is one small, practical step you can take right now to reinforce this new view before you leave here?

I could write down his exact words on a scrap of paper — "Tom, you sure you're okay?" — and put it next to the note on my locker. That way, if I start spiraling again tomorrow, I'll see both reminders: one telling me I'm doing enough, and the other proving he wasn't accusing me. I think that would help me calm down before I even get to my station.

That is a brilliant plan; having two visual anchors—one affirming your worth and one clarifying his intent—creates a strong shield against your anxious thoughts. Before we finish, how does it feel knowing you have a clear, actionable way to manage this worry once you get back to work? Is there anything else you'd like to discuss before we wrap up today?

It feels good, actually. Like I've got a way to fight back against that sinking feeling. I think I can manage this week a little better knowing I've got those notes to look at. No, I think that covers it for now. Thanks for helping me see things differently.

You're very welcome, Tom; it sounds like you left here feeling significantly lighter and equipped with some solid tools to navigate this week. Just remember, even if the worry comes back, taking a moment to glance at those notes can give you the space to pause and choose a different story. How is your energy level feeling right now as we head out the door?

I feel a bit tired, but in a good way — like my mind isn't racing as much as when I walked in. I think I can get a decent night's sleep tonight without lying awake going over every little thing. Thanks again. I'll see you next time.

That is fantastic news, Tom; moving from a racing mind to a resting one without constant analysis is a huge victory for your anxiety. Please remember that this feeling of peace is temporary, but the skills you practiced today will become easier to access each time you use them. Have a wonderful evening and a restful night's sleep.

Hello, thank you for meeting with me today. Last time we spoke, we started looking at how your guitar playing had become such a source of stress, and I hope you found the idea of treating mistakes as just an experiment helpful. How have things been feeling since then, and is there anything new happening regarding your practice routine or your mood that we should focus on today?

Hi. Thanks for seeing me again. I did try that "experiment" thing you suggested, where I was supposed to just play through a mistake without stopping or judging myself. It was really hard. I kept messing up the same chord progression, and instead of feeling like a learning experience, I just felt like a failure all over again. I actually put my guitar away for two days because I felt so stupid.

I hear how difficult it was to stick to that plan, and it makes complete sense that when you keep hitting the same stumbling blocks, your brain quickly jumps to the conclusion that you are failing. Putting the guitar away after two days of feeling that way is a very understandable protective instinct, but let's look closely at what happened during those ten minutes versus what happened afterward. What was the difference between the actual playing you did and the story you told yourself once you stopped?

I guess... when I was actually playing, I was just focused on getting my fingers in the right place and hitting the notes. It was messy, but I didn't really think about it until I stopped. Then I just kept replaying the mistake in my head and telling myself I'll never get it right, and that I'm not a real musician. The actual playing was just a few seconds of messing up, but the story I told myself lasted the whole rest of the day.

That distinction is crucial; separating the few seconds of messy playing from the hours of internal criticism reveals exactly where the pain comes from—it's not the noise on the strings, but the narrative running in your head. It sounds like your brain is trying to protect you from that feeling of being a "failure," but unfortunately, it's doing so by punishing you far harder than the mistakes ever could. Given that setback, what is one small adjustment we could make to your plan tonight so that the ten minutes don't feel like a test you're destined to fail?

Maybe... maybe I could just try playing for five minutes instead of ten? That way, if I mess up, it's over quicker and I don't have as much time to build up the bad feelings. And maybe I could tell myself before I start that it's just practice, not a performance.

Reducing the time to five minutes and adding a pre-play reminder is a very wise adaptation; it lowers the stakes enough that the fear of failure won't paralyze you before you even touch the strings. Since we agreed that the original goal was simply to separate playing from judging, does shrinking the timeframe mean we still have to resist the urge to analyze every mistake afterward, or is the main victory just surviving those five minutes without putting the guitar down?

I think... the main victory is just getting through the five minutes without putting the guitar down. If I can do that, it feels like I actually did something instead of running away. I can worry about the "not judging" part later. Just playing for five whole minutes without quitting might feel like enough.

That is a truly pragmatic win, and recognizing that showing up for five minutes counts as a success is a huge step toward breaking the cycle of avoidance. If your primary goal tonight shifts to simply sitting down and playing for five minutes without leaving, I believe that is absolutely achievable and deserves full credit regardless of how many mistakes occur. Can you picture walking into that room, starting the timer, and trusting that you will stay seated for those five minutes even if your hands are shaking?

Yeah... I think I can picture it. It's scary, but I can see myself just sitting there on the edge of my bed with my guitar, even if my hands are shaking. I'll just tell myself that staying in the room is the only rule. Five minutes. I can do that.

That visualization helps significantly because it grounds the plan in a realistic image of what you *can* do, even when you feel shaky or unsure. Knowing that the only requirement is physical presence—staying in the chair for five minutes—removes the impossible burden of perfection from your shoulders. Before we wrap up, how does it feel to define the night's goal purely as "showing up" rather than "performing"?

It feels... lighter, actually. Like I'm not trying to climb a mountain. It's just sitting down. I think I've been so focused on sounding perfect that I forgot I'm even allowed to just play. Thank you. I'll try it tonight and let you know how it goes.

It is beautiful to hear that lifting the pressure to climb a mountain has given you a sense of relief, and remembering that you are permitted to simply exist in the moment is a profound shift. I am confident you will find that five minutes of just sitting there feels manageable compared to the exhaustion you've been carrying. Let's check in with each other soon to see how that gentle attempt went, and please know that I am cheering you on regardless of the outcome.
Thanks. That really means a lot. I'll text you tomorrow and let you know if I managed to stay in the room for the whole five minutes. I think I can do it this time.

That sounds like a great way to connect, and I truly appreciate your trust in sharing how you're feeling with me. Remember that no matter what happens tonight—even if you drop the guitar immediately—the fact that you chose to try and give it one shot is a victory in itself. I'll be waiting to hear from you tomorrow, whether you succeeded or just survived the challenge.

Hello, thank you for being here. Today, I'd like to review how the new phrase has been working for you, check in on your current mood, and then decide together what specific situation we should focus on improving. To start, how have you been feeling emotionally since our last session, and is there anything particular you'd like to bring up?

Hi, thanks. I guess I've been okay, but... things have been stressful. I tried baking a cake last weekend for a friend's birthday, and I ended up throwing the whole thing away because it didn't look perfect. I felt pretty awful about it, honestly.

That sounds incredibly disappointing, especially when you've already invested time and effort into making something special for someone else. It makes complete sense that you feel embarrassed and frustrated when a project doesn't meet your own high standards. Did you notice any physical signs of stress, like a racing heartbeat or tight muscles, right before you decided to discard the cake?

Yeah, I definitely felt my heart racing, and my shoulders were all tensed up. I just kept thinking, "It's ruined, and everyone will think it tastes terrible," even though I hadn't even tasted it yet. I couldn't stop that thought from taking over.

It sounds like that intense physical sensation and the thought that everything was ruined completely shut down your ability to act rationally. When your body signals such high distress, it often hijacks your decision-making process, making it hard to override the urge to abandon the task entirely. Given that strength, would it help to combine noticing that physical tightness with simply saying, "This is just my old fear talking," to create a tiny gap before reacting?

I think I could try that. It's just... when I'm in that moment, it feels so real, like the cake really is a disaster and there's no fixing it. But maybe if I can pause long enough to say that to myself, I could at least stop before throwing everything out. I'll give it a shot next time I feel that rush.

That is a really smart compromise—you're acknowledging that while the feeling feels real in the moment, it might not reflect the actual reality of the situation. Taking just a few seconds to insert that phrase before acting seems like a very manageable first step to create space between the panic and your reaction. Before we wrap up, how does that sound as a plan to try tonight?

That sounds good. I'll try it tonight when I cook dinner. I'm just making pasta, so it's simpler, but I still get nervous about the sauce being just right. I'll see if I can catch myself before I start overthinking it.

That is a perfect plan; cooking a simple pasta dinner gives us a safe, low-pressure environment to test that pause. If you notice those racing shoulders or that tight chest while waiting for the water to boil, I encourage you to try inserting that phrase right then and there. Does it feel like a realistic goal to catch yourself once before the meal is finished, even if you don't succeed every time?

Yeah, I think once is realistic. I don't want to set the bar too high and then feel like I failed if I can't do it every time. Just catching it once and not throwing out the whole dinner would be a win for me.

That is an excellent and very healthy perspective; aiming for just one success prevents you from feeling overwhelmed if you miss the mark initially. Catching that thought once and choosing to continue cooking, even with an imperfect sauce, would be a massive victory in itself. How does it feel to define that specific moment of stopping and continuing as a true win?
It actually feels kind of... freeing? Like I don't have to be perfect to still succeed. That's a weird thought for me, but I like it. I'll keep that in mind tonight when I'm stirring the sauce.

Hearing you describe that feeling as "freeing" is wonderful news, because it suggests you are starting to loosen your grip on the need for perfection. Defining success simply as "not abandoning the dish" shifts the focus from a high-stakes exam to a practical learning experience. Would you feel comfortable setting a reminder on your phone for around 3 PM tonight so you can pause and check in on yourself while you wait for the sauce to simmer?

Yeah, I can do that. I'll set a reminder for when I'm about to start cooking. Hopefully, just seeing it pop up will help me remember to slow down and breathe before I dive into the stress. Thanks, that actually feels like something I can manage.

Setting that reminder is a brilliant way to create an external anchor whenever you feel caught up in the rush. Knowing you have a gentle nudge to slow down before starting can make the evening feel much less intimidating. How does that sound as a supportive tool to help you catch that old fear before it takes over?

It sounds really helpful, honestly. I think having that little nudge will make me feel less alone in the moment, like I've got a backup plan. I'm actually a tiny bit curious to see how tonight goes now, instead of just dreading it.

That shift from dread to curiosity is such a powerful sign of progress; it means you are starting to approach the challenge with openness rather than avoidance. Having a backup plan makes the unknown feel much safer, and I know tonight will be a great chance to see how that extra bit of space helps you stay with the cooking. I'll see you tomorrow!

Hello again. Since we finished last time feeling more ready for your shift, let's start by checking in on how you're doing this week and what has changed. Could you tell me what's on your mind for our time together today, or do you have any other worries you'd like to bring up?

Hey, thanks. Uh, I guess I’m doing okay, but honestly, this week has been rough. I messed up an order again—nothing huge, just gave someone the wrong sandwich—but my manager gave me this look, and I just froze up. I spent the rest of the shift convinced she’s already Googling how to fire someone.

It sounds incredibly draining to freeze up during a shift and then spend the rest of the time spiraling into a story about being fired based on a single look. That kind of pressure must have felt exhausting for both you and the team. Before we unpack that frozen feeling and the "Googling" worry, what is your main goal for us to tackle while we have time today?

I guess... I just want to figure out how to stop that spiral, you know? Like, when I mess up, my brain goes straight to "you're going to lose your apartment and your cat will be alone," and I can't do my job at all after that. I want to be able to just take a breath and move on, but I don't know how.

That chain of thought—from a small mistake to losing your home—is completely understandable given how scary it feels, but it's important to note that this isn't necessarily a reflection of the actual risk. Your brain is trying to protect you by exaggerating the danger, but it ends up paralyzing you instead. What happens physically in your body right when that "losing everything" thought pops up? Does your heart race, or do you feel tight in your chest?

Yeah, my chest gets really tight, like someone’s sitting on it. And my hands start sweating—I actually have to wipe them on my apron before I can pick up a tray again. It’s like my whole body just screams "danger," even though I’m just standing in a cafe with a coffee in my hand.

That physical sensation of your chest tightening and hands sweating is your body's alarm system going off, signaling extreme threat even though the actual danger is usually much smaller. These symptoms aren't signs that you *are* failing; they are just proof that your brain thinks it needs to protect you from a catastrophe that hasn't happened yet. Since we've noticed this pattern, could we try to separate your body's warning signal from the truth of the situation right now? Would you be open to examining whether there is solid evidence that you truly will lose your apartment because of this one sandwich error?

I mean... when you put it like that, it sounds a little silly. No, one wrong sandwich isn't going to get me fired. I've seen other waiters mess up way worse and still keep their jobs. It makes perfect sense that logic lands firmly against the feeling of impending homelessness, especially since you know others survive bigger errors too. However, the reason it feels so real in the moment is that your brain has learned to treat *any* mistake as a confirmation of your deepest fear, making the physical panic feel like absolute fact. We can use this gap between the logical truth and the overwhelming feeling to build a bridge back to safety. If we focus on that one specific moment when the chest tightens, could we practice saying to ourselves, "My body is scared because I believe I'm a fraud, but the evidence shows I am just a person who made a human mistake"? Would you be willing to try testing that statement against your current experience of being at work?

I think I could try that. It feels weird to say it out loud, like I'm lying to myself, but I get what you're saying. Next time I feel that tightness, I’ll try to tell myself, "This is just my body overreacting because I’m scared, not because I’m actually failing." I guess I’ve got nothing to lose by trying it, right?

That is a brilliant realization—you absolutely have nothing to lose by giving it a try, and noticing that "lying to myself" is actually just speaking kindly to your nervous system is a big breakthrough. Before we wrap up, let's lock in a tiny plan: whenever that tightness hits tomorrow, you'll pause for three seconds and whisper that new phrase instead of spiraling into the disaster story. Would you feel ready to start with that simple reset when the panic comes back?

Yeah, I think I can manage three seconds. That's not too long. I'll try whispering it under my breath next time I feel that panic hit. Thanks—I actually feel a tiny bit less doomed than I did when I walked in.

That is wonderful progress to hear, especially feeling less doomed. You've successfully moved from letting your body hijack your mind to creating a small, safe space where you can speak kindness to yourself. To make sure this sticks, can you imagine walking into the kitchen tomorrow with that new phrase ready, or does the sheer act of preparing for the moment feel slightly daunting?

I think it feels a bit daunting, honestly. Like, I can picture saying the words, but I'm worried the panic will just steamroll right over them. But I guess that's why I'm here—to practice until it's not so scary. I'll give it a shot and see what happens.

That hesitation is completely normal—it's your brain protecting itself from the old fear, so it naturally wants to overwhelm the new tool. Think of it like learning to drive in the rain; you might panic even when holding the wheel correctly, but that doesn't mean the car won't eventually stop skidding. Let's settle on a final commitment: if the panic tries to steamroll over your words, just acknowledge it as a loud voice and repeat the phrase anyway, even if you say it quietly. Does that feel like a manageable step for tomorrow?

Yeah, that feels manageable. I can just say it again, even if my brain is yelling at me. I'll treat it like background noise, not the truth. Thanks for walking me through this—I actually feel like I’ve got something to hold onto now.

That is a powerful shift in perspective, treating the panic as background noise rather than the absolute truth. It sounds like you now have a reliable anchor to hold onto when the storm hits. Is there anything else on your mind before we close our session, or are you ready to head out with this new strategy in your pocket?
No, I think I'm good. I've got my phrase and a plan to just repeat it if the panic gets loud. Thanks for helping me see that it's not the end of the world. I feel a little lighter, honestly.

That is wonderful news to hear, especially feeling lighter after carrying such a heavy burden. Please remember that even if the panic tries to steamroll over your words tomorrow, you now have a clear plan to treat it as background noise rather than the ultimate truth.
