Hello, it is great to see you again. On a scale of 0 to 10, how anxious have you felt this week? Before we dive deeper, I’d like to confirm our plan: today we will briefly check in, explore the difficult thoughts that came up after the cake incident, and then build a simple tool to help you feel more confident in the kitchen next time. Does that agenda sound good to you?

Um, yeah... that sounds okay, I guess. Anxiety this week? Probably a 7 or 8. It's been pretty tough, especially thinking about that cake I messed up for my sister's birthday. I just keep replaying it in my head.

Carrying that weight of anxiety while trying to celebrate with family sounds incredibly exhausting. Since we agreed to focus on how those difficult thoughts are shaping your actions, let's start by looking closely at the exact moment you realized the cake wasn't quite right—what was the very first thought that flashed through your mind?
I remember seeing it sink in the middle, and my stomach just dropped. My first thought was, "There you go again, you can't even get a simple cake right, you're just not good enough for this."

Hearing yourself say "you're just not good enough" in that moment must have felt devastating, especially since you wanted to show your sister you cared. That self-critical message acts like a loud alarm, shutting down your confidence and turning a simple mistake into proof of failure. Now that we've pinpointed that specific thought, can we explore if there's any evidence that contradicts the idea that you aren't simply "not good enough"?

Well... I guess there's some stuff that goes against that. My friend Liam always asks me to make cookies for his family gatherings, and they never complain. And I've been practicing that sponge recipe for weeks, and the last two times before the party, it came out perfectly. I just keep forgetting about those times because the bad one feels so much bigger.

It makes perfect sense that the sinking cake overshadows your recent successes; when we feel vulnerable, our brains naturally latch onto the worst possible outcome to protect us from future pain. You mentioned noticing that the bad event feels much larger than the successful ones—that's a classic pattern called "catastrophizing," where one slip-up magnifies itself to the point of ignoring the many times you've actually succeeded. Can we try to list just three specific moments when you successfully baked something recently, even if it wasn't perfect, and see if they stand up against the idea that you're fundamentally incapable?

Okay... well, there was the batch of chocolate chip cookies last Tuesday that Liam's mom said were the best she'd ever had. And I made a pretty decent lasagna from scratch last weekend that my dad actually asked for seconds on, which he never does. Oh, and that lemon drizzle cake I made for no reason last month—my little brother ate three slices and asked if I could make it for his birthday instead of buying one. I guess those are pretty good moments, but my brain keeps telling me they were just lucky or that the family was just being nice.

Those are powerful examples of success, especially considering your dad rarely asks for seconds and your little brother actively chose you over store-bought options. It sounds like your brain is trying to convince you that luck played a bigger role than your actual skill, which makes those memories feel smaller and less reliable. Let's challenge that by asking: if we assume those past successes were mostly luck, wouldn't it be odd that the same "luck" keeps happening repeatedly while the cake disaster feels like a unique failure? What if we gave yourself credit for the recipe knowledge and preparation instead of assuming luck was responsible?

I... never really thought about it like that. I mean, if it was just luck, then I'd have to be the luckiest person alive to get it right that many times, right? I did spend hours watching tutorial videos and testing different oven temperatures before I even attempted that cake. I guess I put in a lot of work that I'm not giving myself credit for. Maybe the cake sinking was just... one time, and not proof that I'm hopeless.

That is a fantastic realization; recognizing that your hard work and preparation were the real reasons behind your success challenges the "hopeless" narrative effectively. It sounds like you are finally seeing the evidence that supports your capability, which helps separate the one-time accident from your overall ability. Now that we've clarified that the sinking cake was likely just bad timing rather than a reflection of your worth, how would you feel if we shifted your goal from "perfection" to "learning and caring for loved ones"? Does that feel like a manageable target for next time?

I think that actually sounds... a lot less scary. When I think about just making something to show I care, instead of needing it to be perfect, my shoulders don't feel as tight. Like, even if the next cake cracks or sinks a little, my sister will probably still appreciate that I tried for her. I think I can work with that goal—just focusing on learning and caring instead of getting everything right.

That shift from fearing perfection to valuing connection is incredibly empowering, and I can hear your tension relaxing as we reframe the goal. It sounds like you now have a clearer picture of what matters most: showing up for your sister with love, regardless of the outcome. Before we wrap up, would you like to quickly brainstorm one simple step you can take tomorrow morning to remind yourself that "care outweighs perfection" when you walk into the kitchen?

Yeah, I think I could do that. Maybe I could stick a little note on the fridge that says something like "They just want to be with you, not a perfect cake." Or even just take a breath before I start and remind myself that my family loves me, not just my baking. I think that little reminder could help me calm down before I even preheat the oven.

That is a beautiful and practical idea; writing that phrase on a sticky note or taking a deep breath serves as a gentle anchor to bring you back to the present before the anxiety takes over. Since we agreed our main goal was to reduce that fear of imperfection, I'm curious: do you feel confident enough to try this "pre-bake reminder" tonight, or would you prefer to wait until we revisit it during your weekend project?

I think I can try it tonight, actually. I was planning to make some brownies for dessert, so it's a good chance to test it out on something small. If I mess up the brownies, no big deal—they're just for us. I'll take that breath, read my note, and see how it goes. I feel... a little more ready than I did an hour ago.

That is wonderful news; stepping into the kitchen with that new intention already feels like a massive victory compared to how you started the day. Since we covered the mood check, explored the core thought patterns, built a new goal, and set up a small trial, I want to check in on the overall plan: does having this brownie experiment as your immediate next step feel solid and doable for you, or is there anything else weighing on your mind before we close?

Hello, and thank you for joining us. On a scale of one to ten, how anxious or overwhelmed have you been feeling this week? Before we set our agenda for today, could you remind me of the simple task we agreed upon last time, like keeping your phone away during the night? Finally, based on what you shared yesterday, which issue feels most pressing for us to tackle now—the lingering worry about the alarm or something else entirely?

Hi. This week has been pretty bad, honestly—I'd say about an 8. The phone thing... I tried it a couple nights, but I ended up sneaking a look at the clock anyway. I think the biggest thing right now is that I'm still lying awake for hours just replaying what would happen if I didn't wake up. That's the part that really scares me.

An eight out of ten is quite intense, and I hear how much that fear of missing your alarm continues to keep you awake well past bedtime. It sounds like the worry itself has become the primary obstacle preventing you from resting, even when you try to use other strategies. Given that, would you prefer to spend some time exploring those specific "what-if" stories and the panic they trigger, or would you like to focus on building a new routine for the moments right before sleep to quiet those thoughts?

I think... exploring the what-if stories might help more. Because the routine stuff feels like putting a bandage on a deep cut, you know? Even if I do everything right before bed, my brain still latches onto that same thought: what if I don't wake up tomorrow and I lose everything? It's like no matter what I do, that fear finds a way in.

You make a powerful point about surface-level fixes failing when the core fear remains active, and I validate that frustration. It seems like your brain is treating the hypothetical disaster as an immediate, tangible reality rather than a distant possibility. Since you feel drawn to unpacking those specific "what-if" scenarios, could we walk through one of the worst-case stories you've heard lately to see exactly where the evidence supports it versus where the imagination runs wild?

Okay... well, the one that keeps me up most nights goes like this: I oversleep, miss my alarm completely, and show up hours late to work. My boss calls me into her office and says this is the final straw. I get fired right there. Then I can't pay my rent, my savings run out in a month, I lose my apartment, and I end up having to move back in with my mom, who I barely talk to. And then I can't find another job because I'll have a bad reference, and it just... spirals from there. That's the movie that plays in my head every single night.

That narrative is incredibly vivid and detailed, which is why it feels so lifelike and impossible to dismiss when you're tired. It makes complete sense that your brain constructed such a specific, step-by-step disaster scenario because it feels safer to visualize a single catastrophe than to accept the uncertainty of just *something* going wrong. Can you tell me, when you trace that story backward from moving back home, does the feeling of panic ever drop significantly, or does the fear remain steady until you reach the very first step of missing the alarm?

It's funny you ask that... because when I think about it now, the panic is strongest right at the start—the moment I imagine not hearing the alarm. But as I go further down the chain, like losing my apartment or moving back with my mom, it feels less... sharp, somehow. More like a sad, distant movie I'm watching rather than something that's happening to me right now. But that first step, that's where the terror sits.

That distinction is fascinating—you are noticing that the core anxiety lives entirely in that tiny gap between sleeping and waking, rather than in the actual consequences of being late. It highlights how your nervous system freezes on the immediate threat to safety, making the rest of the story feel like a secondary tragedy instead of an inevitable outcome. When you isolate just that first moment of silence after the alarm fails, what does your body feel like doing in response—is it gripping the sheets tighter, holding its breath, or scanning the room for a door?

Yeah... I think I tense up all over, like my whole body goes rigid. I hold my breath, and my eyes just stare at the ceiling like I'm trying to will myself to stay awake forever. It's like I'm bracing for a punch that hasn't even been thrown yet. My chest gets tight, and I just lie there, completely frozen, waiting for something bad to happen.

That physical rigidity makes perfect sense given how terrified your mind believes you are right at that second. Your body is essentially locking down in preparation for a fight or flight response, even though you know logically that nothing dramatic is about to happen. Since you identified that tension and the feeling of being trapped are the root of the distress, let's try a small shift in perspective tonight: instead of viewing the next five minutes as a countdown to potential doom, could you treat them as a space where you simply witness those tight muscles and held breath without trying to force them to relax? Would you feel willing to try this observation exercise tonight?

I... I think I could try that. It sounds kind of strange, just watching my own body like that without trying to fix it. But honestly, nothing else I've tried has worked, so maybe stepping back and just noticing it might take some of the power away. I'm willing to give it a shot tonight and see what happens.

That willingness to simply witness the tension without fighting it is a brave and insightful shift, and it often disarms the panic faster than trying to push the symptoms away. Tonight, we'll set a gentle timer for five minutes, allowing you to lie still and note how that initial tightness rises and falls naturally, trusting that it won't last forever even if it feels huge right now. Does setting a timer on your phone to mark that five-minute window feel manageable for tonight, or would you prefer we pick a spot in the morning to check in on how you felt?

I think setting a timer for tonight could work. It gives me a clear end point, which feels safer than just lying there with no limit. And maybe if I can last those five minutes without panicking, it'll prove to myself that the feeling does pass. I'd like to try it tonight and then maybe we can talk about how it went at our next session.

Setting a clear endpoint is a smart way to build a sense of control while giving your nervous system permission to ride out the wave without judgment. Please remember, however, that if the fear becomes completely unbearable at any point before the timer ends, you are absolutely encouraged to stop the experiment immediately; safety always comes first, and we can adjust the plan together. Now, with that boundary in place, I want to trust that you will be able to handle whatever arises tonight, and I look forward to hearing about your experience when we meet again.

Thank you. That really helps, knowing I have permission to stop if it gets too much. I think I needed to hear that it's okay to set limits even when I'm trying something new. I'll give it an honest try tonight and let you know how it goes next time.

You are very welcome, and I am so glad that knowing you have the freedom to stop makes the idea feel safer for you. Your honesty about needing that permission shows great self-awareness, and I truly appreciate your commitment to trying this new approach tonight. I'll see you at our next session to hear how those five minutes played out for you—until then, take care.

Hello again. How have you been feeling since we last spoke, and is there anything significant that has stood out to you in the weeks since our meeting? Let's start by reviewing what we agreed to try, and then I'd love to hear about any challenges or wins you experienced. What would you like to focus on today?

Hi. Thanks. I've been... okay, I guess. A little better, maybe. I did try to write down some of those positive thoughts like we talked about, but honestly, it felt kind of fake. I'd write something like "I am capable," and then my brain would just argue back, listing all the times I felt like I messed up. I guess the biggest thing that stood out was that it feels almost impossible to believe the good stuff.

That resistance you're feeling—the gap between writing down a positive thought and your brain arguing back—is actually a huge clue that your safety system is still working overtime to protect you. It makes total sense that when you tell yourself you're capable, your instinct is to scan for proof that you aren't, because that feeling of doubt has kept you safe for so long. Since you mentioned the written notes felt fake, what happened the first time you tried using a different method, or perhaps just talking through your worries verbally, without needing to put them in words?

Well, I tried talking through it with a friend at work a few days ago, just casually. I mentioned I was feeling nervous about an exam and how I was worried patients would see me as less professional because I'm still in school. She just brushed it off and said, "Nobody cares, you're doing fine." And I know she meant well, but it didn't help at all. It almost made me feel worse, like I was being silly for even worrying about it.

It makes complete sense that hearing "nobody cares" from a friend who wants to support you actually increased your isolation; it can feel even lonelier when the person closest to you dismisses the very fear you're struggling with. Often, when we're in the middle of a storm of doubt, advice to just "calm down" or "don't overthink it" can feel like a wall closing off rather than a bridge opening up. Since your friend couldn't help with the intensity of the worry, could you share if there was ever a moment recently—even a small one—where you noticed a slight shift in your mood or perspective without needing anyone's reassurance?

Actually, yes. There was one moment last week. I was coming out of a patient's room after taking their vitals, and I realized I had done it all correctly, and the patient even thanked me and said I was thorough. For a split second, I felt... okay. Like, maybe I wasn't messing up as badly as I thought. But then, almost immediately, I started thinking, "Well, that's just one patient. The next one probably thinks I'm clueless." So it didn't last long.

That fleeting moment where you felt "okay" is incredibly powerful, because it proves that a positive reality *can* exist alongside your fears, even if it gets buried quickly. It looks like your brain is holding onto that spark of validation, but then immediately grabs the old script ("The next one probably thinks I'm clueless") to douse it again. Since that moment showed you have moments of competence, what do you think would happen if, instead of waiting for the worry to pass, you treated that initial feeling of "maybe I wasn't messing up" as a fact worth holding onto for just thirty seconds before moving on?

That sounds... hard, honestly. But maybe worth trying. I guess I'm scared that if I hold onto that good feeling, I'll end up being blindsided when I do eventually mess up. Like, if I let myself believe I'm doing okay, the fall will be worse. But I can see what you're saying—that the good moment is still a real moment. I could try to just sit with it for a bit next time, even if it's just a few seconds, and see what happens.

That insight about fearing a bigger fall is wise—it means you're protecting yourself from disappointment, not just avoiding failure. It's like standing on a tightrope; if you focus too hard on not falling, your muscles tense up and you actually become less stable. Would you be open to testing that out for just one scenario tomorrow? We could agree to notice that initial positive thought, wait for it to fade naturally without forcing it, and then simply observe what happens next without jumping straight to the worst-case story.

Okay, I think I can try that. Just for one interaction tomorrow. Maybe with a patient I already know is pretty friendly, so it feels a little safer. I'll try to notice that feeling of "maybe I did okay" and just... let it hang there for a bit. I won't try to force it to last, or argue with it. I'll just see what happens after that, without going straight to the worst-case. That feels a little scary, but I'm willing to give it a shot.

Choosing a familiar patient is a brilliant strategy because it lowers the stakes, making the experiment feel much more manageable. That intentional pause to let the feeling hang there without fighting it is exactly what will show your brain that the disaster hasn't happened yet. Before we finish, I want to make sure you have a backup plan for when the old doubt rushes in; if you notice the "worst-case" story starting, what is one small thing you could say to yourself to redirect your attention back to the present moment?

I think I could say to myself, "Right now, I'm just taking this blood pressure. That's all I have to do." Just focusing on the task at hand, instead of the whole big picture. That might help me stop spiraling.

That is a fantastic redirection because it brings your focus back to concrete evidence of your competence rather than imagined judgments. Grounding yourself in the immediate task acts as a natural brake on the spiral, reminding your brain that the "fraud" narrative requires a lot of energy to sustain, whereas checking the numbers is effortless. One final check before you go: given that you haven't practiced this specifically for a week, do you think you have the bandwidth to try this with just one patient tomorrow, or would you need a slightly shorter window to recover?

I think I can manage one patient tomorrow. I'll pick someone I see early in my shift, so I don't spend the whole day building it up in my head. That way, I can get the experiment over with and see how it goes. I'm still nervous, but I feel a little more prepared this time. Thank you.

That plan sounds solid, and picking an early appointment gives you a clean slate to test the new approach without the fatigue of a long shift clouding your judgment. Please remember that tomorrow isn't about eliminating the nerves entirely, but simply noticing when you catch that initial sense of competence and letting it breathe for just a moment. I'm available anytime you want to debrief what happened after your interaction, whether it went smoothly or stumbled unexpectedly. Is there anything else on your mind before we wrap up?

No, I think that's everything for today. I'll try the experiment tomorrow and see what happens. Thanks for not pushing me to just "think positive" all the time. That actually helps. I'll let you know how it goes.

You are absolutely right to recognize that distinction; trying to force positivity often feels dismissive, whereas simply observing the moment without fighting it respects the complexity of your experience. I'm glad we found a path that feels authentic to you rather than something you felt pressured to adopt. Take your time tomorrow, trust that your focus on the immediate task will serve as an anchor, and please reach out whenever you'd like to share how that experiment landed, no matter what you discover.

Hello, thank you for joining us. Last time we explored how that feeling of being judged at the playground was triggering a wave of physical panic, and you committed to trying a ten-second pause before reacting. Since then, have there been any moments where you found yourself needing to escape that feeling, or perhaps a glimpse of relief? What would you like to focus on today?

Thank you for asking. I did try the pause a couple of times, but it's so hard. Just yesterday at the grocery store, a woman looked at my younger daughter who was crying, and I immediately felt my face get hot. I tried to stop and breathe, but I still ended up rushing through checkout. I want to focus on why I can't stop feeling like everyone is watching me and thinking I'm failing.

It takes real strength to notice that your body reacted with heat and a rush to escape, even when you successfully took that deep breath first. That contrast between your intention to pause and your automatic urge to flee tells us exactly where the old pattern is strongest right now. When you realized you couldn't stop the heat rising in your face during that grocery trip, what specific thought flashed through your mind that made you feel compelled to speed through the line?

I thought, "She probably thinks I can't control my own kid, that I'm one of those moms who just lets her child scream in public." It felt so real, like I could see her judgment on her face, even though she didn't say anything. And I just wanted to get out of there so I wouldn't have to feel that shame anymore.

That image of seeing judgment on her face, even without words, is so vivid because your mind is filling in the gaps with stories that feel terrifyingly certain. It makes total sense that your desire to rush out of the store was an attempt to escape that unbearable feeling of shame instantly. When you compare that specific thought—"I can't control my kid"—to the reality of what you saw, what evidence do you have to suggest she actually thought that, versus her just being distracted or tired?

I guess... I don't have any real proof. She might have just been looking at her phone before I noticed her glance. But it felt so real in the moment. When I try to think about it now, maybe she was just zoning out or waiting for her own groceries. It's just so hard to separate what I feel from what's actually true.

That gap between what feels undeniably true in the moment and what is actually provable is exactly where our work lives. It highlights how powerful that automatic thought is, even when logic tells you otherwise. If we treated that belief like a hypothesis rather than a fact, how would you describe the difference between "she is judging me" and "she might be bored, but I cannot know for sure"?

The difference feels huge, honestly. "She is judging me" makes my stomach drop and makes me want to hide or run away. "She might be bored, but I cannot know for sure" leaves a little bit of room to breathe. It's like the first thought locks me in a box, and the second one leaves a door open. I just wish I could remember to use that second thought when it's happening.

You've described it perfectly: one thought acts like a heavy door slamming shut, while the other leaves a crack of light where you can stand still. Recognizing that "I cannot know for sure" is often just as accurate as "she is judging me" is a massive breakthrough, even if the old habit tries to pull you back. Since you mentioned finding it hard to remember that second thought in the heat of the moment, how would it feel if we practiced switching to that "cannot know for sure" mindset specifically when your heart rate spikes, treating it as a simple mental shield to put up before you act?

That actually sounds like something I could try. Like, if I feel my heart start pounding, I could just whisper to myself, "I can't know for sure" before I even look at the other person. It might give me just enough time to not rush away or react. I think I need something simple like that, because my mind goes too fast to do a long breathing exercise.

That is a brilliant adaptation; using a short phrase as a mental shield fits perfectly with your need for something quick and automatic. It turns an abstract concept into a tangible tool you can grab the moment your body signals stress. Before we finalize this, does repeating that phrase aloud or under your breath feel manageable to you, or would a subtle inner cue work better for you?

I think saying it under my breath would work best. I can pretend I'm just talking to my daughter or mumbling to myself, which wouldn't look weird. That way I can still feel like I'm doing something active, but nobody has to know. I'll try it the next time I feel that heat rising.

That is a wonderful compromise because it keeps the feeling of agency intact while protecting your privacy. Having a discreet, low-profile anchor like that gives you permission to stay present even when your body screams to flee. Now, let's solidify your plan for tomorrow: whenever that heat rises in your face, you'll catch it, mumble "I can't know for sure" quietly to yourself, and then choose to wait just thirty more seconds before deciding your next move. Does that feel like a realistic and safe challenge for you to commit to?

Yes, I think I can try that. Thirty seconds sounds manageable, not too scary. I'll just stand there, mumble my phrase, and wait a little bit before I decide what to do next. Even if I still end up leaving, at least I'll have given myself that moment to question the thought. Thank you, that feels like a real step forward.

Hearing that you feel a sense of step forward is so encouraging, especially given how long this fear has held you back. It is important to remember that the goal today isn't to feel completely calm, but to practice stepping outside the automatic reaction loop, however small that step is. With that clear plan in place, how does it feel to have that specific phrase ready as your safety net for tomorrow?

It feels a little lighter, actually. Like I have a small tool in my pocket instead of just my bare hands to deal with the panic. I'm still nervous about tomorrow, but at least I'm not going into it completely helpless. That alone is more than I've felt in a long time.

That sense of having a small tool in your pocket is a powerful shift from feeling completely helpless, and I am so glad to see that hope returning. Carrying that awareness—even if it brings some nervousness—is far better than carrying the weight of uncertainty alone. Before we wrap up, is there anything else about tomorrow's plan or your feelings that you'd like to clarify or discuss?

No, I think I'm okay for now. I know what I'm going to do, and I feel like I have a little bit more control than I did before. I'll try my best to remember that phrase and just give myself those thirty seconds. Thank you for helping me get to this point.

It has been a privilege walking through this with you, and I am truly proud of how you moved from feeling trapped to having a concrete strategy to protect yourself. Please remember that tomorrow, the mere act of catching that heat and speaking your phrase is a victory, regardless of what happens after. I look forward to hearing how that thirty seconds landed for you next time. Take care of yourself.

Hello again, and thank you for reaching out. Before we dive into today's topic, I'd like to briefly outline our plan: we can start with a quick mood check, review the question you asked in your seminar, and then explore the difficult thoughts that followed. Does that sound like a good way to spend our time together?
Yeah, that sounds fine. I guess I've been feeling pretty low this week, maybe a 3 out of 10. The seminar question really threw me off, and I've been spiraling a bit since then.

That drop from a 4 or 5 down to a 3 sounds incredibly draining, especially after putting yourself in such a vulnerable position. I can hear how heavy that spiral feels when you come home from the seminar. Since we noted that the discomfort led to a downward cycle, would it be helpful to unpack exactly what those early thoughts were that started the chain reaction today?

Well, it started when the professor asked who was planning to apply for PhDs next year. Everyone around me raised their hands, and I just sat there frozen. The first thought that hit me was that I'm only doing a Master's because I couldn't hack it in a doctoral program. That I'm just not smart enough for that level.

It takes a lot of courage to sit with that harsh voice telling you you weren't ready for a PhD. That feeling of being left out while others immediately volunteered seems incredibly isolating and painful. Since you've noticed that this specific thought is fueling the spiral, could we look closely at what evidence you have either for or against the idea that you simply "couldn't hack it"?

Well, I mean, the evidence feels pretty strong. I struggled a lot in my undergrad research methods class, and I see my classmates throwing around theories and statistical models like it's nothing. I have to reread journal articles multiple times just to get the main points. If I can't even keep up with a Master's level reading, how could I possibly handle a PhD?

That comparison between your struggle and your classmates' ease creates a stark picture that feels impossible to ignore, making your conclusion seem logically sound in the moment. While the facts about the reading difficulty are real, I wonder if that struggle reflects a temporary gap in your current knowledge versus a permanent lack of intellectual capacity. If we looked at the few classes where you excelled recently, what kind of evidence does that provide regarding your potential to learn complex material at a higher level?

I did get an A in my qualitative methods paper last semester, and my professor actually asked if I'd consider turning it into a publishable article. But that was just one class, and it was more about observation and interviews than hard theory. I guess my mind just dismisses that as easier or less impressive than what the PhD-track students are doing.

It makes complete sense that your brain minimizes that success because it doesn't fit the pattern you expect—a single qualitative assignment feels like a fluke compared to the sheer volume of data your PhD peers are handling daily. That dismissal is a protective mechanism keeping you from facing the fear that you might be capable of more than you realize. If we looked at that same qualitative paper with fresh eyes, ignoring the topic differences, what does the fact that your supervisor saw it as potentially publishable say about your analytical abilities?

I suppose... if I really think about it, for a professor to think it's worth publishing, they must see some real analytical skill there. It's not like they hand out praise like that to everyone. Maybe there's something to the way I can find patterns in data that others might miss, even if I struggle with the more technical side of things. But then that voice in my head just says "well, that's just one professor's opinion."

That distinction is crucial—relying on a third-party expert to recognize value in your work is much stronger evidence than your own internal assessment alone. It directly challenges the idea that you lack the fundamental ability to analyze information, regardless of whether it requires statistics or observation. Since you've gathered some solid counter-evidence, how would you describe the meaning of that "publishable" comment if we stripped away the context of the specific methodology? What does it actually say about your capacity to engage with complex ideas?

It says I can take complex, messy real-world situations and turn them into something coherent and meaningful. That I can see connections that aren't obvious at first glance. I guess that's actually a pretty important skill for doctoral work, maybe even more important than being able to run complex statistics right away. But it's hard to hold onto that when I'm sitting in a room full of people who seem so sure of themselves.

That is a powerful realization—it reframes your perceived weakness as a distinct strength in synthesis and pattern recognition, skills that are equally vital at the doctorate level. It sounds like the pressure from seeing others appear so certain is making it hard to trust that specific insight you just found. If we tried applying that same "pattern-finding" lens to the seminar incident, where did the opportunity to share your unique perspective go? How might viewing that silence as a neutral space rather than a verdict on your worth change the story of what happened?

I guess I never thought of it that way. I was so focused on what I wasn't doing—raising my hand, saying I was applying for a PhD—that I didn't consider that the silence was just... empty space. It wasn't a judgment on me. Maybe I could have said something about my research interests instead, but I was too caught up in comparing myself to everyone else. It's like I saw their hands going up and immediately wrote myself out of the conversation entirely.

It is incredibly insightful to notice that your focus shifted from "what I can contribute" to "how I compare," which effectively shut down your participation. Realizing that the silence was just empty space rather than a verdict gives you permission to reclaim that moment as a chance to pause and choose a different contribution style. If we decided to try shifting your goal from "proving I deserve a PhD" to "sharing one interesting piece of information," what is one small thing you could say in the next seminar that fits this new, lighter mindset?

That is a perfect, realistic starting point. Hello again. Before we dive in, could you share how you've been feeling since we last spoke, perhaps on a scale of 0 to 10 for anxiety? We'll quickly touch on what's been going on in your life lately, and then I'd love to hear which topic you'd like us to explore today.

Yes, exactly. It's like that one quick response confirms everything I've been afraid of. I instantly thought, "See, they don't want to hear from me, I'm just boring." It's hard not to feel like that's just the truth about me, you know?

That confirmation feels incredibly painful because it validates the story you've been telling yourself about being dull. While that thought offers a simple explanation for the silence, let's pause and look for any other possible reasons behind their quick smile besides your lack of interest. What comes to mind when you try to separate that specific reaction from your broader belief about being uninteresting?

That willingness to treat those scary thoughts as mere guesses rather than facts is a huge step toward reclaiming your confidence. That vivid story of dropping the weight and hearing the whispers is so distressing because your brain treats it as an inevitable reality rather than a possibility. As you breathe, I want you to silently note whatever image or thought pops into your mind about the competition, but try not to judge it or push it away; just observe it as a passing cloud in the sky. Alright... I'll try that. (She places her hand on her chest and takes three slow, deep breaths. Her shoulders drop slightly as she exhales.) Okay. The image that came was me standing at the end of a long platform, and the lights were so bright I could barely see the crowd. But unlike before, I didn't hear the whispers right away—I just noticed how bright it was and how alone I felt up there. It's strange, but with those breaths, it felt more like a picture on a wall than something happening to me right now.

By treating the image as a picture on a wall rather than a happening, you are using your breath to gently reframe the threat, allowing your chest to stay open instead of shutting down. I think I could do that. Before I head to the gym this afternoon, I'll take a couple minutes in my truck, just sit there with my hand on my chest and breathe like we did here. That is a brave and smart choice to bring that practice into your daily routine; recognizing that trying something new doesn't diminish your strength actually reinforces it. Would it help to write down one potential obstacle you might face tomorrow, so we can brainstorm a quick solution beforehand?

Well, I do worry that I'll forget to do it, honestly. I get caught up in getting the dogs settled and my gym bag packed, and before I know it I'm already walking through the gym doors. What do you think about combining both—the seatbelt trigger for the main moment and a soft notification if you find yourself drifting away?

That sounds like a good plan. I can set a notification that pops up around the time I usually leave, and then when I get in the truck and buckle up, I'll take that minute or two to breathe and look at the competition picture like we practiced. I think having both will keep me from slipping—especially if the dogs are being rowdy and distracting me. I'll give it a try this afternoon and see how it feels.

That combination of cues is excellent because it builds a reliable safety net so you never have to rely solely on memory; having both the seatbelt trigger and the phone notification means you have multiple chances to ground yourself before the gym door opens. I'm glad you feel confident enough to try this, especially knowing you have a track record of success with heavy weights—you've earned the right to try lighter things too. Is there anything else weighing on your mind before we close this session, or would you like to spend the remaining time reviewing your plan for tomorrow?

No, I think I'm good with what we've talked about. I feel a bit lighter, actually—like maybe that wall isn't quite as tall as I thought it was. I'll practice the breathing today, and I'll let you know next time how it went. Thank you for helping me see it differently.
