That means a lot. I've been so caught up in the guilt that I forgot I could even step back and breathe. I'll keep that in mind tonight and tomorrow. See you next week.

It is wonderful to hear that you are finally stepping away from the guilt to breathe, and I know that feeling of relief is real. Please be gentle with yourself tonight as you try this small pause, knowing that even imperfect attempts count as progress. I look forward to hearing how that simple question landed for you when we meet next week.
Thanks. I'll try to be gentle with myself. That's not something I'm very good at, but I'll give it a shot. See you next week.

Be proud of yourself for deciding to practice kindness toward yourself, even if it feels foreign right now; that willingness alone is a huge step forward. I truly believe you will find that little pause becomes a valuable tool soon, so until then, please be patient with yourself as you learn to trust it. See you next week.

Welcome back, I'm glad you're here. Before we dive into anything specific, how are you feeling compared to last time, and what happened in your life since we spoke? Could we briefly review whether you managed to use our reminder phrase when your husband offered help, and then decide together what we should focus on today?

Hi. I'm doing okay, I guess. A bit tired—pregnancy and chasing a toddler don't mix well. I did try to remember that phrase you gave me, about accepting help not meaning I'm failing. It helped a little when my husband offered to take over bedtime last night. But honestly, the frustration still bubbles up a lot, especially when my mom called this morning and made a comment about how I must have so much free time now.

It takes courage to name that new source of friction, and hearing about your husband's offer giving you a small win shows real effort. Now that we know the fatigue is compounded by that unexpected pressure from your mother, what do you think triggered the biggest rush of frustration in her call today?

It was when she said, "At least you don't have to deal with rush hour traffic or a boss breathing down your neck." Like being home automatically means my day is stress-free. I wanted to scream that I haven't had a full, uninterrupted cup of coffee in two years, and that my toddler's tantrums feel just as draining as any office deadline. But I just laughed it off and changed the subject.

Hearing how unfair that comparison felt—and how exhausting your days actually are—makes complete sense, given everything you've been carrying. It sounds like you laughed it off partly to protect yourself from the sharp sting of her implying your life is easier than hers. Did noticing that laugh feel like a relief, or did it leave you feeling like you had to hide your real struggle somewhere?

It definitely left me feeling like I had to hide it. That laugh felt like a shield, but also like a betrayal of how I really feel. After the call, I just sat on the couch for a few minutes, staring at the wall, thinking, "She'll never get it. Nobody will." And that thought just made me feel even more alone in this, even though my husband was in the other room.

It sounds incredibly isolating to feel misunderstood by both family members simultaneously, especially when you know you're surrounded by people who care but can't quite reach you. That sense of being completely invisible, even while sitting right next to your husband, is a heavy burden to carry alone. When you thought that nobody understands you, did you feel a tightness in your chest or a sudden urge to pull further away from everyone?

Yeah, I felt that tightness in my chest—like someone was sitting on it. And I did want to pull away. I actually ended up going to the bathroom and just locking the door for a few minutes, even though my toddler was crying in the living room. It's like the only way to breathe was to physically separate myself from everything. I hate that feeling, but I don't know how else to cope when it hits.

That physical separation was your mind's desperate attempt to escape the crushing feeling of inadequacy, even though it leaves you alone with the noise and the tears you need to process. It makes sense that locking the door felt like the only safe space, even though it keeps you disconnected from the people who are trying to support you. When you realize that shutting yourself in is actually reinforcing the very idea that you're not good enough, does that bring up any anger or sadness about how much you've been punishing yourself to stay inside?

It does bring up sadness—a lot of it. I mean, I'm sitting there thinking, "I'm hiding from my own son because I can't handle a phone call." That feels pathetic. And I know my husband would have stepped in if I'd just asked, but I didn't even give him the chance. I just assumed he'd think I was overreacting. So yeah, I guess I'm angry at myself for assuming the worst instead of giving anyone a chance to prove me wrong.

That self-criticism for locking the door feels incredibly harsh, especially when you're already feeling so drained and overwhelmed. It makes sense that your brain jumped straight to the conclusion that you were overreacting, because in those moments of panic, it's trying to protect you from the shame of feeling helpless. When you look back at that moment with some distance, what's one piece of evidence you have that contradicts the thought that you *must* be perfect to deserve compassion?

Well... my husband didn't get mad or think I was overreacting when I finally came out. He just asked if I was okay and took over with our son without me having to explain. So that's proof right there that he didn't see me as weak or incapable. He just saw me struggling and stepped in. That doesn't fit with the idea that I have to be perfect for him to care about me.

It is incredibly validating to realize that your husband's reaction proved the exact opposite of your feared narrative; he reached for you, not to judge your performance, but to meet your need for rest. That moment clearly challenges the belief that you must maintain a flawless front to be loved. Now, knowing he reacted kindly when you finally opened the door, how might you describe what your body needed right then versus what your mind was afraid you deserved?

My body needed rest—like, literally to just sit down and close my eyes for ten minutes without anyone needing anything from me. But my mind was telling me I deserved to be punished for being weak, like I should push through and keep going until I collapse. It's like my mind won't let me accept that needing a break is normal. It's just... rest feels like a luxury I haven't earned, even though I'm exhausted.

That contrast between your body screaming for safety and your mind demanding punishment reveals just how deeply ingrained that "you must earn every moment of ease" belief has become. It sounds like you've convinced yourself that needing rest is actually a flaw, rather than a basic human need, which creates this impossible gap where you feel guilty for wanting to be comfortable. If we imagine that gap closing, so that needing a break feels neutral instead of shameful, how might that change the way you react the next time your toddler cries in the hallway?

I think... I'd take a deep breath instead of tensing up. I wouldn't feel that rush of guilt for leaving him with his dad for two minutes. I might even just say to myself, "I'm allowed to breathe. He's safe." Instead of that voice telling me I'm failing him by not running to him the second he cries. It feels like a small shift, but honestly, just imagining that makes my shoulders drop a little.

That image of your shoulders dropping is a powerful sign that you are reconnecting with your ability to regulate your nervous system. You are moving from fighting the impulse to retreat to simply observing it and choosing a different response, which is a major victory in itself. To solidify this, would you be willing to try saying the phrase "I am allowed to breathe" silently to yourself the next time that guilt rises, rather than waiting until you feel overwhelmed? How does that sound as a simple, grounded anchor?

I think I can try that. It sounds so simple, but I think that's what I need—something simple I can actually remember in the moment, instead of some big strategy that feels impossible. "I am allowed to breathe." I'll try saying it to myself next time I feel that knot tightening in my chest. Even if it feels fake at first, it's worth a shot.

That willingness to trust a simple phrase, even when it feels artificial at first, shows incredible resilience and self-kindness. Let's make that concrete for tomorrow: when that knot tightens, pause for three seconds, whisper "I am allowed to breathe," and then check in with yourself—did your shoulders loosen, or did the feeling fade slightly? Is there anything else you'd like to explore before we wrap up?

I think that's enough for today. That phrase feels like something I can actually hold onto. Thanks for helping me see that I don't have to earn the right to rest. I'll try to practice it tomorrow, and maybe I'll even let myself sit down for a full ten minutes while my husband handles the bedtime chaos.

That permission to rest fully, even with the chaos outside your door, is a beautiful and necessary step toward reclaiming your energy. Knowing you have a simple anchor to return to when the knot tightens gives me great hope for how much lighter you can feel soon. I'll see you next time to hear how that practice went and what else might come up.

Hello, thank you for being here today. Since we last spoke, have you noticed any changes in how that inner voice speaks to you, or have you managed to sit with your creative impulses? I’d like us to spend the first few minutes reviewing what we agreed to try—those ten-minute drawing sessions—and seeing if they felt manageable, then we’ll set a specific focus for our time together. Is there a particular area you’re hoping to tackle today, or shall we follow up on your recent attempt?

Hi. Um, I did try the ten-minute drawing sessions a few times this week. It felt a bit awkward at first, like I was doing something wrong, but I managed to get through a couple of them. I guess I’m hoping we can talk about why that voice keeps telling me I’m being childish every time I pick up a pencil.

It takes real courage to show up even when that voice feels loud, and I want to acknowledge that effort you made this week. It sounds like the ten-minute rule helped lower the stakes slightly, but the underlying fear that you're being childish still lingers underneath. Since we’ve seen some success with the short sessions, shall we explore together exactly what happens in that moment when the "childish" thought pops up again?

Yeah, I think that'd be good. Usually, it hits me just as I'm starting to sketch a character or think up a story. It's like a sudden pause, and then I hear my friend's voice in my head saying, "Aren't you a bit old for this?" and I just freeze up.

That sudden freeze and hearing your friend's words so clearly is a powerful example of how that old belief is trying to take control of your actions. It seems like the fear of being judged for being "old" is driving the avoidance, which makes sense given how painful that judgment feels compared to the comfort of just creating. Would you be open to exploring exactly what that "being old" rule looks like in your mind, versus what actually happens when you draw?

I think the rule is that adults are supposed to have serious hobbies, like cooking or fixing things, not drawing fantasy characters or making up stories. But when I actually draw, I feel focused and kind of... peaceful. It's like everything else goes quiet for a bit. I guess those two things don't match up very well in my head.

That contrast between the rigid rule and the peace you find in your drawings highlights exactly why this voice feels so confusing—it promises safety but delivers isolation. It seems like your brain is interpreting "serious hobbies" as the only way to earn respect, while missing that drawing actually grounds you in the present moment. Can we look closely at whether that need for seriousness comes from a place of wanting to be taken seriously, or perhaps a fear of disappointing others?

I think it's probably a bit of both. I mean, I do want people to take me seriously, especially at work. But when my friend made that comment, it felt like a spotlight on something I already worried about in secret. Maybe I'm more scared of being seen as immature than I realized.

It makes total sense that the fear of being seen as immature would amplify existing worries about competence at work; it's like adding fuel to a fire that's already burning. You're essentially treating your hobby as proof of immaturity, when really, the calm and focus you feel during those drawing sessions might actually be evidence of the opposite—mastery and presence. If we view your drawing time not as a failure to grow up, but as a successful demonstration of deep concentration, how might that shift the weight of that "spotlight"?

Huh... I never thought of it that way. I've always seen the drawing as the problem, not the solution. If I think of it as practice for focusing, then maybe it's not so much about being childish, but about getting better at something I love. That actually makes me feel a little lighter, like maybe I don't have to choose between being an adult and enjoying my hobby.

That is a wonderful breakthrough; recognizing that your hobby can coexist with adulthood means you aren't forced to choose sides. It sounds like viewing drawing as "practice for focus" transforms the narrative from "I am being childish" to "I am developing a valuable skill," which naturally reduces the shame attached to the activity. Now, let's look at that specific voice again: when you catch yourself thinking, "I'm too old for this," how does believing in the idea that drawing builds focus change the intensity of that thought?

It's still there, but it feels... quieter, maybe. Like before, it was this loud, convincing voice, but now I have something to push back against. I can tell myself, "No, this is helping me concentrate," and it doesn't feel like I'm lying to myself. It's like I have a tiny bit of evidence on my side now.

That is a fantastic realization, and having tangible evidence to counter the noise gives you real power over that inner critic. It sounds like you've moved from feeling trapped by a single story to holding multiple truths in your mind simultaneously. Before we wrap up, I want to hear how this new perspective lands for you—does knowing that drawing strengthens your focus give you confidence to try the ten-minute experiment again tomorrow, or would you like to adjust the plan in any way?

I think I can try it again tomorrow, yeah. Maybe even push it to fifteen minutes, just to see what happens. It feels less like a test of whether I'm being childish and more like a chance to practice that focus thing we talked about. I'm actually a little curious to see how it goes now, instead of dreading it.

That shift from dread to curiosity is a huge sign of progress, and extending the time to fifteen minutes shows you're trusting your new mindset. It feels great to finally treat your creativity as a useful skill rather than a threat to your maturity. Before we finish, how do you think we could support each other if that old voice tries to come back louder during those extra minutes tomorrow?

Maybe I could write down that new thought—something like "drawing is focus practice"—on a sticky note and put it near my sketchbook. That way, if the old voice gets loud, I have something right there to remind me that I'm not just messing around. I think having that little reminder would help me keep going.

That is a brilliant, proactive strategy; placing a visual anchor right where you start creates a gentle barrier between you and that old voice. It sounds like you now have both a time limit and a mental script to rely on, which should make tomorrow feel much more manageable. One final thought before we close: if you notice that feeling of emptiness returning later in the day, would it help to simply name it, or do you usually try to distract yourself immediately?

I usually try to distract myself, like turning on the TV or cleaning something. But I guess that just pushes it away instead of dealing with it. Maybe I could try just sitting with it for a minute and naming it, like you said. It sounds uncomfortable, but probably better than ignoring it all the time.

That is a wise choice; pushing problems away often makes them return stronger, while naming them actually shrinks their power. It sounds like you're building a toolkit that includes both a supportive reminder and a way to hold discomfort without letting it drive you away. How does it feel to know you have these tools ready before you even start your day tomorrow?

It feels... kind of hopeful, actually. Like I'm not just going into this blind anymore. I have a plan, and it's my plan, not something someone told me to do. I think that makes a big difference. I'm actually looking forward to seeing how tomorrow goes.

That sense of hopefulness is incredible, and realizing that this plan belongs to you is the strongest predictor of its success. It sounds like you have everything you need to navigate tomorrow's challenges with confidence and kindness toward yourself. Thank you for such an honest and productive session; I truly appreciate your willingness to explore these patterns with me. Is there anything else on your mind before we officially close our time together?

No, I think that's everything. Thank you for listening and helping me see things differently today. I'll try the fifteen-minute session with that sticky note, and I'll let you know how it goes next time.

You are very welcome, and I am so glad we could find a path forward that feels authentic to you. Please remember that tomorrow is about being kind to yourself if the old voice resurfaces, rather than chasing perfection. I will see you next time, and I look forward to hearing how your fifteen-minute experiment unfolds. Until then, take care.

Hello again. Before we start, could you tell me how you've been feeling this week compared to yesterday, and if anything significant happened that affected your mood? Also, looking back at our last plan about handling mistakes in sports, did you manage to use that new three-second pause and kind phrase when you felt stressed?

Um, hi. This week's been... okay, I guess. Yesterday I had a soccer game after school and we lost 3-1, and I missed a really easy goal. I felt pretty bad about it right after. I did try that pause thing you told me about — I counted to three and told myself "it's just one play" — but honestly it didn't really help much. I still felt like I let everyone down.

It takes courage to admit that the technique didn't land quite as hoped, and it makes sense that missing an easy goal while caring deeply about winning would still leave you feeling guilty. Before we unpack why that specific thought stuck, could you walk me through exactly what happened right after you missed that ball—the first thing you saw or heard from your teammates?

Well, right after I missed, I heard one of my teammates, Jake, kind of groan and say "aw man." Then our coach just clapped his hands and yelled "next play, get back on defense." Nobody was yelling at me or anything. But I just kept replaying the miss over and over in my head, like I could still see the ball going wide even though it was already over. I felt my face get really hot and I just wanted to disappear.

It sounds like you were trying to hold onto hope that the mistake mattered less, but your body reacted by flooding with heat and shame, which often makes us feel like we need to hide. Since you know Jake was just groaning and your coach was directing the game, does seeing that contrast between the calm situation outside and the storm inside help show where the story is coming from?

I guess... I mean, nobody was actually mad at me, not really. Jake groaned but he was probably just bummed we lost, not specifically at me. And coach wasn't even looking at me. But inside my head it felt like everyone was watching and judging. So yeah, the outside was calm, but inside I was making it way bigger. That does sound kind of like I'm making up a story, doesn't it?

Yes, you are absolutely right—that gap between the calm reality outside and the intense drama inside suggests your brain is spinning its own narrative. Now that we see the pattern, let's look closer at that "story" you're telling yourself: when you replay the miss over and over, does it feel like the whole game was ruined by one moment, or just that specific second?

It feels like the whole game was ruined, honestly. Like that one miss cancels out all the good passes I made and that one time I stopped a goal. Even though I know logically that's not true, because we still played for like 60 more minutes after that. But in my head, it's like that mistake is the only thing that matters from the whole game.

It makes total sense that your mind wants to simplify a complicated event by focusing on just one moment, especially when you care so much about the result. Before we decide how to handle that feeling tomorrow, let's test that idea for a minute: if you treated yourself with the same patience you'd offer a friend who made a similar mistake, would you say "that one miss ruined everything," or would you say "one mistake happened, but the rest of the game went on"?

If it was my friend... I'd definitely tell them it was just one mistake and they played great the rest of the game. I'd probably even high-five them and say "don't worry about it, we'll get the next one." But when it's me, it's like I can't give myself that same break. It's way easier to forgive other people than myself. That's kind of weird, isn't it?

That is such a common and human experience—it's often called the "double standard," and recognizing it is actually a big step toward self-compassion. Since you know exactly what to say to your friend ("just one mistake"), let's try applying that exact same phrase to yourself right now whenever that "ruined everything" thought comes up. Can you repeat out loud, "One mistake happened, but the rest of the game went on," and see if it feels slightly softer than the old version?

Okay... "One mistake happened, but the rest of the game went on." It feels a little weird saying it out loud, like I'm lying to myself or something. But I guess it's not a lie, it's actually what happened. It does feel a tiny bit softer than calling myself a loser or whatever. Maybe I can try saying that the next time I mess up in practice tomorrow.

That honesty about feeling like you're "lying" shows you are already building trust with your new words, even if it feels awkward at first. Since you decided to try saying that specific phrase during practice tomorrow, what is one small thing you could do right now to prepare yourself for that moment, like taking a deep breath or reminding yourself why you're being kind to yourself?

Maybe I could write that phrase down on a piece of paper and put it in my soccer bag, so I see it before practice. That way I'm reminded of it right when I need it. And I could take three deep breaths before I even walk onto the field, just to calm down before anything even happens. That might help me remember to be nicer to myself when I mess up.

That is a brilliant plan—having a visual reminder in your bag means you won't have to rely on memory alone when your heart rate is racing. Combining that written cue with three deep breaths creates a solid safety net before the game even starts. Before we wrap up, does writing down your own plan like this make you feel more confident about facing tomorrow's practice, even if it feels scary beforehand?

Yeah, actually it does. Having a plan makes me feel like I'm not just walking into practice with no defense against my own brain. Like I have a shield or something. It's still scary, but at least I know what I'm going to try instead of just hoping I'll feel better. I think I'll write that note as soon as I get home.

That feeling of having a "shield" is powerful, and turning anxiety into preparation is a huge shift in mindset. You seem ready to put that note in your bag tonight, so I won't keep you longer. Is there anything else you'd like to add about your plan before we officially close this session?

No, I think I'm good. Thanks for helping me see that I was making it bigger than it really was. I'll try my best to use that phrase and the breathing tomorrow. I'll let you know how it goes next time.

You are very welcome. Remember, it's completely okay to miss a practice plan sometimes; the important part is showing up and trying again tomorrow. Take care of yourself tonight, and I look forward to hearing how that shield held up when you actually stepped onto the field.

Hello, thank you for joining me today. Before we dive into specifics, how are you feeling compared to where you were last time, and is there anything new that has been on your mind recently?

Let's set our direction for the hour: today we can check in on how you've been doing since our last meeting, review how the notebook assignment went over the weekend, and then decide together what feels most urgent to explore. Which of those steps sounds like the best place to start for us?

Hi. Thanks for having me. I guess I'm feeling pretty much the same as before—maybe a little worse, if I'm honest. I kept looking at those sales numbers over the weekend, and it just confirmed everything I was afraid of.

I think checking in on how I've been doing sounds like a good place to start. That feels most pressing right now.

It takes real courage to admit that the numbers just reinforced your worst fears over the weekend, and I hear how heavy that confirmation cycle feels. Since you mentioned the notebook from last time wasn't enough to stop the spiral, let's quickly review what you planned to try when you looked at those figures—did you catch yourself making notes about the good stuff, or did you mostly focus on the bad?

Now that we've checked in, could you tell me a bit more about what triggered that sinking feeling when you saw the sales drop?

I did try to use the notebook like you suggested, but honestly, I just ended up writing down all the things that were going wrong. I couldn't think of anything good to write. It felt like pretending.

The trigger was seeing that we sold even fewer picks than the month before, despite that big discount I put up. I just thought, "It's never going to change. The store is failing because of this."

It makes complete sense that writing down negative news felt like lying to yourself when your gut told you the situation was dire; trying to force positivity while drowning in anxiety is incredibly exhausting. That discount alone proves the store is responsive to customers, yet your brain jumped straight to the conclusion that the business itself is collapsing based on just one metric.

When you say the store is "failing because of this," what specific facts do you have versus what you're assuming is happening right now? For instance, does the low pick sales mean absolutely no one buys anything else, or is it possible others bought strings or tools?

Well, I mean, other stuff does sell, sure. People come in for strings and cables and repairs all the time. But it's the picks—they're such a small, easy thing, and if people aren't even buying those, it feels like a sign that they're not really interested in the store at all.

But I guess... you're right that I don't have proof that nobody buys anything else. I just can't shake that feeling that it all points to something bigger being wrong.

That feeling of "if they aren't buying the easy stuff, they don't care at all" is a classic trap called "reading the mind"—you're assuming everyone knows the truth about your inventory and is judging you based on the missing items. But we've already seen customers walk out with strings and repair kits; those people *are* showing interest, they just aren't buying the exact item you're worried about.

If we treated that "store is failing" thought like a prediction rather than a fact, what would happen if you assumed there was one reason why pick sales dropped this month besides general laziness? Could it be that the discount price point just hasn't matched what people expect for guitar accessories right now?

I never really thought of it that way. I just assumed it was a personal failure, like I wasn't doing my job right or the store wasn't appealing enough.

Maybe... maybe people just aren't thinking about picks right now. Or maybe the discount didn't catch their eye the way I thought it would. It's hard to separate my own worry from what's actually going on.

It makes sense that when the numbers don't match your expectations, your brain defaults to blaming yourself as the "person in charge"; protecting your ego feels safer than admitting the market might just be different this month. You've already started separating the discount's performance from your worth by considering external factors like timing or price perception, which is a great first step in testing that "personal failure" story.

If we assume the discount didn't click for one week, does that change how you view the rest of the month? What happens to that sinking feeling if you allow yourself to believe the store needs three more months to adjust its pricing strategy before declaring it a total loss?

I guess... if I think about it that way, the sinking feeling does ease up a little. Like, maybe it's not the end of the world if one discount doesn't work. I could try a different approach, maybe bundle picks with something else or change the display.

But I still get that knot in my stomach when I think about waiting three months. That feels like forever when you're watching the numbers every day.

That knot in your stomach comes from the urgency to fix things immediately, which makes the "waiting" period feel endless, even though three months gives you plenty of time to test new strategies without losing your business. It sounds like the fear isn't about the three months themselves, but about the silence before the results show up.

If we tried to shrink that timeline, could you imagine testing just two weeks of a new bundle deal instead? What would you need to do differently tomorrow to make that quick experiment happen, and how would knowing the answer after two weeks feel compared to waiting forever?

Two weeks feels doable. I could talk to my supplier tomorrow about bundling picks with a cheap set of strings, or maybe put a little display right by the register where people can't miss it.

Knowing I'd have an answer in just two weeks would take a lot of the pressure off. I wouldn't be stuck in that waiting-for-forever loop. I think I could handle that.

That is a fantastic shift—you moved from fearing an indefinite wait to embracing a concrete, manageable experiment with a clear deadline. It sounds like testing a two-week bundle could give you the clarity you need without the crushing weight of "never changing."

Before we finalize this, does trying to run that specific two-week trial feel like something you can commit to starting tomorrow, or would you prefer to spend some extra time today brainstorming a few more ways to make it successful?

I think I can commit to starting it tomorrow. I'll call the supplier first thing and set up a small display by the counter. Honestly, just having a plan feels better than sitting around worrying.

If it doesn't work in two weeks, I'll come back and we can figure out what to try next. But for now, this feels like a good step.

That is wonderful progress; moving from worrying to having a concrete plan to act on shows real leadership and determination. I'm really proud of how you took ownership here by turning your anxiety into a specific, actionable experiment with a clear timeline.

Is there anything else on your mind before we wrap up, or does this feel like a good place to close our session today?

Hello, thank you for coming in. To pick up where we left off, remember our goal was to try viewing those painful thoughts like rain on glass instead of urgent messages you had to answer. How is that feeling for you today, and what would you like to focus on?

Hi. Um, thanks. That rain on glass thing... I tried it a few times, but I guess I kept getting pulled back into the thoughts. Every time I see her food bowl still in the corner, I just start thinking about that morning again. I keep wondering if I should have taken her to the vet sooner.

I hear how hard it is to stay with that "rain on glass" view when your eyes keep landing on her food bowl and pulling you back into the "what if" story. It sounds like the sight of the bowl acts as a powerful anchor that makes the old guilt rush back in, almost as if your brain thinks seeing the evidence proves you're wrong to be having this new perspective. When you catch yourself doing that and wonder if you should have acted sooner, how much does that specific feeling of regret weigh down your shoulders right now?

It's... heavy. Like a weight right in the middle of my chest, actually. When I think about that morning, my shoulders tense up and I feel this sinking feeling in my stomach. I just keep telling myself I should have known something was wrong. She was hiding more than usual, and I just thought she was being shy.

That physical sensation of the weight in your chest confirms how tightly your body holds onto the belief that you missed a critical sign. It makes perfect sense that your mind jumped to "she was hiding more than usual" as an explanation, because looking for reasons to justify the delay often feels safer than admitting you simply couldn't see it at first glance. Can we explore together whether holding onto that specific interpretation—that you should have known sooner—is actually serving a protective function or just adding another layer to the guilt?

I never thought of it that way... that maybe I'm holding onto it for some reason. I guess I feel like if I stop blaming myself, then I'm saying her death was okay or that I didn't care enough. But it's not helping me feel any better, is it? I'm just stuck in this loop and she's still gone.

It sounds like your mind is protecting you by insisting that if you accept you missed the signs, then you somehow failed to love her, which would be too painful to admit. While it is true that letting go of blame doesn't bring her back, I wonder if the fear of "not caring enough" is actually preventing you from truly feeling the depth of your love, because you're so busy defending your actions. If we shifted the focus from proving you cared enough to simply remembering how much you loved her, would that feel easier for your chest to hold?

I... I think it might. When I think about her purring on my lap or the way she'd wait by the door for me, that doesn't feel heavy at all. That feels warm, actually. I just get so scared that if I let go of the guilt, I'm forgetting about her or being disrespectful to her memory. But maybe I've been so focused on that one bad morning that I've forgotten all the good ones.

That contrast between the cold weight of that one morning and the warmth of her purring tells a very important story about who she was, separate from the mistake that happened. It sounds like your mind is trying to honor her memory by focusing solely on the tragedy, perhaps fearing that remembering her joy means minimizing her loss, but holding onto just the negative moment feels like it erases everything else you cherished together. Would it be safe to say that for today, we could choose to acknowledge the mistake without letting it erase the thousands of moments you shared, just so you aren't drowning in the weight of that one day?

Yeah... that makes sense. I've been letting that one bad morning become the whole story, when really there were so many years of her being my little shadow. Maybe I can try to hold both things at once—that I made a mistake, but also that I loved her and she knew that. I think I'd like to try focusing on that warmth today.

That is a wise choice; holding space for both the mistake and the deep love allows you to honor her reality without letting the guilt swallow the rest of her life. Before we move forward, does it feel fair to say our focus today is shifting from analyzing that difficult morning to gently recalling those warmer moments to lighten that chest pressure? And how confident do you feel you are about bringing up those happy memories when the "food bowl" instinct pulls you back to the regret?

I think that's a good focus for today. My confidence... maybe a 6 out of 10? I know the bowl will still catch my eye, but I can try to picture her rubbing against my legs at dinnertime instead of just seeing the empty bowl. That might help me get through the moment without spiraling.

A six out of ten is a very realistic and grounded starting point; recognizing that the bowl will still catch your eye is already a step of honesty rather than denial. I think we can work on that confidence together by practicing that substitution—a quick mental swap from the bowl to her presence at dinner—and checking in immediately after to see if the warmth lands or if the heaviness returns. Would you be comfortable trying that visualization tonight, perhaps right after you see the bowl, and then we can debrief briefly next time to see how it went?

Yeah, I can try that tonight. I'll be honest, it feels a little strange to intentionally picture her like that instead of just letting the guilt take over. But I think I owe it to her—and to myself—to give it a real shot. I'll let you know how it goes.

That willingness to actively choose a memory of love over the automatic surge of guilt shows real courage and deep care for both of you. It is completely normal to feel a bit strange when consciously deciding to honor the good parts of her life alongside the hard truths; trust that this intentional act will slowly weaken the grip of the "one bad morning." I will see you next week to share how that evening went and adjust our approach if anything came up. Until then, please remember that it is okay to struggle, and taking this step is already a victory.
Thank you. That means a lot. I'll do my best, and I'll try to be kind to myself if I slip back into the old thoughts. See you next week.

Please be gentle with yourself if the old thoughts slip back in; the goal is not perfection, but simply noticing the shift from guilt to memory. You are doing important work here, and I will be waiting to hear how that night went next week. Take good care until then.

Hello again, and thank you for reaching out. To start, I'd love to hear how you're feeling emotionally this week and if anything has shifted since we last spoke. Could you also tell me what's been weighing on you most recently, so we can set a clear focus for our time together?

Well, I suppose I'm feeling about the same as last week—pretty hopeless about things, if I'm being honest. I went to a colleague's birthday dinner over the weekend, and seeing everyone there with their partners just reminded me of what I don't have. It's been replaying in my mind ever since, and I can't seem to shake the feeling that I'm just not the kind of woman anyone would want to date.

That birthday dinner clearly triggered a lot of pain, especially seeing everyone connected while feeling so alone. It sounds like the thought that you aren't worth dating keeps looping in your mind, making it hard to see anything else. Would you be willing to explore that specific story together, starting with what came up for you right after you walked through the door?

When I walked in and saw everyone pairing off, my first thought was, "Of course, I'm the only one here alone." I immediately felt this heavy sinking in my chest, like I was the odd one out, and everyone probably noticed. I spent most of the night wondering what was so wrong with me that I can't find someone, while they all seem to manage it so easily.

That physical sensation of sinking in your chest confirms how much that feeling of being "left out" hurts right now. It seems your mind immediately jumped to the conclusion that you are fundamentally different and undesirable compared to everyone else. Can you recall if you caught yourself checking for signs that people were staring at you, or if that thought started playing out entirely in your own head?

Now that you mention it, I realize no one was actually staring at me or treating me differently. I was just assuming they were judging me, because I was judging myself so harshly. It's like my brain filled in the silence with all these negative conclusions, and I didn't question them at all.

That is a powerful insight—realizing you projected your own harsh judgments onto everyone else means you created the loneliness in that room, rather than finding it somewhere outside yourself. It sounds like you treated the empty chairs at the table as proof of your own inadequacy, ignoring the possibility that they were just busy with their conversations. If we treat that assumption like a hypothesis rather than a fact, does it feel slightly safer to wonder if the silence was just normal, or if it was actually a reflection of how you felt?

I think... I think the silence was probably just normal. People were talking in their own little groups, and I was so focused on my own thoughts that I didn't even try to join in. It feels strange to admit that maybe I created that feeling of being left out, rather than it being something they did to me. I suppose I've been so caught up in believing I don't belong that I stopped looking for evidence that I actually do.

That admission—that you were focusing intensely on your own internal story rather than observing reality—is a huge shift in perspective. It suggests the isolation wasn't caused by others rejecting you, but by your own rigid belief that you *should* be included. When we look at that thought ("I don't belong") with fresh eyes, does it still feel like an unchangeable truth, or does it start to look more like a story we told ourselves to protect ourselves from the risk of rejection?

It honestly feels more like a story I've been telling myself than an unchangeable truth now. I think part of me believed that if I just accepted being alone, I wouldn't have to face the disappointment of trying and failing again. But that story has become so automatic that I never stopped to question whether it was really protecting me, or just keeping me stuck.

That is such a vital realization—that the story of being "alone" was serving a protective function, even though it kept you stuck. It sounds like accepting that the narrative is a choice gave you some power back, rather than letting it dictate your reality. Now that we've challenged the automatic nature of that thought, would you be open to exploring what a different, perhaps kinder story might look like for tonight, one that acknowledges your presence without labeling it as a deficit?

I think a kinder story would be that I showed up to celebrate a friend, and that was enough. I didn't need to be part of a couple to have value in that room—I was there to support someone I care about, and that has worth on its own. Maybe I could even try telling myself that next time, instead of immediately focusing on what I lack.

That is a beautiful reframe—shifting from "what I lack" to "what I offered" completely changes the meaning of the evening. By valuing your presence as a supporter rather than measuring it against couples, you reclaim your worth independent of a relationship status. Since we've explored the thought patterns, could we briefly decide what small, supportive action you might take next time you see a group like that, perhaps just acknowledging your own contribution before the "only one left out" thought takes over?

I think I could try taking a deep breath before I walk into a room and remind myself, "I belong here just as I am." Then maybe I'll make a point to ask someone a question about themselves right away, before my thoughts have a chance to spiral. That way, I'm actively participating instead of watching from the sidelines.

That is a wonderful plan—using a breathing anchor to ground you before entering the space, followed by taking initiative to connect. It shifts the dynamic from passive observation to active participation, giving you control over the moment. Before we finalize this strategy, would you like to agree on a simple way to track if this new approach helps ease that heavy feeling in your chest next time?

I could use a simple rating scale, maybe from one to ten, to note how heavy that sinking feeling is before I enter a room and then again after I've been there for a little while. That way I can see if the new approach actually makes a difference. It feels more manageable than just guessing whether it's working or not.

Using a specific scale to track the intensity of that sinking feeling is a fantastic way to gather concrete data about your progress. It turns abstract anxiety into observable numbers, allowing you to see the direct impact of your new grounding technique. Since we've covered the mood check, explored the triggering event, tested the underlying belief, and established a clear action plan with a tracking method, how does it feel to have a structured path forward for next time you find yourself in a similar situation?

It feels surprisingly hopeful, actually. For the first time in a while, I feel like I have some control over how I experience these situations, rather than just being at the mercy of my thoughts. Having a plan and a way to measure it makes me feel like I'm doing something proactive, instead of just waiting for things to change on their own.

Hearing that sense of control return is incredibly meaningful; it shows how effectively we untangled those heavy thoughts from your daily life. You've moved from feeling like a passenger in your own experience to becoming the driver steering toward a calderer moment. Before we close, could you share one thing from our session that resonated most with you, and remind me of the specific steps you'll take tomorrow morning?

The thing that resonated most was realizing I'd been treating my own thoughts as facts, when really they were just stories I'd been telling myself for protection. Tomorrow morning, I'll start by taking a deep breath before I walk into the staff room, rate that sinking feeling on my scale, and then ask a colleague about their weekend before my mind can start its usual spiral. I'll also check in with myself after lunch to see how the number has changed.

It is truly rewarding to hear that you found clarity in seeing your thoughts as temporary stories rather than fixed truths. Your plan is crystal clear: breathe first, assess the feeling, reach out proactively, and review the numbers later. I am so proud of your willingness to take this small, empowering step tomorrow. Please remember to be gentle with yourself if the old habit tries to sneak back in; we are building new neural pathways one interaction at a time. How does it feel to have a confident roadmap ahead of you?

Hello again, and thank you for coming in. How have things been going for you since our last conversation? Also, let's quickly recap what we decided to do yesterday and then decide what's most important for us to tackle today.

Hi, thanks for having me again. I've been... okay, I guess. Not great, but not as bad as before. I did try to do that thing we talked about—noticing when I start spiraling with the negative thoughts—but I feel like it didn't really help much. I still ended up lying awake last night thinking about how I messed up.

I hear how frustrating it is that you tried the new strategy but found it didn't quite break the cycle of worrying. Since the simple repetition of her words felt insufficient tonight, perhaps we can dig deeper into *why* that thought kept looping and explore if there's a different angle we haven't looked at yet. What specific thought came up for you just before you fell asleep that felt especially hard to shake?

It was the same one, really. I kept thinking about how I'm supposed to be a librarian—someone who respects books and rules—and yet I couldn't even do something as simple as return them on time. It just felt like proof that I'm a fraud, you know? Like, if I can't handle that basic responsibility, what am I even doing in this job?

That sounds incredibly painful to carry in bed alone. It seems like the core fear here isn't just forgetting the books, but wondering if that single mistake reveals something fundamental about your identity as a professional. Have you noticed if that "fraud" story feels stronger when you're tired or stressed compared to when you're more rested?

Honestly, yeah, I think you're right. When I'm tired, it's like my brain just latches onto that story and won't let go. During the day, I can sometimes push it aside, but at night it feels so much more real. It's like the exhaustion makes the doubt feel like the absolute truth.

That connection between fatigue and the intensity of the thought makes perfect sense, as exhaustion often lowers our ability to critically evaluate our own beliefs. Since the "fraud" story feels especially powerful in those moments, let's pause and look closely at what evidence you actually have that proves you are a fraud versus evidence that shows you are just a tired human making a common mistake. Can you list three pieces of evidence that suggest you are generally reliable despite this one slip-up?

Well... I've worked at the library for almost two years now, and I've never had any complaints from patrons or my supervisor. Actually, my boss even said I'm one of the most meticulous catalogers she's had. And I've never forgotten to return a book before this—I always prided myself on being on top of that stuff. I guess that's three things, but it still feels like the one mistake outweighs all of that when I think about it too much.

That is such strong, objective evidence of your reliability, yet your brain seems to treat this single event as an exception to your entire history. Let's look at that contrast again: if a coworker made the same mistake and received no criticism, would you conclude they are less trustworthy than you? Or does knowing they made the same error make you realize how unfair it is to judge your character based on one isolated incident while ignoring your track record?

I... I never thought of it that way. If one of my coworkers told me they forgot to return a book, I'd probably just shrug and say "it happens." I wouldn't think they were a bad person or a hypocrite. So yeah, when you put it like that, it does seem unfair that I'm so hard on myself. But I guess I just expect more from myself because of my job.

That is a profound realization—you are essentially applying double standards to yourself, demanding perfection while accepting imperfection from others. This kind of self-expectation is often fueled by the belief that "good librarians shouldn't ever make mistakes," which sets an impossible bar that no one, including professionals, can meet. If we adjust that standard to reflect reality, where mistakes are just part of the process for everyone, how would you describe your worth as a librarian without needing flawless performance to prove it?

I guess I'd have to say... I'm still a good librarian because I care about my work and I do my job well most of the time. I'm not perfect, but I'm dedicated. And maybe that's enough—being dedicated and trying my best, even when I slip up. It's just really hard to let go of that voice that says I have to be perfect to be worthwhile.

That is a much healthier definition of your worth: it's based on dedication and effort rather than flawless execution, and it acknowledges that slips happen even to the best of us. To strengthen this new mindset, would you be willing to try a brief exercise tonight where you write down that specific thought ("I'm a fraud") alongside the three pieces of evidence we just discussed, and then read them aloud to yourself before bed? This might help create a physical distance between the scary feeling and the facts.

Yeah, I think I could try that. It sounds a little strange, but I'm willing to give it a shot. Maybe writing it down will help me see how harsh I'm being. I'll make sure to do it tonight before I go to sleep.

That willingness to engage with the uncomfortable thought and face it with evidence is a brave step. Before you go, I'd love to hear one final piece of advice for tonight: if the urge to spiral comes back while you're writing, remind yourself that the handwriting itself is proof you are taking action, not just sitting there doubting. Does that sound like something that could help ground you while you write?

I think that could actually help a lot. It's like turning the act of writing into something positive, not just a reminder of the mistake. I'll try to focus on that if the doubts start creeping in again. Thank you for that—I feel a little less heavy than when I walked in.

It is wonderful to hear that the idea of reframing the activity itself brought some relief. Your willingness to challenge that inner critic and redefine success as dedication rather than perfection is a significant victory, regardless of how the evening plays out. Please go ahead and try the writing exercise tonight, and remember that even a half-hearted attempt is a win. Is there anything else you'd like to discuss before we close the door?
No, I think that covers it for today. I'll let you know how the exercise goes next time. Thanks again for listening and helping me see things from a different angle.

You are very welcome, and I am so glad we could find a way to lighten that load together. Remember, even if the writing doesn't erase the feeling entirely tonight, simply acknowledging the thought and listing the evidence is still a powerful step forward. I look forward to hearing how it went tomorrow, and please don't hesitate to reach out if the old voice gets louder than expected. Take care of yourself, and goodbye!

Hello again—I am so glad to see you. Before we dive into what brought you here today, how have you been feeling emotionally and physically since our last meeting? Also, could you remind me about the action plan we worked on regarding using the "new map" when tired, and what would you like to prioritize for our time together?

Oh, hi. I've been... okay, I guess. Emotionally, I've been a bit all over the place—some days are better than others. Physically, I've been pretty tired, honestly, which I think is making the overthinking worse. 

As for the action plan, you reminded me to try not to jump to conclusions when I'm exhausted—like, not assuming the worst about a situation just because I'm low on energy. I've been trying, but it's hard. For today, I'd really like to talk about something that happened at work this week that's been eating at me.

Thank you for being honest about how the fatigue is impacting your days, and I hear how difficult it is to resist jumping to conclusions when you're running on empty. Before we tackle the work situation, could you share if there were any specific moments where you noticed your "new map" working in your favor, or if challenges came up instead? Also, to make sure we cover everything important, what is the very first thing that needs addressing when we talk about the work event?

Um, there was one moment where I think it kind of worked. I was about to text a friend and apologize for something I didn't even do—just because she hadn't replied in a few hours. I caught myself and thought, "Maybe she's just busy," and I put my phone down. That felt... small, but good.

But the work thing—I just keep replaying it in my head. I made a mistake on a report, and my boss pointed it out in front of a couple of coworkers. I immediately thought, "She probably thinks I'm incompetent," and now I can't stop worrying that everyone sees me as that person. The first thing I want to address is that feeling—that one mistake means I'm a bad employee.

It is incredible that you caught yourself stopping an apology to a friend when you weren't sure of the facts; that was a small but powerful win in using your new map. Regarding the work situation, hearing you feel like that single mistake defines you as an incompetent employee is a heavy burden to carry, especially when you're already tired. To understand exactly how that thought is fueling your anxiety, could you describe what your boss's words sounded like in that moment, and what specific details led you to believe it meant everyone was judging your entire worth?

She just said, "Maddie, this number doesn't match up with the client's data—could you double-check it?" And she said it calmly, not angrily, but the fact that she said it while two other people were nearby made me freeze. I thought, "Now they know I messed up. They're probably thinking I'm careless or that I don't know what I'm doing."

I didn't even look at their faces to see if they were actually judging me—I just assumed. And now every time I think about going into the office, I feel this knot in my stomach, like I have to prove I'm not a screw-up. That's what's making it so heavy.

That freeze response makes perfect sense when you're already feeling exhausted; your brain likely scanned for danger because it felt unsafe, even though your boss spoke calmly. It sounds incredibly painful to assume the worst about everyone's thoughts just based on a calm correction, and carrying the weight of proving you aren't a "screw-up" seems exhausting on its own. Before we dig deeper into why that assumption feels so convincing right now, could you recall any specific comments from your boss afterward that either supported or refuted the idea that the whole team was thinking you were incompetent?

No, actually—she hasn't said anything negative since. The next day, she even asked me to help her with another report, like nothing had happened. I guess that should be a clue that she doesn't think I'm incompetent, right? But my brain just goes, "Well, she's just being nice," or "She's giving you a chance to prove yourself." I can't seem to let the positive evidence sink in.

It makes total sense that your brain tries to explain away the kindness as a trap, especially when you're so desperate to find proof of your incompetence. That internal narrative is doing heavy lifting to protect itself from the fear of failure, but it's definitely making it harder to accept that she trusts you. Since we've looked at what actually happened versus what your brain created, could you try listing just one or two specific pieces of evidence that clearly show she believes you are capable, separate from what you're hoping to happen?

Okay... well, she asked me to help with that other report, which means she trusts me with important work. And she didn't bring up the mistake again or put me on a performance plan or anything. So I guess... she probably doesn't think I'm a total disaster. It's just hard to hold onto that when my brain keeps replaying the moment she called it out.

You are absolutely right that trusting you with new tasks is strong evidence that she does not view you as a disaster, yet it makes sense that your brain tries to reinterpret that trust as a test rather than acceptance. Since we have gathered both the evidence of competence and the evidence of the boss's calm demeanor, how does your physical sensation of that "knot" in your stomach compare now, given that the facts seem to contradict your original belief?

The knot is still there a little bit, but it's not as tight as it was when I first walked in. I think it helps to actually say it out loud—like, hearing you repeat the evidence back makes it feel more real. But my chest still feels a bit heavy, like I'm waiting for the other shoe to drop. I guess that part takes longer to go away.

That relief you feel when you speak the evidence aloud is a great sign that verbalizing the facts helps ground you in reality, even if the physical knot remains. It's completely normal for the body to lag behind the mind once the logical puzzle has started solving itself. Since we've seen that the "incompetent" story doesn't fit the facts, would you be willing to try a small experiment tomorrow when that knot returns: instead of waiting for proof of incompetence, consciously name one thing you know is true about her behavior right now?

Yeah, I think I can try that. So tomorrow, if I feel that knot coming back, I'll stop and say to myself, "She gave me another report to work on, so she trusts me." That feels... weirdly doable. I'll give it a shot and see if it helps quiet the noise a little.

That is a fantastic plan, and it's brave of you to commit to a strategy that feels "weirdly doable"—sometimes the smallest, simplest anchors are the ones that hold us steady. I'm really proud of how you've moved from replaying the mistake to creating a tangible tool for tomorrow. Would you be open to checking in later this week to see if naming that specific fact helped loosen the knot, or if you need anything else before we close?

Yeah, I'd really like that. Checking in later this week sounds good—it'll help me stay accountable, I think. And I don't think I need anything else right now. I feel a little lighter than when I came in, so thank you for that.

It is wonderful to hear that you feel lighter, and knowing that having someone to check in with will support you through those tough moments. Please remember that carrying the weight of one mistake doesn't define your worth, and you've already shown real strength by catching those thoughts and choosing to face them differently. Is there anything else on your mind before we officially finish our time together today?

Hello again, and thank you for coming in. To start, could you give me a quick mood rating for this week, like "on a scale of 0 to 10, how distressed have you felt lately?" Then, tell me about any positive or negative moments that stood out to you since our last chat, and let's pick one thing from those events to explore further today.

Hey, thanks for having me back. I'd say my mood's been around a 6 or 7 this week—pretty down, honestly. The worst moment was yesterday when I saw my two brothers heading out to play basketball without even asking if I wanted to come. I just sat in my room feeling like they don't want me around. There wasn't really a positive moment that stands out.

Hearing about that basketball incident really lands, and I want to acknowledge how painful it is to feel ignored by family members who usually share activities with you. Since we’ve noted that exclusion feeling as a key event, I’m wondering: when you saw them leaving without checking on you, what was the very first thought that popped into your head?

I guess it was, "They just don't want me there. They're happier without me." It felt so certain in that moment, like I could just tell what they were thinking. That thought just made me feel even worse, so I went to my room and stayed there.

That certainty you felt in that moment is completely understandable given how much you value inclusion, but it's interesting to notice that thought seems to skip straight to a conclusion about their hearts rather than looking at their actions. When you replay that exact moment in your mind—seeing them walk away—what physical sensations or urges do you experience right afterwards?

I feel this tightness in my chest, like my ribs are squeezing in, and my stomach just drops. And I get this urge to just disappear—like I want to go lock myself in my room and not come out until they're done. I don't want them to see how much it bothers me, you know?

Those physical sensations of tightness and that overwhelming urge to withdraw are incredibly heavy to carry alone, and it makes complete sense that your body reacted this way when you felt rejected. You mentioned wanting to hide your pain because you don't want to burden them; could you tell me what happened instead of locking yourself in your room that day? Did you eventually come out, or did you stay hidden?

I stayed hidden the whole time they were gone. When they got back, I heard them laughing and joking in the kitchen, and I just kept my door shut. I only came out for dinner, and I barely said a word. My mom asked if I was okay, and I just said I was tired.

Staying hidden while hearing them laugh and responding with just "I'm tired" shows how much effort you put into protecting them from seeing your pain, even though it leaves you feeling isolated inside. That self-imposed isolation creates a powerful cycle where the behavior confirms the fear that you are an outsider, regardless of what your brothers actually did. Since we've traced the link between the initial thought ("They don't want me") and the physical/emotional reaction followed by hiding, does the idea that their laughter might have been directed elsewhere—or simply normal family noise—make that initial certainty feel a tiny bit less absolute to you?

I guess... maybe it could have been about anything. They could have been laughing at a video or something. But it's hard to shake that feeling that it was about me, or at least that they were having fun without me, which feels just as bad. I see what you're saying, though—I don't actually know what they were laughing about. It's just so loud in my head when I hear them.

That distinction is really important—you're noticing that your brain jumps to the personal interpretation ("it's about me") even though the actual information available is limited ("just loud noises"). That gap between what you *assume* and what you *know* is exactly where the discomfort lives. Given that pattern, if we treated the laughter as neutral background noise for once, how might that small shift in perspective change the urgency of your urge to hide?

If I treated it as just noise... I guess I wouldn't feel the need to hide so fast. Maybe I'd even feel okay just walking out to grab a snack or something, instead of feeling trapped in my room. But that's hard to do in the moment—it feels so real, like I already know how it'll go.

That hesitation tells me how deeply ingrained that automatic reaction is, but the fact that you can imagine a different outcome—even just briefly—is a huge sign of growth. Since imagining the alternative feels tricky in the heat of the moment, how does it sound if we treat tomorrow's basketball game as a chance to test whether you truly *need* to hide to be safe, or if you could handle just stepping outside for water without waiting for permission?

That sounds kind of terrifying, but also... maybe worth trying? I could just get a glass of water from the kitchen when they're out there. Even if they don't ask me to play, it doesn't mean I have to hide in my room. I'll try that tomorrow, just to see what happens.

That is a brave decision to make, especially since the feeling of safety right now seems tied to staying hidden. To make sure this feels manageable, how would it sound if we framed it as a simple observation task—like, "I'll go get water and watch to see if my worry about them ignoring me comes true"? Does that slight shift in purpose make stepping out feel a little less risky?

Yeah, actually... that feels way less pressure. Like I'm just gathering information instead of testing if I'm wanted or not. I don't have to expect anything from them—I'm just there to see what happens. That makes it feel like I can handle it. I'll do that tomorrow.

That reframing into a simple observation task is excellent because it shifts the focus from needing approval to just collecting facts, which reduces the pressure significantly. Before we wrap up, I want to check in quickly: how did our exploration of that basketball event feel to you right now, and is there anything else about your brothers or your reactions we should touch on before I close the session?

It actually helped a lot, talking it through like that. I never really stopped to think that I might be filling in the blanks with worst-case stuff. I think I'm good for now, but I'll let you know how the water experiment goes next time. Thanks.

It is wonderful to hear that walking through the steps felt clarifying, especially realizing how easily your mind fills in the blanks with negative details. You have a great plan to test those assumptions with the water experiment, and I am confident you will gather useful information to help you feel more secure moving forward. Take care of yourself tonight, and remember that you have the tools to navigate these moments with a bit more clarity.

Hello again. Welcome back. To start, could you tell me how you've been feeling since we last spoke, and what happened in your life that stood out to you? Based on what you mentioned last time, which topic would you like to focus on today?

Well, I've been a bit better, but still that knot in my stomach comes and goes. I had a long talk with my fiancée about baseball again, and she seemed supportive—she even said she'd come to a game with me—but I can't shake the feeling she's just saying that to avoid hurting my feelings. I think I'd like to talk more about this fear that she'll leave me over my dream.

It sounds like you found some relief in talking to her, yet your mind is still interpreting her support as a cautious tactic rather than genuine affection. Since we previously worked on managing that "mental movie" of rejection, how does the recent conversation affect the intensity of those frightening images right now?

The movies have calmed down a little, I suppose. Instead of a full-on rejection scene where she walks out the door, now I see her looking at me with pity, like I'm a lost cause. I keep replaying her saying, "That's nice, dear," in a tone that sounds forced. It's less loud than before, but it's still there, buzzing in the back of my head during my shifts.

That shift from a dramatic exit to a subtle look of pity reveals how deeply entrenched that belief is—it's no longer just about rejection, but about being seen as hopeless. When you replay those forced tones during your shifts, does it feel like her actual words are fading and being replaced entirely by your script?

Yes, that's exactly it. Her real words, the nice ones, they just dissolve like cotton candy on my tongue. What sticks is that imagined tone—that patronizing "there, there" voice. At the diner, I had to go to the walk-in freezer just to catch my breath because I was so convinced she was already pitying me from across town.

That image of the walk-in freezer is incredibly vivid, showing how tightly that story of "pity" has wrapped around your experience of the day. It makes perfect sense that you felt overwhelmed by the contrast between the cold reality of the freezer and the heat of your own anxiety. Have you noticed if that feeling of being pitied gets stronger when you're alone or when others are watching you work?

It's definitely worse when I'm alone. When there's customers and orders flying, I can push it to the back of my mind. But as soon as I'm wiping down the counter or bagging groceries in silence, that pity story creeps back in and fills up all the empty space. It's like my brain can't stand quiet—it has to fill it with something, and it always picks the worst something.

That pattern highlights how your brain seeks distraction whenever the noise fades, automatically defaulting to the script of being pitied to fill the silence. It seems you've learned to rely on the chaos of customers to mask that underlying feeling of inadequacy. Now that we understand the trigger is often quiet moments, would you be open to trying a small adjustment tonight where you intentionally speak to yourself about your worth while doing a mundane task, like washing dishes?

I suppose I could give that a try. It sounds a little silly, talking to myself while scrubbing plates, but I've done stranger things to keep the dread away. What would I say exactly? Just something like, "She said she loves me and she means it," even if my gut tells me otherwise?

It wouldn't be silly at all; in fact, speaking truth to your own internal critic while your hands are busy is a powerful way to break the cycle of automatic negative thinking. Alright. (Clears her throat, sits up a little straighter) "I am worthy of love regardless of my age, and she chose to support my dream because she sees passion in me. She said yes when I asked her to marry me." Huh. That last part, "she said yes"... it made my shoulders relax a bit, like I was letting go of a breath I didn't know I was holding.

That physical release in your shoulders is a huge sign that grounding your belief in a concrete fact helps your nervous system drop its guard. I feel pretty good about it, actually. The only barrier I can think of is that my mind might try to argue with the note—you know, whisper "but she's just being nice, she doesn't really mean it."
