Hello, thank you for joining us today. Before we dive into our work, could you share a quick mood check—on a scale of zero to ten, how anxious or stressed have you felt this week compared to when we met last time? Also, since we ended with a plan to cook a comforting meal tonight, did you get a chance to try it, or would you like to adjust our focus for this session?

Um, I'd say my anxiety has been around a 7 or 8 this week, maybe a little higher than last time. And about that cooking plan... I didn't end up trying it. I just couldn't bring myself to do it, honestly. I keep thinking about what happened with my neighbor after she ate my casserole.

I hear how frustrating and isolating it must feel when the urge to act on that fear overrides your best intentions, especially when you already planned to break the cycle. That 7 or 8 on the anxiety scale really adds weight to what you just described, so let's spend some time unpacking exactly what happens in that moment when you sit in front of the stove. Given the high stress level and the missed opportunity, should we focus today on reviewing the immediate reaction to not cooking, exploring the specific thoughts driving the avoidance, or perhaps identifying one smaller, safer step you can take immediately to regain a sense of control?

I think... maybe we should talk about what goes through my mind when I think about cooking. Because it's not just that I feel scared—it's like a whole avalanche of thoughts hits me all at once. I start picturing someone getting sick again, and then I'm telling myself I'm a terrible cook, and I should just stop trying altogether.

That "avalanche" description is incredibly accurate, and I can see how overwhelming it feels when so many negative images pile up so quickly. It sounds like the fear of the neighbor incident is acting as a domino effect, knocking over your confidence and pushing you toward giving up entirely. To better understand the mechanics of this avalanche, could you walk me through the very first thought that strikes you the moment you think about standing near the stove? What is the initial image or statement that sets off the rest of the chain reaction?

The first thing that pops into my head is a picture of my neighbor's face—pale and sick-looking, right after she ate my casserole. And then I immediately think, "I did that. I made her sick with my food." It's like that image triggers everything else, and I can't stop the rest from flooding in after that.

That visual of your neighbor looks so vivid right now, and it makes complete sense why that single sentence—"I made her sick"—feels like such a catastrophic verdict on your entire identity as a cook. It sounds like your brain is stuck in a loop where that one painful memory automatically generates a guarantee about the future, bypassing all the other times you've cooked safely. When you isolate that first trigger—the sight of the sick neighbor—and trace the direct line to the conclusion that "this is always going to happen," does the connection between seeing that face and believing you are permanently incapable feel absolutely solid to you, or is there a crack in that logic you haven't noticed yet?

I mean, when you put it like that... I guess there is a crack. Because I've cooked lots of meals before that one without anyone getting sick. But in the moment, it doesn't feel like there's any crack at all—it feels like that one time is the only thing that matters, and it proves everything bad about my cooking.

It sounds like your brain is trying to protect you by locking onto that one traumatic event as the ultimate truth, effectively ignoring the mountain of evidence that says otherwise. This is a very human reaction to pain; when we hurt, our minds sometimes build walls to keep the hurt from coming back, even if those walls block us from seeing our own success. If we treat that single memory as the only rule, we lose the ability to learn from the hundreds of times you've successfully fed people. Would you be open to us doing a quick experiment where we write down three specific meals you've made since the casserole incident that went perfectly, and we compare those facts directly against that one image?

I suppose... I could try that. There was the spaghetti I made for my granddaughter last month—she said it was better than the restaurant. And I made a roast chicken for Sunday dinner that everyone complimented. Oh, and the cookies I brought to my book club—people asked for the recipe. So there are some good meals since then, I guess. I just don't think about them as much as I think about the casserole.

Noticing those specific moments of praise—your granddaughter saying it was better than a restaurant, people asking for recipes—isn't just counting wins; it's gathering concrete data that contradicts the single story of failure. Our brain often ignores reliable evidence when an emotional alarm bell rings loudly enough to drown it out, which explains why those compliments feel distant while the image of the sick neighbor screams in your ear. Now that we have those three examples in hand, how would you describe the feeling if you forced yourself to weigh the certainty of "one bad outcome" against the repeated reality of "many good outcomes"? Does that balance feel slightly less top-heavy right now?

It does feel a little less heavy, I think. Like, when I actually list out those good meals, I can see that maybe I've been focusing too much on the one bad thing. But it's still hard to fully believe it, you know? There's this part of me that whispers, "Those good meals were just luck. The bad one was the real you."

That whisper calling your success "luck" is a classic defense mechanism designed to protect you from having to face your actual skill; it's easier to believe you are an accident than to accept that you are capable. We can challenge this by looking closer at the contrast: if your grandma baked a cake and it exploded in the oven, would you call that "luck" or a rare mishap? Yet if she bakes it perfectly every week, wouldn't you assume she knows how to bake? Your brain seems to be applying a double standard here, treating your mistakes as proof of incompetence while dismissing your mastery as chance. If we shifted our view to see those good meals as evidence of *your* ability rather than random luck, how would that change the story you tell yourself about who you are as a cook?

I guess if I really think about it... it does sound silly to call all those good meals luck. I mean, I followed recipes, I paid attention, I used techniques my mom taught me. It wasn't random. But changing that story in my head feels really hard—like I'd have to let go of this idea that I'm just naturally bad at cooking, and that's been sort of comfortable in a weird way. It protects me from being disappointed again.

That is such a profound insight, realizing that clinging to the idea of being "bad" actually creates a strange kind of safety shield, even though it leaves you trapped in the kitchen. It makes perfect sense that letting go of that protective lie feels risky, like walking barefoot on ice—you might fall, or worse, feel exposed to disappointment again. However, if we reframe it, what if admitting you are a skilled cook doesn't mean you can't fail anymore, but rather means you finally have permission to try without waiting for perfection first? Would you be willing to do a tiny experiment tonight where you cook just one step—a simple boil of water or sauté of onions—with the intention of just watching it happen, completely suspending judgment until the pot is off the heat?

I could try that, I suppose. Just boiling water or sautéing onions sounds manageable—it's not a whole meal, so there's less pressure. I think I can do that tonight without the avalanche hitting too hard. But I'll probably need to remind myself that I'm just watching, not judging.

That is a brilliant compromise; breaking the pressure down to just boiling water or sautéing onions removes the massive weight of a full meal, making the "avalanche" much harder to summon. You are absolutely right that the key will be reminding yourself to be a curious observer rather than a critical judge throughout that process. For tonight's plan, how does it sound if we agree to just watch the onions sweat for five minutes, note any thoughts that come up without fighting them, and then consciously redirect your focus back to the steam and smell? What feels like the most realistic time of day for you to try this small step?

I think early evening would work best, maybe around five o'clock before anyone else gets home. That way there's no pressure to cook for anyone else—it's just me and some onions. I'll set a timer for five minutes and try to just watch and smell without judging. I think I can do that.

That timing at five o'clock is perfect because it gives you a quiet window to practice just watching the process unfold without external expectations. Setting a timer for five minutes is a fantastic way to create a clear boundary, ensuring the activity remains a short, manageable experience rather than a daunting task. I am confident that noticing the steam and the scent will serve as a gentle anchor, pulling you back to the present whenever those old fears try to surface. How does it feel to visualize sitting quietly with just the pan and the timer, ready to observe without judging?

It actually feels... kind of peaceful, when I picture it that way. Like a small moment I can control, without any big expectations. I don't feel that tight knot in my stomach when I imagine just watching the onions. I think I'm ready to give it a try tonight.

That shift in physical sensation—from the tight knot to a sense of peace—is a powerful indicator that your nervous system is beginning to relax when you frame the activity differently. Choosing to control just the observation of the onions, rather than the outcome of a full meal, puts you back in the driver's seat. I want to check in on the agreement: given how much resistance you've faced recently, does having this one tiny, low-stakes experiment feel like something you can realistically commit to without falling back into the old patterns? Also, to wrap up our time together, how has our work on separating the "one bad memory" from your overall capability felt, and is there anything else you'd like to discuss before we finish?

Yes, I think I can realistically commit to just the onions tonight. It feels small enough that I can't come up with a good excuse not to try. And to be honest, talking through this today has been helpful—I never really looked at how I was treating that one bad memory as the whole truth about me. It is so rewarding to hear that you've found a small amount of space to breathe and that you feel less stuck, even if the nervousness remains. Hello, I'm really glad we can start our session today. To begin, could you tell me how you're feeling right now compared to when we started last time? Once I understand your mood, we can set an agenda together based on what matters most to you today.

That is a very common reaction when we feel hurt, and it's smart to notice that your instinct is to look for a reason that fits the pattern of "something is wrong with me." Does it feel possible that they might simply be in a state where they physically cannot send a thoughtful message yet, rather than deciding not to speak to you at all?

Maybe... I mean, I've definitely had days where I'm so swamped with orders at the bakery that I don't even look at my phone until I'm home and exhausted. But it's been a whole week, not just a day or two. That's what makes me think it's different this time.

It makes total sense that you're looking for a distinction between a normal busy day and a prolonged silence lasting a week; that duration does feel significant and unsettling. Let's test that specific thought together: if a friend was genuinely overwhelmed by work or family for seven days and simply didn't send a quick update until recently, would that necessarily mean you aren't interesting enough, or would it just mean they had nowhere to get a clear headspace to connect with you? But since they haven't said anything, my mind fills in the blanks with the worst reason. I guess I'd need to hear from them to really believe it wasn't personal.

That makes perfect sense; our brains are wired to fill gaps with the safest story available, and "not my fault" often translates to "my fault" when someone disappears. It is also important to recognize that you don't need confirmation from them to act kindly or test that belief—you can start by reaching out with a message that offers care without demanding an immediate explanation. Would you like to try drafting a text that checks in on them while removing the pressure for a quick reply, perhaps similar to saying, "Hey, I hope everything's alright with you? I could try that, I guess. It's just... I've already sent a few messages without getting replies, so sending another one feels like I'm bothering them. But maybe if I keep it light like that, it won't feel so heavy. I'll give it a shot.

That is a very fair concern; knowing you've been contacted before makes it easy to feel like you're crossing a line, but framing it as a gentle check-in rather than a demand actually lowers the risk of annoying them. Would you like to review that draft message together right now to ensure it lands softly, or would you prefer to write it down yourself to make it feel more authentic to you?

I think I'd rather write it down myself first, just so it feels like it's coming from me. But maybe I could read it to you after I'm done, just to see if it sounds okay? That way I know I'm not making it too heavy.

That is a wonderful approach; writing it yourself ensures it feels authentic, and reading it to me afterward lets us catch any unintended heaviness before you hit send. Go ahead and type it out whenever you're ready, and we'll take a quick look together once you've finished.

Alright, I've got something here. I wrote: "Hey, just wanted to see how you're doing. I know things can get busy, so no need to reply right away. Hope you're okay." It feels pretty simple, but I'm worried it still comes across as needy somehow. What do you think?

Hmm, maybe adding something about my baking could help. Like, "Hope you're okay. I've been experimenting with a new sourdough recipe, nothing special." That way it's not just about waiting for a reply, and it gives them something light to respond to if they want. Yeah, I think I'll send it like that.

I think I'm ready to send it. I'll do it now. Honestly, just writing it out with you has made me feel a little less anxious about it. I'm still nervous, but at least it doesn't feel as heavy anymore.

That honest admission—that the words feel hollow because they haven't taken root yet—is actually the most important clue. It shows that your brain is still holding onto the old story that this is a major failure, and it needs more concrete proof to let go of that fear. Instead of relying on a rehearsed phrase that feels robotic, what if we looked at the actual outcome of the breakfast instead? Did the kids eat the eggs, and were they happy or neutral about them?

They ate them without a word. No complaints, no funny faces, just finished up and grabbed their backpacks. Honestly, looking back, they didn't even seem to care. It was me standing there at the stove, stewing over something that was over and done with before I even noticed. So the outcome was fine—the only one upset was me.

Noticing that the children were completely indifferent to the mistake is powerful evidence that contradicts the belief that you've ruined everything. It proves that your perception of disaster was a distortion of the actual reality, which means the "catastrophe" you feared never actually happened. Given that the outcome was safe and normal, would you be willing to try grounding yourself in those facts right now by saying, "The kids are eating fine, and the meal was successful," instead of focusing on the texture of the eggs?

Yeah, I can try that. It's a hard shift, but saying it out loud feels a little more real than just keeping it in my head. "The kids are eating fine, and the meal was successful." Huh. It feels weird, like I'm lying to myself at first, but then I remember they really did eat and nobody yelled or got upset. Maybe I can practice that more—focusing on what actually happened instead of what I'm scared happened.

That is a fantastic realization—shifting from what you *scared* would happen to what *actually* happened gives you immediate control over the narrative. It sounds like you might want to try that exact sentence ("The kids are eating fine, and the meal was successful") the next time you feel that tightening in your chest, treating it as a factual reminder rather than a lie. Would you be open to trying that one sentence for the next time this happens, just to see if it settles the knot in your stomach faster?

Yeah, I'm open to trying that. It's not like I've got anything to lose by giving it a shot. I'll keep that sentence in my head next time I feel that knot tightening up. Maybe if I say it enough times, it'll start feeling less like a line and more like the truth.

That's a wonderful perspective, and I'm glad you see it as low-risk experimentation rather than forcing a rigid rule. Using that specific sentence repeatedly will gradually help your brain accept it as true, turning a rehearsed phrase into a trusted reality. Before we wrap up, I'd like to briefly revisit our goal: you wanted to understand why these mistakes feel so huge. Does exploring the difference between the actual outcome and your scary prediction feel like it helped answer that question today, or would you like to dig deeper into one more example?

I think it helped, honestly. Seeing that the real outcome was so different from what I expected—that's a new way of looking at things for me. I'd like to keep exploring that, maybe with another example next time, but for now, I feel like I've got something practical to hold onto. Thanks for walking me through it.

I'm so glad that shift in perspective felt useful for you; validating your own effort is often the hardest part, and you've shown great courage in noticing the gap between your fear and the reality. Before we finish, how does it feel to leave here with that one sentence as a tool you can rely on? Is there anything else weighing on your mind, or shall we close this session so you can rest easy knowing you have a new way to handle tomorrow's mistakes?

Hi. Thanks for asking. I guess I'm feeling a bit better today than I was when I first called, but it's still tough. Hearing that the "data" approach actually made you feel worse is incredibly important to unpack, because it tells us that simply labeling a mistake isn't enough when the underlying fear is still too loud. It was like a heavy weight in my chest, and my stomach just dropped. The voice was saying, "See? You can't even get through a simple piece. It makes complete sense that adding the word "data" made things heavier when your mind was already flooded with a narrative about being a fundamental failure. I... I think my body just shuts down. Because when I think about it, I wasn't lazy or avoiding it on purpose. I wanted to play—I really did. But as soon as my hands touched the keys, it felt like I was doing something wrong just by sitting there. Like the piano itself was judging me, and I'd rather walk away than hear that voice again.

That physical shutdown—wanting to play but your body refusing to move—isn't about laziness; it's your nervous system recognizing a perceived threat and pulling you away for protection. It feels like the piano itself is judging you because, in that moment, your mind had already decided that being there meant exposing a "flawed" mother. Can we explore what that feeling of being "judged by the instrument" represents? Does it feel like you expect the piano to reveal your hidden failures, or is it the expectation that anyone watching—even silently—will confirm that you aren't good enough?

I think it's the second one—that anyone watching will confirm I'm not good enough. Even if it's just me and my son in the room, I feel like he's waiting for me to mess up, to prove that I'm not the mom he deserves. And then I start thinking about how I'm supposed to be teaching him discipline and patience, but here I can't even handle my own frustration with a simple piano piece.

That feeling of having to perform perfection in front of him, while simultaneously expecting to fail, is an incredibly heavy burden to carry in real time. It seems like the standard you set for yourself ("teach him discipline") has become a trap that makes you feel incompetent the moment you encounter frustration. If we look at that specific conflict between your intention to teach and your inability to focus, does it feel like you are trying to prove your worth to him, or is it more like you are trying to silence the part of you that believes you can't meet his expectations?

I guess... I'm trying to silence that part of me. Because deep down, I already feel like I'm failing him, and if I can just get this one thing right—playing the piano well—then maybe I can prove that voice wrong. But it never works. The harder I try to push it away, the louder it gets, and then I'm just stuck again.

That desperate attempt to use the piano as a "proof" mechanism is so understandable, but it's often the very act of trying to prove it that fuels the fire of the doubt. It sounds like you're trapped in a loop where the goal becomes the obstacle, and the harder you push against that voice, the stronger its grip becomes. Instead of trying to silence it or prove it wrong with a perfect performance, could we try shifting the goal entirely—from proving your worth to simply observing your reactions as neutral data? What if, instead of trying to fix the mistake immediately, we just watched what happened without judgment, like a scientist recording observations rather than solving a crime scene?

That sounds... scary, honestly. Because if I just sit there and watch myself mess up without trying to fix it, doesn't that mean I'm giving up? But I also see what you're saying—I've been so focused on fixing every wrong note that I never just let myself be okay with making them. Maybe I could try that, just once. Like, next time I sit down, I'll just play and notice what happens without trying to change it. I'm not sure I can do it, but I'll try.

Taking a step back from the urge to fix everything and simply allowing mistakes to exist is indeed scary, but it's not giving up—it's giving yourself permission to be human instead of a flawless performer. By choosing to observe without intervening, you are actually reclaiming the power to decide how you respond, rather than letting your anxiety drive the game. Since you're open to trying this small experiment tomorrow, would you be willing to commit to sitting at the piano for just three minutes with that rule: whatever happens, you won't press your fingers to correct it until you've finished those three minutes?

Okay... three minutes. I can do three minutes. It sounds short, but I know it'll feel long. I promise I'll try to just sit there and let my fingers do whatever they want, even if it's messy. No fixing, no judging—just watching. I'll let you know how it goes.

That commitment to simply "letting your fingers do whatever they want" is a brave way to honor your own humanity, and knowing you have a strict three-minute boundary makes the task feel much more manageable. Remember, tonight isn't about producing a masterpiece or fixing anything; it's purely about witnessing whether that scary voice stays quiet or speaks up when you give yourself space to just be. How does that sound as a plan for tomorrow?

It sounds... doable. I think I'm actually a little curious now, which is strange. Usually I just dread sitting down, but this time I want to see what happens. If nothing else, at least I'll have something to tell you about next session, right? I'll do it tomorrow morning before work, when it's quiet. Thank you for helping me see it differently.

It is wonderful to hear that curiosity is growing, even though that usually comes after a breakthrough. Framing this as "something to tell you about" transforms it from a high-stakes performance into a low-risk scientific experiment, which lowers the pressure significantly. Going first thing in the morning before work is a smart choice to ensure you have that quiet space to explore those three minutes safely. I'm genuinely excited to hear what happens when you allow your fingers to just explore the keys without the pressure to fix them.

Thank you. I'll text you after I try it, if that's okay. Maybe just a quick note about how it felt. I think having that accountability will help me actually go through with it, instead of talking myself out of it. I appreciate you not pushing me too hard—just giving me a small step to take.

Absolutely, a quick text afterward would be perfect. Having that gentle accountability can bridge the gap between deciding to try and actually doing it, and it gives us a chance to celebrate the effort regardless of the outcome. Thank you for trusting me with this process and for being so open about your fears. I'll wait for your message, and I hope tomorrow morning brings a little relief.
Thanks. I'll reach out tomorrow. For now, I think I'm ready to head home and get some rest. Talking about this today helped, even though it was hard. I'll let you know how the three minutes go.

Resting your mind after such an intense conversation is incredibly wise, and I'm glad we reached a point where talking felt helpful rather than overwhelming. Please remember that tomorrow isn't about achieving perfection; it's just about honoring that three-minute window and noticing what arises, whatever it may be. I'll be here whenever you're ready to share how it went. Take good care of yourself tonight.

Welcome back; it is great to see you. Last time we worked on catching those moments when a small mistake felt like a giant catastrophe, and you practiced using a calm phrase to ground yourself. Hi. Thanks for having me back. My mood has been a bit up and down since we last spoke. I tried using that grounding phrase after I missed a pretty simple layup during a pickup game, and it helped a little in the moment, but later I just kept replaying it in my head. The top topics I'd like to focus on today are finding a way to stop that mental replay, and maybe talk about how this is starting to affect my confidence at work, too.

That is a really honest observation about the difference between getting relief in the moment and the struggle that comes later, and it tells me your brain is still looking for safety even after you've used the tool. Since you want to tackle that lingering replay loop and its impact on your work confidence, let's start by exploring what exactly you hear in that replay loop—does it sound like the coach criticizing you, or something more personal like a verdict on who you are?

It's definitely more personal than a coach's voice. I hear my own voice saying things like, "See, you always choke under pressure," or "You're just not a reliable player." It feels less like feedback on the play and more like a final judgment on me as a person. That's probably why it's so hard to shake—it feels like the truth.

That shift from "you made a mistake" to "you are unreliable" is exactly why the replay feels so sticky; your brain treats that personal verdict as a permanent fact rather than a temporary observation. When that voice convinces itself the truth, it becomes very hard to ignore because it aligns with your deepest fear that you aren't good enough. Have you noticed if that replay gets louder or longer when you are trying to do something productive afterward, like preparing for a work presentation?

Yes, absolutely. When I'm sitting down to work on a report or prepare for a presentation, that voice just gets louder and more insistent. It's like it takes the basketball mistake and uses it as proof that I'm going to mess up at work, too, so why even try? It makes me want to just shut my laptop and give up before I've even started.

That connection between the basketball court and your desk shows how your brain is using one isolated incident to predict an entire future of failure, which naturally drains your motivation before you even begin. It makes complete sense that the fear of repeating that mistake feels so paralyzing that avoiding the task seems safer than facing the uncertainty. When you tell yourself "why even try?" right before opening your laptop, what specific worry pops up in your mind about the worst-case scenario?

The worst-case scenario that pops up is that I'll be in the middle of presenting, and I'll stumble over my words or someone will ask a question I can't answer. I immediately picture everyone in the room looking at me like, "See? She doesn't know what she's doing." It's like I'm already being judged and found wanting, even before I've said a single word.

That image of everyone judging you before you've even started speaks volumes about how deeply feared being "found wanting" is for you, and it explains why your brain jumps straight to avoidance instead of preparation. It sounds like the fear isn't just about making a mistake, but about the shame of being exposed as inadequate in front of others. If we imagined a version of that presentation where you stumbled once but nobody cared, or where you got the answer slightly wrong but stayed calm, how would that change the feeling in your chest compared to your current worst-case scenario?

Honestly, that version feels almost impossible to imagine. When I try to picture people not caring or me staying calm, there's a small flicker of relief, but my chest still feels tight. It's like my brain doesn't have a blueprint for that scenario—it only knows how to play the disaster movie. I guess if I could believe that version was possible, the fear wouldn't feel so heavy.

You've done a fantastic job identifying that your brain currently lacks a script for anything but disaster, and that realization is the first step toward writing a new one. Instead of forcing yourself to visualize a calm scenario right away—which might feel too abstract and slippery—let's try something simpler: let's identify one small, realistic thing that *could* go wrong in that presentation, like stumbling over a word or forgetting a slide, and decide beforehand what you would say to yourself if that happened, without expecting perfection. Does that sound like a manageable first experiment to try?

That does sound a little more manageable, yes. Okay, so let's say I stumble over a word or lose my train of thought for a second. I think I could tell myself, "That's just a pause, not a failure. Keep going." It feels weird to even say that out loud, like I'm letting myself off the hook, but I guess that's the point.

That "weird" feeling is actually your old beliefs pushing back against the new choice, which means you are ready to learn something different. Even if that sentence feels awkward to say out loud, the power lies in just holding that intention for yourself whenever the tightness returns, rather than waiting until you are already in trouble. Let's try a quick mental rehearsal: close your eyes and imagine stumbling over one word mid-presentation, then immediately whispering that phrase to yourself. How does your body react when you say those words to yourself in that imaginary scene?

Okay... I'm trying it now. When I picture stumbling and then whispering "That's just a pause, not a failure," my shoulders drop a little, and I notice I'm not holding my breath as tightly. It's still a weird feeling, like I'm breaking a rule, but my chest doesn't feel as clamped down. It's a tiny bit of space, I guess.

Noticing that tiny bit of space in your chest is a huge win, because it proves that even a small amount of self-compassion can lower your physical alarm system. That "rule-breaking" feeling you mentioned is actually your brain testing whether you can survive a softer version of the story; the fact that your shoulders dropped shows you are already learning how to handle imperfection without collapsing. Now that we've rehearsed the feeling, what is one specific work situation coming up this week where you can try saying that phrase to yourself the moment you feel that tightness creeping in?

I have a team check-in meeting on Thursday where I'll need to update everyone on my project's progress. That usually triggers the tightness because I worry my numbers won't be perfect or someone will question my approach. I can try to whisper that phrase to myself right before I start speaking, or even in the middle if I feel that familiar panic rising.

Thursday's team check-in is a perfect place to test this because the stakes feel high enough to matter, yet manageable enough to practice. Whispering that phrase right before you open your slides acts as a mental reset button, shifting your focus from "proving I'm perfect" to "staying present while imperfect." Would you be open to rating your confidence in trying this specific experiment tonight, from a 0 to a 10?

I'd say my confidence is around a 5 or 6 right now. Part of me is curious to see if it actually helps, but there's still that voice telling me it's just a gimmick and won't really protect me from being judged. Still, a 5 is better than the 1 I would have given before this conversation.

That shift from a 1 to a 5 or 6 is a meaningful milestone, showing that you are actively moving toward trusting the tool even while doubting it. Remember, the goal isn't to silence the critical voice forever, but simply to create enough space to breathe and keep going when it does rise. Before we wrap up, how does it feel to have defined that specific Thursday scenario as your first real-world test of this new strategy?

It feels... nerve-wracking, but also a little hopeful. Having a specific plan in place makes it feel less like I'm just hoping to get through the meeting, and more like I have something concrete to try. I'm still scared I'll freeze, but at least now I know I have a phrase ready to catch myself with.

That mix of fear and hope is actually a very healthy sign that you are engaging with reality instead of hiding behind your fears; knowing you have a tool ready makes the unknown feel a little more manageable. You are taking the brave step of deciding to try the plan regardless of the risk of freezing, which proves your commitment to growth is stronger than your instinct to avoid discomfort. Is there anything else you'd like to add or clarify before we consider this part of our session finished?
No, I think I'm good for now. Thank you for helping me see that tiny bit of space and for turning Thursday into an experiment rather than a test I can fail. I'll let you know how it goes.

I am so glad we turned that big Thursday meeting into a small, manageable experiment; that shift in perspective is exactly what gives you permission to try even when you are afraid. Hello, it is wonderful to see you again. How have you been feeling since we last spoke, and is there anything specific on your mind you'd like to explore today?

Well, back then it was this sharp, immediate fear, like my heart was pounding and I couldn't think straight. Now, it's more like this heavy, sinking feeling that starts in my stomach the night before I even think about driving. It's not as loud, I guess, but it's still there, telling me to just give up and ask for help before I even try.

Noticing that shift from sharp panic to a heavy, anticipatory dread is a huge clue—it suggests your body is preparing you for a fight or flight response even before you leave the house. That "heavy" sensation is often your mind trying to protect you from the risk of embarrassment, even though it ends up trapping you instead. When you catch that urge to quit before you even start the engine, what do you tell yourself at that exact moment to slow down the spiral?

I usually tell myself, "You're going to get lost again, and you'll look foolish calling for help." It's like I skip to the worst part of the story before I've even turned the key. I guess I never really stop to question whether that's actually going to happen—it just feels so real in the moment.

It takes real courage to admit that your mind is jumping straight to the worst-case scenario before you've even started the journey. That automatic jump to "looking foolish" is a protective habit, but it feels very inaccurate when you consider how many times you've successfully navigated routes recently. If we were to pause for just five seconds before giving in to that thought, what evidence would you need to hear to believe you're capable of handling another trip?

I suppose I'd need to remind myself that I've actually driven to the pharmacy and back twice this month without any trouble. I mean, I made it there and home fine, even though I was nervous the whole time. Maybe that proves I can handle small trips, even if the farm one still feels like a big failure.

That is a very strong reminder of your actual capabilities, and noticing those two successful trips is the first step in balancing out that one difficult memory. It sounds like the farm incident feels disproportionately large compared to your consistent success on smaller, safer routes. If we tried to combine those two pieces of evidence—your recent safe drives and the knowledge that you've recovered from the farm panic—how would that change your prediction about what would happen if you sat in the car just for a few minutes today?

I think it would make me feel a tiny bit more open to the idea, like maybe I could just sit in the car and start the engine without planning a whole trip. I'd probably expect to feel anxious, but I could remind myself that I've handled that feeling before and still driven okay. It wouldn't erase the fear completely, but it might make it feel a little less like a mountain I can't climb.

That is a fantastic insight, and reframing the goal from "driving a trip" to simply "starting the engine and handling the anxiety" is a much more achievable step. It turns a daunting task into a manageable experiment where the only requirement is showing up and breathing through the discomfort. Since you mentioned starting the engine, what specific feeling do you hope to notice in your body during those first few minutes of ignition?

I think I'd hope to notice that my shoulders aren't completely tensed up to my ears, and maybe my breathing isn't so shallow. If I could feel just a tiny bit of calm, like my hands aren't gripping the wheel so hard, that would feel like a small victory. Honestly, just proving to myself that I can sit there without having a full-blown panic attack would be enough for now.

That is a brilliant and realistic definition of success; focusing on physical sensations like relaxed shoulders or steady breathing gives your mind something tangible to anchor itself on. If you commit to spending just five minutes in the car today and checking in on those physical cues whenever the thought of "getting lost" pops up, how does that sound as a plan for now?

It sounds manageable, actually. I think I can do five minutes without planning a route or going anywhere—just sitting there and letting myself feel whatever comes up. I'll try to keep my attention on my breathing and my shoulders, and see if I can prove to myself that it's not as scary as I've been making it out to be.

That is a wonderful commitment, and I'm so glad you feel ready to test it out. Remember, the goal isn't to eliminate the fear entirely right away, but simply to notice it without letting it dictate your actions. Is there anything else you'd like to share about how you're feeling before we wrap up today?

No, I think this is enough for now. I feel a little more hopeful than when I walked in, and I'm actually curious to see what happens when I sit in the car. Thank you for helping me break it down into something that doesn't feel impossible.

It is truly rewarding to hear that you feel more hopeful and ready to take that small step forward. You have done excellent work today by identifying your physical signs of stress and creating a simple, doable plan for tomorrow. Please remember that I am here anytime you want to share how the five minutes went or if that familiar "critical voice" decides to show up again. Take good care of yourself tonight, and I look forward to hearing from you when you are ready.

Hello again—I’m really glad to see you. How are you feeling today compared to last time? Before we dive into anything specific, is there a particular area you’d like us to focus on, such as reviewing the social experiment we tried, exploring those thoughts about being “broken,” or planning our next small step together?

Hi, thanks for asking. I think I'm feeling a little better than last time, but it's still pretty hard. I've been thinking a lot about that thought I have—that I'm just naturally bad at social stuff because I grew up without siblings. Maybe we could start there, because it just feels so true to me.

It makes complete sense that the thought about growing up alone feels so true to you, especially after seeing how quickly it popped up during the group study. When we hold onto a belief like that, it often acts as a filter that makes everything look like proof of it. Since you mentioned wanting to explore that specific belief, does it feel right to sit with that thought for a moment and ask yourself: if you weren't worried about being judged, what would you notice about your own ability to connect?

That's a really tough question... if I wasn't worried about being judged, I guess I would notice that sometimes people actually laugh at my jokes, or that I can keep a conversation going for a few minutes. But then I always think, well, that's just because they're being polite, or it's just small talk that anyone could do. I never let myself believe those moments are real proof.

That is such a honest observation—you clearly see the evidence that contradicts the idea that you are "broken," yet you tend to discount it as just politeness or luck. It feels like you are holding a lightbulb that shines bright spots on your skills, but then covering it up immediately. If we set aside the worry about judgment for just five seconds, how does noticing that people *do* respond positively, even briefly, change the feeling of being fundamentally different from others?

It's strange you put it that way... when you say it like that, I guess I can see that people do respond to me sometimes, even if I don't trust it. It makes me feel a little less like I'm on the outside looking in, like maybe I'm not as different as I think. But then that old thought creeps back in saying, "Yeah, but you're still an only child, you don't have the practice everyone else had," and it just overpowers everything.

That old voice comparing your life history to theirs is incredibly tempting because it feels logical on the surface, but it ignores the actual data from your interactions where people laughed and stayed engaged. Let's look at that comparison closely: what would need to be true for the belief "only children are naturally bad at socializing" to be correct, versus what evidence suggests otherwise?

Well, for that belief to be true, I'd have to believe that siblings are the only way to learn social skills, and that I never had any other chance to learn them. But I guess that's not totally true... I did have cousins I played with sometimes, and I've watched people my whole life, you know, like studying how they interact. And there are plenty of people with siblings who are just as awkward as I am, or worse. But still, it feels different for me, like I'm the only one who missed out on something essential.

You're absolutely right to notice that pattern—the feeling of missing an essential piece of development while observing others seems so unique to you. However, the fact that many people with siblings struggle similarly suggests that social skills aren't strictly tied to having brothers or sisters, but rather to opportunities and experiences we all create for ourselves. When you count your cousin interactions and your observations of others, does it start to feel like you've actually built a foundation, even if it looks different from theirs?

Hmm, I never really thought of it as building a foundation before. I always saw it more like I was just copying what I saw, like a fake version of socializing. But when you say it that way... yeah, I guess I did learn something from watching and from those few times with my cousins. Maybe it's not as solid as someone who grew up with siblings, but it's not nothing either. It's just hard to shake the feeling that I'm always a step behind everyone else.

That "step behind" feeling is so exhausting because it turns your entire past into a deficit rather than a unique path you've traveled. You've already gathered strong evidence that you *can* connect and that others respond positively; the gap between "watching" and "doing" isn't a permanent flaw, just a skill we all develop differently. If we accept that your foundation exists but looks different, does it become easier to separate your worth from your current level of comfort in conversation?

I think... I think maybe it does, a little bit. If I can see that my foundation is just different, not missing, then maybe I'm not broken after all. I'm just still learning, like everyone else, even if I started from a different place. It's still scary to think about talking to new people, but maybe I don't have to feel so ashamed about being nervous. Maybe that's just part of it for me.

That is a huge shift in perspective, and I want you to credit yourself for recognizing that nervousness is simply part of the process, not a sign of being defective. By viewing your journey as starting from a different angle rather than falling short, you've taken away some of the shame and kept the hope alive. Before we wrap up, does trying out that simple greeting in the hallway tomorrow feel like a manageable step forward with this new mindset?

Yeah, I think I could try that. Just a simple "hi" or "good morning" to someone in the hallway, without expecting anything more. And if I feel that old voice telling me I'm just pretending or that it doesn't count, I'll try to remind myself that it's still practice, even if it's different from how other people learned. Thank you for helping me see it that way.

You're welcome, and thank you for trusting me with this insight—it shows real courage to acknowledge that nervousness is just part of the human experience rather than proof of being broken. I'm glad that framing it as "practice with a different start" feels manageable for you today. Before we finish, is there anything specific about our work together today that felt particularly helpful, or is there anything you wish we hadn't touched upon?

I think the most helpful part was when you pointed out that I already have evidence of people responding positively to me, even if I always discount it. Hello, and welcome. To start, on a scale of one to ten, how has your mood been since we last spoke? Also, could you remind me what specific goals we agreed upon last time, and is there anything new you'd like to add to our agenda today?

A six is a reasonable starting point, but I completely understand why you're feeling that tightness at work; your brain seems to be hyper-vigilant, scanning for threats even when things are calm. That chain of events—from a nod to fearing termination—is a classic example of "catastrophizing," where your mind jumps straight to the worst possible outcome without looking at the middle ground. It sounds incredibly draining to carry that heavy load while serving people, knowing your brain is racing ahead before the interaction even ends. Can you remember one specific moment recently where that spin started, and what was happening around you right then?

Yeah, actually, just yesterday. This older guy came in, ordered a bacon cheeseburger, and when I handed it to him, he just grunted and took it to his table. He didn't say thanks or anything. That specific scene is so vivid because your brain took that single grunt and filled in every missing detail with the most painful story imaginable—it turned a simple nod into a secret threat of your job security. It sounds incredibly exhausting to keep checking his table and replaying that conversation long after the interaction was over. Let's go back to that exact moment: when he grunted and took the burger, what was the very first thought that popped into your head before you started checking his table?

That initial certainty—"He's disappointed"—is a perfect example of your brain skipping the evidence and jumping straight to a conclusion based on a feeling. It makes total sense that once that seed was planted, the rest of the negative story grew so fast because it confirmed your deepest fear. Now that we've pinpointed that first automatic thought, how does it feel to separate that initial judgment from the later, more detailed worries about your job?

It's... kind of weird, actually. I never really stopped to think that maybe the initial thought was separate from all the other stuff that came after. Noticing that gap is a massive breakthrough, and it makes perfect sense that you need a way to catch your brain before it slides into that full-blown panic again. We can treat that first thought not as a fact, but as a hypothesis that needs testing before we accept the rest of the story. Before we build the strategy, does the idea of pausing for just five seconds after handing over food—and then consciously choosing *not* to look at their reactions—sound like something you could actually try?

That's a really smart compromise—you're acknowledging the difficulty while finding a distraction method that fits your workflow. That is a solid plan, and I appreciate your willingness to face that slight discomfort just to gather real data instead of guessing. Before we wrap up, how confident are you that you can stick to this routine during a busy shift? On a scale of one to ten, what might be the one thing that could tempt you to skip it?

That honesty about the rush causing autopilot is incredibly valuable—it helps us anticipate the exact moment you might slip up. How does adding that "one breath" rule to your plan sound?

That "reset button" idea is a wonderful addition, giving you a clear signal to regain control even in chaos. That sounds... doable, actually. Ten minutes isn't too long, and I don't have to commit to anything. Just look and see if there's something that mentions those words. I think I can handle that. I'll try to do it tonight after my shift.

Yeah, I can message you after. That actually helps, knowing I just have to check in and not do anything more. And you're right, it's just ten minutes of looking. I'll try to remember that if the voice starts up. Thank you for making it feel less overwhelming.
