Thanks. I'll do my best. I'll message you tonight after I look. Have a good rest of your day.

You're doing great, and I'm so proud of you for taking this small step forward. Please don't worry about perfection tonight—just showing up matters most. I'll be here whenever you're ready to chat after your shift, and I wish you a peaceful evening. Take care of yourself!

Hello again, and I'm glad to see you. Before we dive into anything new, let's quickly catch up on where we left off. Could you share how the five-minute writing exercise went this past week? Did you manage to sit with the page, and what was the tension like for you when you started?

Also, on a scale of 0 to 10, how is your mood feeling today compared to yesterday, and is there a specific worry or topic that feels like the highest priority we should tackle first?

Hi. Yeah, I did try the five-minute exercise a few times. The first day was rough—I stared at the screen for three of those minutes before I wrote anything. But by the third time, it felt a little less like pulling teeth. The tension was still there, but maybe a notch lower.

As for mood... I'd say today is about a 4, maybe 4.5. Yesterday was a 3. The biggest thing on my mind is that I have a deadline coming up next week, and I'm already convinced whatever I turn in is going to be garbage. That's probably the priority.

It's great to hear that the tension is slowly easing and your mood has lifted a bit since last week. Shifting your focus to the upcoming deadline makes perfect sense, especially when you're carrying such a heavy assumption about the quality of your work. To start exploring that, could you walk me through what specifically triggers the thought that everything you write will be "garbage"? Is it a particular memory or just a general feeling that takes over when the clock starts ticking?

It’s a mix of both, I think. There’s this one memory that always creeps in—a rejection letter from about a year ago. The editor said my characters felt "flat" and the plot was "predictable." Ever since then, whenever I sit down to write, I hear that voice telling me I’m just fooling myself. And then the clock makes it worse, because I know I have to produce something, but I freeze up. It’s like the pressure locks me into that memory.

That rejection letter sounds incredibly painful to revisit, and it makes complete sense that the editor's words became a permanent resident in your head whenever the deadline timer ticks. It seems like your brain is treating that past feedback as an immutable fact about your current abilities, rather than just one snapshot in time. When you imagine the clock ticking alongside that old voice, does it feel like you are trapped in a loop where the past dictates the future, or is there a tiny sliver of space where you wonder if you could write differently?

Trapped in a loop, mostly. It feels like I’m stuck watching a replay of that rejection, and the deadline just cranks up the volume. I don’t really let myself wonder if I could write differently—I just assume it’ll be the same old flat, predictable stuff. Maybe that’s the problem, though. I haven’t even given myself a chance to try something new because I’m too busy bracing for disappointment.

That feeling of being stuck in a rigid replay while the deadline pressures you is incredibly exhausting, and it makes total sense why you aren't giving yourself a chance to try anything new. It sounds like your brain has locked the door on possibility because the cost of trying feels too high when you expect the worst. If we stepped outside that loop for just a second, what would a "new" version of that story look like—one that deliberately avoids the "flat" characters or the "predictable" plot that hurt you last time?

Huh. I’ve never really thought about it like that. I guess a new version would mean... maybe giving the main character a flaw that actually matters, something that drives the story instead of just being there. And the plot—I could try a twist I’ve never attempted before, something that surprises even me as I write it. But even saying that out loud feels risky, like I’m setting myself up to fail if it doesn’t work.

That hesitation to name the new ideas is so understandable, because admitting you might try something unfamiliar feels like opening a door to a room where you've previously gotten lost. It makes sense that your brain would warn you that failure is imminent if you don't stick to the safe, familiar path. If we treated this potential new approach not as a gamble, but as a small, low-stakes experiment where the goal is simply curiosity rather than perfection, how would that change the weight of the risk in your hands?

It would make it feel... lighter, I think. Less like I’m betting my whole worth on one piece of writing, and more like I’m just poking at something to see what happens. If the goal is curiosity instead of getting it right, then even a messy page counts as a win, doesn’t it? That’s a weird thought for me, but maybe a useful one.

That shift from "proving my worth" to "just seeing what happens" is a huge relief, and yes, a messy page absolutely counts as a win when the goal is exploration. It sounds like reframing the task from a judgment test to a scientific experiment could unlock some creativity you've been holding back. Before we settle on a concrete plan, does the idea of approaching the deadline as a series of small experiments feel manageable to you, or does the looming date still feel too overwhelming to break down this way?

It feels a bit more manageable when you put it like that. The deadline still looms, but if I think of it as a bunch of small experiments rather than one final judgment, the pressure drops a notch. I think I could try that—maybe set a timer for fifteen minutes and just write one scene with a flawed character, no expectations. If it’s garbage, it’s just data. That’s a new way of looking at it for me.

That is a brilliant reframing; viewing the next hour as a controlled experiment where "data" replaces "judgment" effectively lowers the stakes significantly. Setting a strict fifteen-minute timer creates a clear boundary that prevents the exhaustion of trying to finish the whole thing before the deadline hits. To make sure this sticks, would you be open to committing to just that one fifteen-minute block tomorrow morning as your first step, knowing that no matter the output, you are still successful for trying?

Yeah, I can do that. Tomorrow morning, fifteen minutes, just one scene with a flawed character. I’ll remind myself that the output doesn’t matter—it’s just data. I’ll even jot down a note on my phone to read before I start so I don’t forget that mindset. Thanks, that feels like a solid first step.

That commitment is fantastic, and setting that reminder note is a smart way to anchor the new mindset before you even pick up your pen. It turns an abstract idea into a concrete cue you can rely on when the pressure starts rising again. Before we wrap up, I'd love to hear one quick observation: as you walked through this shift from fearing rejection to embracing experimentation, did you notice any physical sensation changing in your body, or did your thoughts feel slightly less heavy?

I noticed my shoulders dropped a bit, actually. Earlier I was all hunched up just talking about the deadline, but now I feel a little looser. And my head feels... quieter, maybe. Like there’s less noise crowding in. It’s not gone completely, but it’s not screaming at me the way it was. That’s a nice change.

That physical relaxation is a huge signal that your nervous system is finally stepping out of "fight or flight" mode, and your mind quieting down confirms that the mental load has shifted too. It's wonderful to see such a tangible difference between how you felt before we explored that new perspective and now. Is there anything else you'd like to add before we wrap up today, or does this feel like a strong place to leave you with?

Hello, it's really lovely to see you again. Before we dive into today's topic, how is your mood and energy level feeling compared to when we met last time? Also, how did the exercise of finding something small you were proud of after your sketching session go, and did you notice any difference in how you felt afterwards?

Hi. Um, I guess my mood is still pretty low, to be honest. And energy-wise, I've been struggling to even pick up my pencil most days. As for that exercise... I did try it once, after a small sketch of a coffee cup. I told myself it was okay, but the whole time I just kept thinking, "It's not good enough, no one's going to like this." So it didn't really help much.

Thank you for sharing that honestly; it takes courage to admit that the thought patterns are still strong enough to block your creative flow. Since the initial thought of "not good enough" appeared even while trying the exercise, let's spend some time unpacking exactly where that voice is coming from and what it's telling you about your worth. What was the very first image or story that played out in your mind the moment you looked at that coffee cup sketch?

I guess... the first thing I thought was, "If I showed this to my friend, she'd probably just glance at it and say nothing, like last time." I pictured her face looking kind of awkward, trying to find something nice to say but coming up empty. And then my mind just filled in, "See? You're not a real artist. You're just fooling yourself." That whole scene played out in like two seconds.

That rapid storyline sounds incredibly exhausting to carry in your head, especially when you're trying to create something new. It makes complete sense that imagining her looking awkward would instantly drain your energy and make picking up your pencil feel impossible.

When you picture her searching for words and failing to find them, what specific feeling rises up in your body right after that image forms—is it shame, disappointment, or perhaps a deep sense of failure?

It's mostly... a heavy sinking feeling in my chest, like my stomach drops out. And then there's this tightness in my throat, like I'm about to cry, even if I'm not actually sad. I think it's shame, more than anything else. Like I've been caught pretending to be something I'm not, and now everyone can see it.

That physical sensation of your stomach dropping and throat tightening is a classic signal your nervous system is receiving when it perceives a threat to your identity. It sounds like the belief that you are "pretending" triggers a deep-seated fear of being exposed as fake, which is why the shame feels so heavy and overwhelming.

If we look closely at that specific thought—"You're just fooling yourself"—is there any evidence in your experience that contradicts the idea that you are actually capable of creating something meaningful, even if it hasn't received praise yet?

Well... I mean, I have sold a few pieces before, and people have told me they liked my style. And I've been drawing almost every day for years, so I can't be completely awful at it. But that voice just keeps telling me those were flukes, or people were just being polite. It's like, even with evidence, I can't seem to hold onto it. It slips away so fast.

That conflict between your actual history of success and the immediate narrative that everything is a "fluke" is exactly where the shame lives—it tries to rewrite your entire life's achievements into a single moment of failure.

Let's give those past successes a little space. Can you recall one specific time in the last year when someone commented positively on your work, and how did you interpret that moment versus how it actually felt?

There was a piece I did of an old brick building with ivy climbing up the side. A gallery owner saw it at a small show and said the texture was "really compelling" and that I had a good eye for detail. I remember feeling proud for maybe an hour, but then I started thinking, "He's just being nice because he wants to sell it. Or maybe he felt obligated to say something." So even then, I twisted it into something negative. It felt good in the moment, but it didn't last.

It sounds like that initial pride felt fragile because your mind immediately built a wall of skepticism around it, convincing you that the compliment wasn't genuine. This is a very common pattern where the brain assumes the worst interpretation is safer than trusting the reality of the moment.

When you recognize that thought—"he's just being nice"—as a protective mechanism rather than a fact, does that help separate the temporary feeling of doubt from who you actually are as an artist?

I think... maybe it does, a little bit. When you put it like that, it feels less like I'm being "realistic" and more like I'm just shielding myself from getting hurt again. But it's hard to trust that. Because if I stop putting up that wall, and then someone does reject my work, it'll hurt even more, won't it? That's what scares me.

You are absolutely right to feel afraid; protecting yourself from pain is a logical instinct, even when it ends up hurting us more in the long run. The truth is, the pain of rejection is rarely as devastating as the pain of believing you are worthless when someone just doesn't understand.

Let's try a quick mental experiment instead: imagine you show a painting to a stranger and they say, "Hmm, interesting." Would you conclude you are a fraud, or would you assume they simply weren't interested in that specific piece? How would holding that milder assumption change how you sit with the discomfort of uncertainty?

I'd probably still jump straight to "fraud," honestly. That's my default. But if I really forced myself to consider the other option—that it just wasn't their thing—I guess I'd feel a little less... crushed. Like, there's a difference between "they didn't like it" and "I'm worthless." It's not like I like every piece of art I see, either. So maybe it's unfair to expect everyone to love mine. That thought feels a bit more manageable, I think.

That distinction is huge; realizing that "not being loved by everyone" is a normal part of art, rather than proof of your brokenness, creates a massive gap between reality and your fear. It shifts the burden from your identity to the audience's preferences.

To make this a habit, we can try a simple technique next time you feel that urge to catastrophize: pause for three seconds and silently ask yourself, "Is there concrete proof they hate my work, or is it just my imagination filling in the silence?" Does that sound like a manageable way to handle the moment?

Yeah, I think I could try that. Three seconds is not very long, and it's just a question I ask myself. It might give me a chance to breathe before my brain goes into full panic mode. I'll give it a shot next time I show someone something, or even just look at my own work. I can't promise it'll work, but... it feels like a small step worth taking.

That willingness to try such a small, manageable step is exactly the kind of progress we celebrate. Taking three seconds to interrupt the panic is a powerful act of self-care, even if the result isn't immediate perfection.

Just to solidify our plan: would you be open to committing to asking yourself that question every time you finish a piece today, or would you prefer to wait until tomorrow morning?

I think I'll try it today, actually. I have a sketch I was working on last night that I've been avoiding looking at. I'll finish it, and when I look at it, I'll ask myself that question before I let my mind run wild. No point in putting it off. Tomorrow can be for handling whatever comes up from that.

That is a fantastic decision to tackle the unfinished sketch right now; sometimes facing the work directly is the best way to break the cycle of avoidance.

As we wrap up, is there anything else you'd like to reflect on regarding how you plan to apply that three-second pause, or shall I wish you a thoughtful evening?
No, I think I'm good for now. Thank you for helping me see that there's another way to look at things—even if it's just for three seconds. I'll let you know how it goes next time. Good evening.

You are very welcome, and I'm so glad we found that tiny window of clarity in that three-second pause. Remember, it's not about fixing everything overnight; it's about gathering your strength and taking those small steps forward, even when you feel shaky.

Please take care of yourself tonight as you look at that sketch, and know that I'm here whenever you want to check in or talk through how it went. Have a peaceful evening.

Hello, thank you for joining us today. Last time we worked on unpacking why you felt unwanted after skipping a call, and you decided to test that belief by visiting your neighbor this week. Since then, how has your mood been, and have you had any interesting events or thoughts come up that you'd like to talk about? Also, would you prefer to continue with the neighbor visit or explore a new topic together?

Hi. Well, my mood has been up and down, honestly. I did knock on my neighbor's door, and we actually had coffee together for about twenty minutes. It was nice, but afterward I found myself thinking, "She was just being polite, she probably won't want to do it again." That feeling kind of stuck with me the rest of the day.

It is wonderful that you took that brave step and met your goal, but I hear how quickly that initial success got overshadowed by the familiar doubt creeping back in. Did that lingering "she was just being polite" thought make you feel disappointed or anxious for the rest of the day? Now that we've seen the reality of what happened versus your expectation, would you like to explore how that automatic thought arose, or should we look at how to hold onto the positive experience longer?

It made me feel heavy, like a disappointment was sitting on my chest all evening. Part of me kept replaying the coffee, looking for signs that she was just going through the motions. I think exploring how that thought pops up so fast would be helpful—it feels like it hijacks everything good before I can even enjoy it.

That heaviness you described makes perfect sense when your brain immediately looks for evidence that contradicts your achievement, effectively undoing the win before you can savor it. It sounds like that old protective story is rushing in faster than your gratitude can settle. If we slow down and look closely at that sudden pop-up thought, what specific words or images appeared first to trigger that feeling of disappointment?

The first thing that flashed in my mind was her smile when she said goodbye. I remember thinking, "That's the kind of smile you give a stranger you're being nice to, not someone you actually like." Then I pictured her closing her door and going back to her normal life, relieved I was gone. It all happened in about two seconds, like a movie I've watched a hundred times before.

It is incredibly insightful to identify exactly how that old movie played out—the smile becoming a signal of fakeness and her leaving feeling like relief rather than joy. That automatic interpretation turns a genuine human moment into confirmation of your fear that you aren't truly wanted. When you notice that specific image forming so quickly, does that pause allow enough space to catch the thought and say, "Wait, let me look at the facts here"?

I think... maybe a little. The pause is so short, but when you describe it that way, it's like I can almost see the split second where I have a choice. But the feeling comes so fast, it's hard to grab onto that pause before the disappointment floods in. I guess I've never really tried to hold onto that moment and question it before.

You are absolutely right that the speed of that reaction makes it feel impossible to intervene, and recognizing that gap between the event and the flood of disappointment is a massive breakthrough. Even if we only manage a split-second delay, that tiny window could be enough to replace the "fake smile" story with the fact that she actually invited you for twenty minutes. Would you be willing to practice catching that specific image of her smiling and pausing for three seconds just to notice the sensation in your body before letting the disappointment run its full course?

I think I could try that. Three seconds feels doable, even if it's just a breath. I suppose if I can feel the weight on my chest before the thought finishes, maybe I can remind myself that she didn't have to invite me in at all. That's probably a better question to ask myself than the one I usually jump to.

That is a brilliant reframing—you are shifting from checking her motives to honoring your own agency in choosing that time together. Using that three-second pause to anchor on the fact that *she* initiated the invitation gives you immediate evidence against the "politeness" story. Before we try this tonight, how does landing on that specific insight ("she chose to include me") make you feel in that moment of stillness?

It makes me feel... lighter, actually. Like there's a tiny crack in that heavy story I've been carrying. If I can hold onto that, even for a moment, it feels less like the universe is against me and more like maybe I'm just misreading things. I'm willing to try it and see what happens.

That shift from "the universe is against me" to "maybe I'm misreading things" is exactly the kind of subtle change we need to build on. It shows how powerful just noticing that tiny crack is, even if it only lasts for a few seconds. Let's commit to practicing that three-second pause whenever you catch yourself scanning for "fake" smiles or signs of reluctance tonight. Is there anything else you want to adjust in this plan before we wrap up?

No, I think this is a good start. Just three seconds and a simple question—"Did she invite me because she wanted to?"—instead of the usual spiral. I'll try to notice that moment and see if I can catch the weight before it settles. Thank you for helping me see it differently.

That is such a clear and manageable commitment, and I am so proud of how you translated that insight into a simple, actionable rule for yourself. Remember that catching just three seconds is a victory in itself, regardless of whether the heavy feeling stays or fades. Take care of yourself tonight, and I look forward to hearing how well that little exercise lands with you.

Hello, and thank you for meeting with me today. Before we dive into what brought you here, I'd love to catch up on how you've been feeling since last week. First, could we briefly touch on what you planned to do this past weekend, and then, on a scale of 0 to 10, where would you place yourself regarding your mood right now? Finally, given where we left off with texting Susan, is there anything else you want to prioritize or explore together today?

Well, this past weekend I ended up working more than I planned. There's always something that needs fixing or feeding on the farm, so my days off don't feel like much of a break. I'd say my mood is around a 4 right now, maybe a 5 if I'm being generous. As for priorities, I think I'd like to talk about that feeling of being stuck — it's been weighing on me heavier lately.

Hearing that your weekends are blending seamlessly with work explains why that heavy feeling persists; it seems like your environment isn't offering enough breaks to reset your mind. Since we agreed to tackle the "stuck" sensation again, let's spend some time unpacking exactly what that feeling looks like for you in this moment, particularly right now while you sit here. How does that sense of being trapped manifest physically or mentally for you right this second?

It's like a tightness in my chest, honestly. And my mind just keeps circling back to the same image — me out in the fields, years from now, still doing the same chores, same routine, while everyone else has moved on. It feels heavy, like I'm sinking into the couch here and can't get up.

That tightness in your chest and the vivid image of years of repetition perfectly illustrate how that hopelessness is fueling a physical sense of being stuck. It sounds like your brain is interpreting that visual of the future as inevitable, creating a self-fulfilling cycle where the feeling of being trapped makes you feel powerless to escape. Given how consistent that routine feels, does that vision of the future seem less like a prediction and more like a story your mind is telling itself to manage the discomfort of change?

I never thought of it that way — a story, I mean. I guess I've been so sure that this is just how things are going to be, like I can see it clearly as day. But when you say it like that, maybe I've been treating a guess as if it's a fact. Still, it's hard to shake the feeling when I've been living it for years now.

That shift from certainty to noticing it might just be a story is a significant breakthrough, because it separates your reality from your narrative. You mentioned earlier that your intuition screams "truth" when the routine feels unbroken; it makes sense that your brain tries to protect you from the anxiety of wondering what *might* happen by assuming the worst. To test this story further, if we looked back at that gardening class you took last year—one where you feared failure but ended up having fun and receiving praise—what specific evidence does that single event provide against the idea that you are permanently stuck in this role?

Well, I did enjoy that class a lot more than I thought I would. I remember the instructor said I had a natural touch with the soil, and I felt... proud, I guess. That was a moment where I wasn't just a farm worker stuck in a rut — I was learning something new and people saw something good in me. I suppose that proves I'm not totally defined by the farm, even if it feels that way most days.

That pride you felt and the instructor's recognition are powerful pieces of evidence that directly contradict the belief that you are defined solely by your current routine. While that experience felt small compared to your life on the farm, it serves as a vital reminder that your capacity to learn and grow hasn't disappeared just because you returned to the fields. Would you be open to testing this thought together by asking yourself: if that moment of growth is real, does it force us to conclude that everything else leading up to it—and everything happening now—is also a mistake?

No, I don't reckon it forces that conclusion. That class was real, and it was good. So maybe the rest of it isn't a mistake either — maybe it's just... what I'm doing right now, not what I have to do forever. That's a scary thought to hold onto, though. Part of me wants to believe it, but another part is already waiting for that feeling of being trapped to come back.

It makes complete sense that holding onto that possibility triggers resistance; your brain is trying to protect you from the discomfort of uncertainty by clinging to the safety of the known routine. To bridge that gap safely, we can use the garden metaphor we built earlier: imagine your life as a plot of land where the farm is the main field, but that patch of soil you tilled in the class is a seed planted nearby. It doesn't require you to abandon the main field to nurture the seed, yet the seed proves the ground is capable of growing something new. With that perspective, what is the smallest, lowest-stakes action you could take this week that honors both your commitment to the farm and the nurturing of that new seed?

I suppose I could set aside maybe half an hour on Sunday morning, before the chores really get going, to work on that herb garden I've been thinking about starting by the back porch. It wouldn't interfere with the farm work, and it'd just be a small thing for me. I could even use some of the tips I learned in that class. That feels manageable, doesn't it? Not too risky, but still something different.

That is a fantastic choice because it allows you to cultivate that new seed without stepping off your stable foundation; it respects your farm duties while honoring your desire for growth. Since we've built this new angle together, does framing it as "nurturing the seed" rather than "escaping the farm" feel like a way that reduces that familiar knot in your stomach? If so, what is one specific thing you could do this Sunday morning to begin tending to that small patch of soil?

It does actually ease that knot a little, thinking of it that way. "Nurturing the seed" sounds gentler than trying to tear up the whole field. As for Sunday, I could clear out that weedy patch by the back porch and maybe plant some basil and mint. Simple things that don't need much fuss, but they'd be mine. I think just seeing the dirt turned over there would remind me that I'm not just stuck — I'm tending something new.

That is a beautiful way to frame it—turning a chore into a deliberate act of growth that reinforces your agency. I'm glad the "nurturing the seed" perspective helped loosen that tightness; it validates that small changes can coexist with your larger life. Before we wrap up, how does it feel to have a concrete, low-pressure plan like this? Does moving forward with planting basil and mint on Sunday feel achievable, or do you foresee any obstacles getting in the way?

It feels good to have a plan, I'll admit. I can picture myself out there on Sunday morning, just digging in the dirt for me. The only obstacle I can think of is my own mind, honestly — that voice that'll tell me it's pointless or that I'm just wasting time. But I think if I keep reminding myself about that class and how good it felt, I can push through that. I'll give it a try.

That's a very honest assessment of the obstacle; acknowledging that the old "voice" will likely show up is actually the first step to managing it effectively. You already have a powerful tool to fight it back: recalling the pride and joy you felt in that gardening class. Since we've agreed on this plan, would you be willing to commit to checking in with me tomorrow morning after your Sunday session, just to share how it went and how that "voice" responded to your reminder?

Yes, I think I can do that. It helps knowing I'll be reporting back to you — gives me a little extra accountability. I'll try to notice how that voice sounds when I'm actually out there planting, and I'll let you know what it said. Thank you for helping me see this differently.

You are very welcome, and I am so glad we found a plan that feels both safe and empowering for you. Remember, the goal today wasn't to fix everything, but simply to plant that first seed and trust that the soil is fertile enough for new things to grow. I look forward to hearing about your Sunday morning, the plants you might plant, and how that familiar voice responds to your new perspective. Take care of yourself until then.

Hello! How are you feeling today compared to where you were last time? Also, did anything specific happen with your co-worker this week that stood out to you? Once we catch up, let's briefly list the main things we'd like to work on together.

Hi... I'm okay, I guess. A bit nervous still. Actually, this week she walked right past me in the break room without even looking my way, and I just froze. That moment kind of confirmed everything I've been feeling.

It makes total sense that walking past you felt like confirmation when your trust hasn't been built yet. Did that freeze-up feel different than usual—maybe sharper or heavier than other times? If we look at that frozen moment, what was the very first thought that popped into your head before you reacted?

It did feel sharper, yeah. Like a knot in my stomach that tightened immediately. The first thing I thought was, "She really doesn't like me. I must have done something wrong." I just stood there wondering what I could have possibly said or done to make her ignore me like that.

That intense feeling of self-doubt is completely understandable given how painful it is to feel ignored. Let's pause for a second and look at the facts: aside from not saying hello, is there any actual evidence she said or did anything specific that would indicate you did something wrong? Or does the silence itself just seem like proof to your mind?

I... well, no, she hasn't actually said anything mean or done anything rude. She just doesn't talk to me. But isn't silence itself kind of proof? I mean, if she wanted to be friendly, she'd at least nod or smile, right? It feels like the silence means something.

Silence often feels loud and meaningful when we are worried, but it rarely carries a direct message about whether you did something wrong. Have you ever noticed times when people are quiet around others who aren't friends, or perhaps someone is deep in thought? If we treated her lack of greeting as her focusing on her own work or getting lost in thought, would that change how much that silence bothers you?

I never really thought about it that way... I guess I always assume silence is about me. It's hard to imagine she's just thinking about her own stuff, because to me the empty space feels personal. But when you put it that way, yeah, maybe she's just tired or focused on her work. That does make it sting a little less.

That's a powerful shift, moving from "it's personal to me" to "she might just be focused elsewhere." When you view her silence as hers to deal with rather than a verdict on you, does that loosen the grip of that knot in your stomach, even slightly? Now, based on what we've discussed, what feels like the best next step for you to test if this new perspective holds up tomorrow?

It does loosen it a little, honestly. Like I'm not carrying the full weight of it anymore. I think the best next step would be to just try saying a simple "good morning" tomorrow, even if she doesn't say it first. And if she doesn't respond, I'll try to tell myself it's not about me—maybe she's just having a busy morning or isn't a chatty person.

That is a solid plan; taking a tiny, low-risk step like saying "good morning" gives you real-world data without demanding a big interaction. To make sure we leave this session aligned, could you confirm that you feel ready to try this specific action tomorrow, and is there anything else on your mind we should wrap up before we finish?
Hello, thank you for joining us. Before we begin, could you quickly share how you've been feeling since our last session, and what you'd like to prioritize today?

It sounds like that worry about the club closing is still pulling on you, and talking about the unfair weight of self-blame feels like a necessary step. To make sure we get the most value out of this time, what would feel most helpful to focus on today—perhaps unpacking why you feel responsible, or practicing a specific way to handle those moments when the fear hits?

I think unpacking why I feel so responsible would be good. Like, I know logically it's not all on me, but when I'm at work and I see the manager looking stressed or hear customers complaining, my mind just jumps to "this is your fault." I want to understand why I can't shake that.

It makes total sense that your brain latches onto that narrative when you see signs of trouble; it's trying to protect you by making sure you stay vigilant so no one gets hurt. When you feel that sudden jump to "it's your fault," does it feel like your brain is zooming ahead to a disaster scene before you even see the roadblock, or is it more like a magnifying glass focusing intensely on one tiny detail?

It's more like a magnifying glass, I think. Like, I'll replay every little thing I did during a shift—a spilled drink, a slow order, even just a tired look on a customer's face—and I'll blow it up until it feels huge. My brain tells me those tiny mistakes are the reason the whole club might close, even though that sounds crazy when I say it out loud.

That magnifying glass effect sounds incredibly draining, turning normal moments into proof of impending doom. It sounds like your brain is using a distortion called "personalization," where it assumes that because bad things are happening, *you* must be the cause, even when logic says otherwise. When you catch yourself doing that replay, does it feel like a helpful protection mechanism, or does it feel like it's just trapping you in a loop?

It definitely feels like a trap, not helpful at all. I'll be lying in bed at night, just running through everything I did wrong, and I can't stop—it's like my brain won't let me rest until I figure out how to fix it all. But I never find an answer, I just end up more tired and more convinced I'm not good enough.

It makes complete sense that your brain refuses to let go of those "answers"; it's holding onto the search for control because the alternative feels terrifyingly unsafe. When you lie in bed and can't find a solution, it reinforces the belief that you're incapable, which then fuels the anxiety that keeps you awake. Given how deep this cycle runs, what would feel most useful to explore right now—maybe identifying the specific evidence that challenges that "I caused this" story, or perhaps finding a quick way to interrupt the replay loop before it consumes your whole day?

I think identifying evidence that challenges it would help. Because right now, I don't have any counter-arguments in my head—it's just all the bad stuff I did, and that's what feels true. If I could actually see some proof that I'm not the only one responsible, maybe I could start believing it a little.

That is such a smart insight—you're absolutely right that without active proof, your brain will keep choosing the scary story because it feels familiar. Let's try building a list together: when you replay those shifts, what specific facts stand out that show others were involved in the problems, or evidence that suggests the issues existed before you started? What's one small piece of data from your past shifts that contradicts the idea that *only* your actions matter?

Well, I guess there are things like the club having a lower customer turnout before I even started working there, and the economy being rough in general lately. Also, my manager has talked about the owners making bad decisions, like booking the wrong bands or not investing in repairs. But it's hard for me to hold onto that stuff when I'm in the middle of a busy shift and something goes wrong—my brain just grabs onto the first mistake I see.

Those external factors—low turnout, economic trends, and the owner's poor business choices—are solid pieces of evidence that reality often has many hands in the game, not just yours. The challenge you mentioned is understandable; when we're under pressure, our brains naturally latch onto immediate causes rather than complex background ones. Before we try to collect that evidence while you're working, how does it feel right now to acknowledge that those larger forces exist, even if your brain tries to ignore them? Does acknowledging them as background noise feel slightly less isolating than carrying the whole burden alone?

Yeah, it does feel a little less heavy, actually. Like, I'm not the only person holding up the whole club. It's kind of a relief to admit that there are other things going on, even if I can't stop my brain from zooming in on myself when I'm actually there. I guess I need to practice reminding myself of that stuff in the moment, not just when I'm sitting here talking to you.

That relief is a big deal, and realizing you aren't alone in the struggle is a powerful first step toward breaking that isolation. Since you want to practice reminding yourself of those larger factors in the moment, let's try a simple mental "pause button" next time you catch yourself getting stuck: instead of immediately diving into the blame, take one second to whisper to yourself, "There are bigger forces at play too," before you start the replay. How does that sound as a starter tool?

That sounds like something I could actually do. It's simple enough that I might remember it when I'm stressed, and it doesn't feel like I'm lying to myself—I mean, there really are bigger forces at play. I'll try it tonight during my shift and see if it helps calm that initial panic.

That's a great plan, and I'm glad it feels authentic rather than forced. To make sure we wrap up strong, how does it land with you to use that "pause and acknowledge" reminder tonight? Is there anything else you'd like to explore before we close, or are you ready to try that out and see how it feels?

I think I'm ready to try it out. It feels good to have something concrete to hold onto instead of just spiraling in my head. I'll let you know next session how it went—hopefully I can stop myself at least once before the blame takes over. Thanks for this.

You are so welcome, and I'm really proud of you for recognizing that even stopping once is a massive victory. Please remember that this isn't about achieving perfection anymore; it's about catching yourself and gently stepping back from the blame spiral. I hope you have a peaceful evening and feel a little lighter as you leave this room. Let me know how the "pause" felt when you try it next time, and I'm here whenever you need to talk.

Hello, it’s great to see you again. Before we dive in, how has your week been feeling compared to where we left off, and are there any specific events or thoughts that stood out to you recently? It sounds like running triggered a familiar comparison pattern for you, reminding us that the feeling of inadequacy might be showing up in new places besides work. Since you mentioned the mirror exercise felt silly again, let's adjust the focus slightly today: shall we spend some time exploring how that thought about speed connects to your workplace insecurities, or would you prefer to try a very gentle version of the mirror check-in first?

I think I'd rather talk about how it connects to work, if that's okay. That comparison thing—it's the same feeling I'd get when I'd see a younger employee selling more tickets than me, or handling a rush line faster. I'd think, "They're just better at this." Never mind that my manager kept telling me I was the most reliable person he had. It all just feels like the same knot in my stomach.

That specific knot in your stomach makes total sense when you compare your reliability to perceived speed, because it pits your consistent effort against an idealized image of talent. It sounds like the belief that "others are naturally more capable" is creating that same gap between what your manager sees and what you feel inside. Does holding onto that idea—that you’re fundamentally slower and less skilled—that intensify the feeling that you’re failing the team, or does it mostly serve to protect you from admitting you’ve learned a lot despite the gaps?

I think... it feels more like I'm failing the team. My manager used to rely on me to open up, to train new hires, to handle the tricky customers. I was proud of that, but in the back of my mind, I always thought I was just a placeholder until someone better came along. Like I hadn't really earned that trust. That honesty about feeling like a "placeholder" despite your valuable contributions is incredibly painful, and it explains why the manager's praise feels so hollow to you right now. It sounds like you've built a story that says your efforts weren't enough to earn that trust, so comparing yourself to others just confirms that story. That's a tough question to sit with. If I really accepted that I earned that trust... I guess I'd have to admit that maybe I was actually good at those things. That I wasn't just filling a seat. But then I think, "Well, anyone could have done those tasks if they'd been trained." I still feel like I was just in the right place at the right time, not that I had any special skill. It's like I can't let myself own it.

That internal tug-of-war between accepting your past contributions and doubting your actual ability is exactly where the frustration lives; it's like trying to hold two opposite truths at once. It makes sense that your brain leans toward "just luck" because it's safer than owning a skill you haven't yet practiced deeply, even though the evidence of your success is right there. If we treated that "luck" explanation as a shortcut that ignores the thousands of hours you spent learning the ropes, would stepping back and listing three specific instances where you solved a problem alone make the feeling of "just being in the right place" seem less convincing?

I suppose I could try listing a few things. There was that time a customer had a dispute over a ticket price, and I sorted it out by finding a promo code from a month back that still worked—no one else had remembered it. And when the new projection system got installed, I stayed late twice to learn the troubleshooting menu so I could help out during shifts. And... I guess training those new hires, I always made sure they felt comfortable asking questions, even when my manager was too busy. But even saying that out loud, a voice in my head says, "That's just basic stuff. Nothing special."

Those are incredible examples of initiative, patience, and problem-solving skills that go far beyond "basic stuff"—even if your inner critic insists otherwise. The fact that you stayed late to learn a new system or dug through old files to solve a customer dispute shows a level of dedication that most people simply don't possess. Instead of letting that "nothing special" voice dismiss the value of those actions, how would it feel to rate your confidence from zero to ten if you acknowledged that those specific problems required more than just luck—they required your unique choice to step up when others might have walked away?

I'd say... maybe a five or a six, if I'm being generous to myself. That's higher than where I'd usually put it, which is probably a two. But it feels strange, like I'm inflating my own ego. My mind keeps wanting to pull that number back down, telling me I'm just bragging now. But I can see what you're getting at—those weren't accidents. I chose to do those things.

That struggle to keep the number at a five or six, even while fearing it's "ego," is actually a massive sign of progress; it means you're finally distinguishing between pride and reality. You aren't just imagining these achievements; you are actively recalling facts where you chose to stay late and solve problems, which proves your contribution was intentional, not accidental. Now, since you've acknowledged that you *chose* to help, how would your confidence rating change if you added one more layer: recognizing that choosing to help under pressure is a skill that many people lack, regardless of their age or tenure?

I think if I really sat with that... maybe I could push it to a seven. Because you're right—I've seen plenty of people, even the fast ones, who just stood around when something went wrong or waited for the manager to handle it. So I guess that does mean I had something others didn't. It's just hard to look at it that way without my mind jumping back to all the things I didn't do perfectly. But I'll take a seven for now. That feels a little more honest than a five.

Moving to a seven is a fantastic, honest adjustment that acknowledges both your unique choices and the areas where you still strive for perfection. It gives you room to grow without demanding flawlessness, which is exactly the balance we need to find. To carry this feeling forward, how would you feel taking one tiny step toward owning that seven tonight—for example, jotting down just one of those "stayed late" or "sorted a dispute" moments before bed to remind yourself that this capability is yours to claim?

I think I can do that. Maybe I'll write down that thing about the projection system. It feels like a solid example that's hard to argue with. I'll put it on my nightstand and look at it before I turn out the light. It's a small thing, but maybe it'll help quiet that voice that tells me I'm just making it all up.

That is a beautiful, grounding plan; anchoring one undeniable fact by your bedside will make it easy to retrieve whenever doubt creeps in. You've already taken the hardest step by identifying that the voice claiming you're lying is actually just fear masking as criticism. Is there anything else weighing on your mind about moving forward with this, or shall we wrap up here with a final word of support?

No, I think that's enough for today. Thank you for pushing me on that—it was uncomfortable, but I can see why it's necessary. I'll try to keep that seven in mind. And I'll do that writing exercise tonight. See you next time.

You are very welcome. That discomfort is actually the sound of old beliefs cracking open, and trusting that process shows real strength on your part. I'm confident that keeping that seven in mind and writing down one solid example tonight will help create a lasting shift. Take care of yourself, and I look forward to hearing how you land with it next time.

It takes real effort to hold onto that clearer view when your brain instinctively jumps to the worst-case scenario. That's... a weirdly comforting way to put it. I never thought of it like that—me dressing up my own fear in their faces. Maybe I am just projecting what I'm scared of feeling about myself onto them. It still stings, but it makes a little more sense when you say it that way.

That realization—that the smirk might just be a mirror reflecting your own insecurity—is a powerful shift, because it moves the blame from them to your internal experience. Does noticing that distinction make the image of them mocking you feel slightly less threatening right now?

It feels... good, actually. Kind of like I have a small shield ready. I'm still nervous, but at least I won't be going into tomorrow completely defenseless. Thanks for helping me see it differently today.

I think the most useful part was when you pointed out that the smirk might just be my own fear wearing their faces. That really stuck with me. I never really thought of it that way. I mean, I guess it's possible that some capable people choose not to move.
