Hi. Well, I'm here, so that's something. I did try that gentle question you suggested—asking myself "is this really as bad as it feels?"—and it helped a little on the first part of the trail. But by the end, the soreness was just... there, and I couldn't shake the thought that it's only going to get worse. I guess I'd like to figure out why I keep focusing on the pain instead of the good parts of the hike.

It takes courage to try the question even when the old habit tries to pull you back in. You noticed a very important detail—that while the check-in helped initially, the worry about worsening pain eventually took over, pushing the focus entirely toward discomfort. When you say you want to figure out why the pain grabs your attention so strongly, what comes up for you when you look at those moments where the "good parts" of the hike feel invisible?

Honestly, it feels like the good parts just don't count as much. Like, I can have a beautiful view or a great conversation with a friend on the trail, but the second I feel that ache in my legs, it's like none of that matters anymore. It's as if the soreness is the only real thing, and everything else is just temporary or fake.

That sensation of the pleasant things fading into the background, leaving only the physical discomfort as "real," points to a pattern where your brain is filtering out positive details once the warning signal appears. It sounds like you are unconsciously deciding that the pain is the only truth worth attending to, effectively dismissing the beauty and connection you experienced just because of the ache. Can you tell me what usually happens right after you notice that ache taking over—is it that the memory of the nice moment suddenly feels hazy, or does your mind actively ignore it to focus solely on the pain?

It's more like the nice moment gets erased, or at least it feels that way. I'll be halfway down the trail, my legs are burning, and I can barely remember the summit view or the joke my friend told. It's like the pain writes over everything else, and all I'm left with is this heavy feeling that hiking just isn't worth it anymore. And then I start thinking, "If I can't even enjoy hiking now, what else is going to fall apart?"

That image of the painful sensations literally "writing over" your memories is powerful, and it perfectly illustrates a common pattern called selective attention, where your brain filters out the positives once the threat signal arrives. Because you've learned to associate pain with disaster, your mind shortcuts itself to assume that if the pain is present, the whole experience—and perhaps your ability to handle challenges generally—is ruined. Does that shortcut feel helpful in protecting you from disappointment, or does it mostly serve to amplify your anxiety?

I guess it's supposed to protect me, but it doesn't feel that way. It just makes me dread the next hike before I even start. I end up thinking, "Why bother if I know I'm just going to end up miserable and sore?" So I guess it's more like it amplifies the anxiety, not protects me from anything. I never really thought of it as a shortcut before—it just felt like the truth.

That realization—that the protection mechanism is actually fueling your dread—is a crucial turning point. It highlights how your brain, in its attempt to safeguard you from past disappointments, has ended up building a bridge straight to anxiety instead. Now that we've seen how the pain hijacks your focus and distorts the value of your experience, how might we shift that lens slightly so you can remember the beauty alongside the burn? Perhaps we could try treating the ache as a separate event from the joy you already earned, rather than letting it erase it.

I like the sound of that—treating the ache as separate. It's like I've been letting the pain rewrite the whole story, but maybe I can keep the two things apart in my mind. Maybe I could try, on my next hike, to consciously note one good thing every time I feel that soreness starting, like a kind of counterbalance. It feels weird, but I'm willing to give it a shot.

That is a wonderful strategy—creating a deliberate "counterweight" to the negative story. Instead of letting the ache define the entire experience, you will actively anchor yourself to a specific piece of evidence (a view, a laugh, a feeling) whenever the alarm goes off. It's like reminding your brain, "Yes, there is pain, but here is also proof that this was a meaningful time." Before we finalize this plan, how does the idea of intentionally naming a "winning moment" feel safe to you, and do you see any potential hurdles that might make it hard to stick with?

It feels a little forced, if I'm being honest—like I'm tricking myself. But I guess that's the point, right? Retraining my brain. The biggest hurdle I see is that when the soreness is really bad, I just want to give in to it and stop fighting. It takes a lot of energy to push back against that feeling, especially when I'm already tired. But I think I can try it for one hike and see what happens.

That honesty about feeling "forced" is incredibly valuable—it shows you're listening closely to your internal resistance rather than forcing a technique that feels unnatural. Acknowledging that energy conservation is real, not just a barrier, helps us frame the counterbalance as a tiny effort to preserve the memory of the good, rather than a fight against exhaustion. Let's lock in this plan: on your next hike, as soon as you feel the first significant ache, you'll name one specific thing you enjoyed (even if it's just the smell of pine) before the dread takes over. Is that clear, and do you feel ready to try this specific sequence once more?

Yes, I think I can do that. One thing, one moment, right when the ache starts—I'll grab hold of a good detail before the dread floods in. It feels like a small enough step that I can manage it, even when I'm tired. I'm ready to give it a real try on my next hike.

That is a smart way to frame it—grabbing a specific detail acts like a quick anchor to hold onto the positive before the tide of dread pulls you under. Taking that small step to reconnect with a good memory is exactly how we begin to rebuild trust in the experience, even when the body is tired. Please remember to send me a quick update after your next hike about how that "one good thing" landed for you and whether it helped shift the focus. How are you feeling right now knowing you have a clearer path forward?

I feel a bit lighter, honestly. Like I have something concrete to do instead of just bracing for the pain. It's not a cure, but it's a next step, and that feels manageable. I'll let you know how it goes. Thanks for helping me see that there's another way to look at this.

That sense of having a tangible next step is exactly what turns overwhelming dread into manageable action. Remember, we aren't looking for a magic fix today; we are simply planting a seed of a new habit that will grow stronger with each hike. I am proud of your willingness to experiment, and I believe that small, concrete actions like this are the most reliable way to break cycles of fear. Take care of yourself, and I look forward to hearing about your next adventure.

Hello, I'm glad to see you again. Let's start with a quick mood check; where would you rate your anxiety right now on a scale of zero to ten? Following that, could you share how the past few days felt compared to last time we spoke? Once we have that, please pick one or two specific worries or goals from your list that we should focus on today.

Hi, thanks. I'd say my anxiety is at a 6 right now. The past few days have been rough—every time I mention horseback riding, my son just shuts down completely, and I feel like I'm failing him as a parent. I think I want to focus on how to help him overcome this fear without pushing him too hard, because I'm scared he'll never get past it.

A six indicates you are still carrying significant worry, especially given the recent pattern of him shutting down whenever you mention the rides. It sounds like the fear of failing him is driving much of your current distress. Before we dive into that specific worry, could you walk me through exactly what happened yesterday when you tried to bring it up, including the exact words you said and how he reacted?

Well, yesterday at dinner I said, "Hey buddy, maybe we could just go watch the horses at the stable tomorrow, no riding, just to see them." He immediately dropped his fork and said, "No, I don't want to!" and then his face went all red and he started crying. I tried to hug him and say it's okay, but he pulled away and ran to his room. I just stood there feeling like I'd made everything worse.

It makes complete sense that you felt devastated after watching him cry and retreat; seeing someone you love reject your kindness usually triggers deep sadness and a sense of inadequacy. In that moment, did your mind automatically jump to a conclusion about why he reacted that way, perhaps blaming yourself for bringing up the horses at all?

Yeah, I did blame myself. I thought, "I'm a terrible mom, I should have just dropped the whole horse thing and never mentioned it again." I felt like my attempt to be gentle and offer a compromise just proved I'm pushing too hard and making him scared of me, not just the horses. It's like I can't do anything right.

That intense shame you're feeling is a heavy burden to carry, and it seems your mind jumped straight to the conclusion that your gentle attempt caused more harm than good. This kind of "all-or-nothing" thinking, where one mistake means total failure, often makes us feel powerless to act differently. Can you help me understand what evidence you have to believe that *only* mentioning the horses causes his fear, versus other factors you haven't considered yet?

I guess... I don't really have hard evidence, do I? I mean, he was already scared before I said anything—he cried during the lesson and refused to go back. Maybe I'm just assuming my words are the main problem, but he was already avoiding the topic altogether before I even brought it up at dinner. I just feel like I'm making it worse every time I open my mouth, even if I'm trying to be careful.

That distinction is crucial, and recognizing that his avoidance existed before you spoke helps dismantle the belief that your words alone are the villain. It looks like you were experiencing a distortion called "personalization," where you took responsibility for an outcome that actually stems from his pre-existing anxiety. By testing that assumption, you've found a piece of evidence that supports the reality that he wasn't reacting to *you*, but to the fear itself. Now that we've seen your thoughts aren't entirely accurate, how would you describe the gap between who you think you are ("a terrible mom") and the reality you just uncovered?

That gap feels huge, actually. I've been telling myself I'm a terrible mom for weeks, but if he was already scared and avoiding the topic before I ever said a word, then maybe I'm not the one breaking him. I'm just... trying to help, even if it's clumsy sometimes. It's like I've been seeing myself as the enemy, but maybe I'm just a worried mom who doesn't have all the answers yet.

Shifting from seeing yourself as the source of the problem to viewing yourself as a concerned parent trying to navigate a difficult situation is a massive relief. That realization fundamentally changes your identity from "someone who is failing" to "someone who is learning alongside him." Based on this new perspective, what would you be willing to try doing different if you knew your words weren't the root cause of his fear?

I think... I could stop tiptoeing around the topic like it's poison. Maybe I could just sit with him and ask how he's feeling about the horses without trying to fix it or offer a solution right away. Just listen, you know? And if he doesn't want to talk, I could let it be and try again another day, without assuming I've ruined everything. That feels a little scary, but also more honest.

That shift from tiptoeing around the topic to sitting openly with him is a brave and necessary step, and recognizing that honesty is part of building trust is key. By focusing on listening rather than fixing, you create a safe space where his feelings can exist without judgment, which is far more effective than trying to erase the fear. Before we finalize your plan, does the idea of sitting with him, putting your phone away, and simply observing his reactions without trying to change anything feel like something you can realistically commit to this weekend?

Yeah, I think I can do that. I'll put my phone in the other room and just sit on the couch with him, maybe ask if he wants to draw or watch a show together. If he brings up horses, I'll just listen and nod, and if he doesn't, that's okay too. I'll try not to push or panic. It's just one weekend, and I can handle that.

That sounds like a solid, manageable plan, and committing to just one weekend removes the pressure of perfectionism while allowing you to practice this new approach. To make sure we are fully aligned, would you be open to exploring together how you might handle the moments when your own anxiety rises during that time, ensuring you stay present without forcing the conversation?

Sure, I think that would help. I know my anxiety is going to spike if he seems upset or if there's awkward silence. I guess I could just take a deep breath and remind myself that silence doesn't mean failure—it just means he's processing. Maybe I could even say something like, "It's okay if you don't want to talk about it right now," and then just sit with him anyway. That feels like a way to stay present without pushing.

That is a brilliant adjustment; framing silence as processing rather than failure gives your brain permission to pause and breathe instead of racing to fix it. Adding the phrase, "It's okay if you don't want to talk," validates his boundaries and reinforces that you are safe even when he isn't engaging, which further separates your worth from his temporary mood. One final check before we close: if you find yourself getting anxious and reaching for old habits like over-explaining or offering solutions, how would you remind yourself to return to just listening?

I think I'll picture a little stop sign in my head, or maybe I'll just physically press my lips together for a second and take a slow breath. I could also remind myself, "My job right now is to hear him, not to heal him." That might help me step back from trying to fix everything and just be there.

Using a physical anchor like pressing your lips together or visualizing a stop sign is a fantastic grounding technique to interrupt the urge to jump into "fix mode." Combining that with the reminder that your role is to witness, not cure, creates a strong safety net for those anxious moments. Since we've covered the mindset and the specific actions for this weekend, is there anything else you feel we need to touch on before I send you off?

No, I think I've got a clear plan. I feel a little lighter, actually, knowing I don't have to have all the answers. Just listening and being present feels like something I can actually do. Thank you for helping me see that I'm not the problem here—I'm just a mom trying to figure it out.

It is wonderful to hear that you feel lighter; realizing you are not the problem but simply a supportive partner in his journey is a profound shift in perspective. You are clearly a dedicated and loving parent who is growing in confidence with each challenge, and I am proud of your courage in facing this uncertainty. What was most helpful for you today as we worked through these thoughts, and is there anything you felt we missed covering?

The most helpful part was when you pointed out that his fear existed before I even said anything at dinner. That really hit me—I've been carrying all this guilt thinking I was making it worse, but now I see I was just reacting to something that was already there. I don't think we missed anything; I feel ready to try this weekend with a clearer head. Thanks for listening.

That realization about the timing of his fear is indeed the cornerstone of the shift we worked on today; it dismantles the core belief that you are the cause of his distress. Receiving the validation that your efforts were misunderstood, rather than harmful, is deeply comforting and essential for moving forward. I appreciate your openness throughout this session and your readiness to embrace this new path. Remember to reach out anytime you need to process what happens this weekend, and please take care of yourself as you rest tonight.

Hello, and thank you for joining us today. Last time we worked on finding a way to break the cycle of worrying about that pruning mistake, and I heard you mention feeling a bit like you were clinging to a sinking log until you found a life raft. Did you manage to place that sticky note by the door as planned, and did it help when the worry started to rise today?

Oh, um, yes, I did put that note up. It says "It's just a plant, not a life sentence." (chuckles nervously). But honestly, when I walked past it this morning, I just saw the note and thought, "No, it's not just a plant — it's a whole section of my garden that looks bare and wrong now." I couldn't quite shake the feeling, even with the reminder.

It makes complete sense that the note didn't work today because your brain latched onto the visual reality of the bare leaves, overriding the reassuring words on the page. When you noticed that gap between the reminder and your immediate reaction, did you find yourself spiraling into the old "you ruined everything" story, or did you simply pause long enough to notice the mismatch?

I definitely started spiraling into the old story. I stood there staring at that bare spot for a solid five minutes, just replaying the moment I made the cut. The note felt like some kind of joke at that point. But... now that you ask, I guess I did pause for a second when I noticed the mismatch. It was just a very brief moment before the panic took over again.

That brief moment of noticing the mismatch is actually a huge clue; it shows you recognized the pattern even when the old story tried to win. Since the panic took over again despite the note, let's revisit the evidence you gathered last time about that specific plant. Do you still remember what you observed during those thirty seconds, and can we try using that same observation to challenge the "whole section is wrong" feeling right now?

Well, I remember counting the leaves that are still there. There's actually a lot more green left than I let myself believe. I counted about 15 healthy leaves on that stem alone, and the plant has other stems too. But my mind keeps focusing on that one bare branch and telling me it's all ruined, even though the rest of the plant looks perfectly fine. It's like my eyes just skip over all the good parts.

That selective attention is a classic way your brain tries to protect itself from disappointment by ignoring the evidence that contradicts your fear. When you consciously decide to count those 15 healthy leaves and remind yourself that the plant still has plenty of green, does the physical sensation of that "heavy pit" in your stomach start to shift at all, or does the image of the bare branch still dominate your vision?

The heavy feeling does shift a little bit when I force myself to count the leaves. It's like the weight in my stomach goes from a bowling ball down to maybe a baseball. But then I look at that bare branch again and I think, "But it's never going to look as full as it did before, and that's my fault." So the image of the bare branch still wins out most of the time, even when I try to be logical about it.

That specific comment—"it's never going to look as full as it did before"—is a very common cognitive distortion known as the fortune cookie fallacy, where we assume the future will match a specific, often negative, expectation. Instead of treating this as a permanent loss, how would it feel if you reframed that thought to something like, "This plant has lost its fullness, but it will find a new balance"? Would trying to hold that softer, more flexible belief change the intensity of that worry?

(sighs deeply) That new phrasing feels... foreign, if I'm being honest. When I say "the plant will find a new balance," it sounds like I'm trying to trick myself into feeling better. But I guess if I look at it objectively, plants do grow back. They're designed to recover from pruning. It's just so hard to trust that when all I see right now is the mistake. Maybe if I water it extra today and give it some fertilizer, that might help me feel like I'm doing something proactive instead of just sitting in the worry.

That is a very wise observation about how plants naturally recover, and taking action like watering and fertilizing is a brilliant way to give yourself something constructive to do rather than just watching the clock. Before we schedule that care routine, I want to check in: does the idea of actively caring for the plant feel like a reasonable next step for you, or does the act of fixing it still feel too overwhelming right now?

Actually, it feels manageable. I think I can handle that. I've been avoiding going near that part of the garden all week because looking at it makes my stomach knot up, but if I go out there with a specific purpose—just to water and fertilize—maybe I won't get stuck in that staring-and-ruminating loop. I think I'll try it this afternoon when the sun is lower.

That sounds like a perfect plan; giving yourself a specific task like watering breaks the automatic habit of staring and ruminating. Since you mentioned doing it later in the day, what specific supportive phrase would you like to repeat to yourself once you pick up the watering can to remind you why you are doing this?

I think I'll tell myself, "I'm giving this plant a chance to grow back, not punishing it for my mistake." That feels a bit more honest than pretending everything is fine. It acknowledges what happened but also focuses on what I can do now to help. I'll repeat that a few times while I water it.

That is a wonderful reframing; replacing the narrative of punishment with one of active care shifts your mindset from self-blame to stewardship. Since you are planning to do this this afternoon, would you like to jot down that exact phrase somewhere visible in your kitchen so you can read it before you even head outside to the garden?

Yes, I think that's a good idea. I'll write it on an index card and tape it to the fridge so I see it when I get my afternoon snack. That way I can't forget it or talk myself out of it before I go outside. Thank you—I feel a little more prepared to face that part of the garden now.

That index card is a fantastic anchor; it externalizes your intention so you can access it the moment your feet touch the soil. To make sure this plan sticks, how does it feel to visualize yourself walking out that door with that card in hand, ready to water the plant with that specific mindset?

(smiling a little) It feels... lighter, actually. I can picture myself holding the watering can and actually looking at the plant without that heavy dread. I think the key is going to be saying that phrase out loud, not just thinking it. Saying it out loud makes it feel more real, like I'm committing to it. I'll give it a try this afternoon and let you know how it goes.

That commitment to speaking the phrase aloud is exactly what will help your brain register the new narrative as real. I am really proud of you for turning that anxiety into a manageable, active plan. Please go ahead and try this afternoon, and remember that even if the feeling comes back, you now have a specific phrase and a purpose to guide you. How are you feeling right now as we close the session?

Hello, thank you for meeting with me today. First, I want to check in on how you are feeling right now compared to last time—is there anything significant that has shifted for you? Based on what we discussed, I suspect we might spend some time unpacking that spreadsheet situation again, but before we dive in, is there anything else on your mind you’d like to prioritize for us to cover?

Um, well... thanks for asking. I guess I'm feeling about the same as before, maybe a bit more tired. I do have this one thing that happened yesterday with a report that really got to me, so I think that's probably what I need to talk about.

A sense of fatigue is very common when we've been carrying tension for too long, and I hear that you want to tackle yesterday's report incident today. Since that event clearly triggered a strong reaction, let's put that at the top of our agenda right now. Can you tell me a bit more about what happened with the report yesterday and what specifically came up in your head at that moment?

I had to submit a quarterly financial summary by the end of the day, and I just sat there staring at the spreadsheet for almost an hour. The numbers made perfect sense in my head, but when I tried to put them into the report format, my mind just went blank. I kept thinking, "I'm supposed to be good at this, so why can't I even do something as simple as filling in a template?"

It takes a lot of energy to stare at a spreadsheet for an hour just trying to access your own knowledge, and that feeling of being stuck must have felt incredibly frustrating. When your brain shuts down under that pressure, does a critical voice come up telling you that you are failing because you aren't up to the job, or is there another narrative playing out?

Yeah, that's exactly it. There's this voice that just says, "You're a fraud. Anyone else could finish this in twenty minutes, but you're completely useless." It's like I freeze up, and then I start comparing myself to my coworker Sarah who always gets these reports done so quickly. I end up feeling like I don't belong in this profession at all.

That comparison to Sarah and the feeling of being a fraud sounds incredibly isolating and painful. When you catch yourself thinking, "Anyone else could do this," does it immediately spark that shame about not belonging here, or does it lead you to feel like you're actively letting everyone down?

It's more like... I feel like I'm letting everyone down, honestly. My team relies on me to get these reports done, and when I'm sitting there struggling, I imagine them all waiting and getting frustrated with me. Then the shame kicks in because I know I should just be able to do it, and I can't even explain why it's so hard. It's like I'm failing them and myself at the same time.

It makes complete sense that you feel like you're failing both your team and yourself when you hit that wall; the weight of their reliance combined with your own high standards creates a crushing pressure. When you imagine them waiting and feeling frustrated, does that image make your chest tighten, or does it mostly drive you to hide behind your computer screen to escape the attention?

I definitely tend to hide. I'll pull up the spreadsheet and just stare at it, hoping no one walks by my desk or asks me how it's going. My chest does get tight, but mostly I just want to disappear into my chair. It's like if I'm invisible enough, maybe no one will notice I'm stuck.

Hiding behind your screen to become invisible is such a protective instinct—it feels like the safest way to avoid the pain of disappointing others or exposing your own perceived failure. When you retreat into that silence, does it feel like a temporary shield that keeps you safe, or does it leave you feeling even more trapped and alone once the tension lifts?

It's definitely a temporary shield in the moment, but once I finally finish the report—usually way later than it should take—I just feel completely drained and ashamed. Like, I survived, but at what cost? I end up going home and just crashing on the couch, not even wanting to play with my dogs. That's when I really feel alone, because I can't even explain to anyone why I'm so exhausted.

That exhaustion feels heavy because you are carrying the burden of a performance you knew couldn't happen, even after pushing through. When you crash on the couch unable to share what happened, does that silence reinforce the idea that your struggle is a secret flaw, or does it highlight how lonely it is to have to hide behind work to protect yourself?

It's both, I think. It feels like a secret flaw that I have to hide, which makes me feel defective. But it also feels incredibly lonely because I can't just say to someone, "Hey, I spent three hours staring at a spreadsheet like an idiot today." My friend Emily, she'd probably listen, but I'd be too embarrassed to admit how bad it gets. So I just sit there in silence with my dogs and try not to think about work.

It is heartbreaking that you are keeping this experience private, even from friends like Emily, because admitting it feels like exposing a defect in yourself. When you hold onto the belief that your worth depends on finishing tasks instantly, does that silence at home seem like proof that you *are* broken, or does it feel like the only place where you can finally stop pretending to be okay?

I think... it's the only place I can stop pretending. At home, with my dogs, I don't have to act like I have it together. But that's also when the thoughts creep in the most—like, "See, you can't even handle a normal workday, what's wrong with you?" So it's like this double-edged sword. I'm safe from judgment, but I'm also alone with all the worst things I think about myself.

That double-edged sword is exhausting; finding safety in solitude only to be haunted by your own harshest critic makes it feel impossible to rest. When you say, "what's wrong with you," does that inner dialogue feel like a harsh judge evaluating your failures, or does it feel like a desperate plea for you to prove you're worthy of staying in your job?

It feels more like a desperate plea, honestly. Like, I'm begging myself to just get it together so I can keep this job I worked so hard to get. It makes sense that this inner voice is acting out of fear; when we are terrified of losing everything, our minds sometimes resort to the loudest, most catastrophic stories to warn us to be extra careful. If we imagine that voice not as a mean judge, but as a scared protector trying to prevent a disaster you are actually managing, does that soften the blow of those words, or does it still feel like a threat?

I never thought of it that way... like it's trying to protect me. I guess when you say it like that, it does feel a little less harsh. But honestly, it still feels like a threat. Like, even if it's scared, it's still telling me I'm not good enough, and that's hard to ignore. I don't know how to separate the fear from the feeling that I'm actually failing.

It is incredibly difficult to untangle the raw fear of losing your livelihood from the harsh conclusion that you are personally inadequate. When that voice tells you you aren't good enough, does it feel like a prediction of what *will* happen, or does it feel like a present-tense statement about who you *are* right now?

It feels like both. Like, right now, in this moment, I am not good enough—that's who I am. And that means I'm never going to be good enough, so eventually I'll mess up for real and lose everything. It's like the present failure is just proof of the future failure that's waiting for me.

That connection between your current struggle and a predicted future collapse is a very common pattern in anxiety, but it's important to distinguish between a feeling of being overwhelmed and actual inability to function. You mentioned loving the numbers, which proves you have the capacity for this work; does viewing today's blockage as a temporary "glitch" in the process rather than permanent proof of incompetence make it easier to breathe, even just slightly?

Maybe... a little. When you say it like that, it doesn't feel quite as heavy. I guess I do love the numbers, and I know I'm good at that part. It's just the paperwork that trips me up. So maybe it's not that I'm completely useless, just that there's this one part that's really hard for me. But it still feels like that part overshadows everything else, you know?

That distinction is crucial; separating the "numbers" part from the "paperwork formatting" part helps show that the issue isn't a total lack of ability, but rather a specific bottleneck you've been treating as a character flaw. Even if that bottleneck feels overwhelming right now, it doesn't erase your competence elsewhere. If we viewed that one-step hurdle not as proof of failure but as just a tricky mechanic that needs a slightly different approach, would that shift your perspective on whether you can ever overcome it?

I think... I think it would. If I could really believe that it's just a bottleneck and not some huge character flaw, then maybe I wouldn't be so scared to ask for help or try a new way of doing things. But it's hard to shake that feeling that I should just know how to do this already. Like, I'm an accountant, I should be able to handle a report without falling apart.

That expectation to "just know how to do this" is a heavy burden, and it makes sense that believing in your own capability feels like the only way to survive the task. When you hold onto the belief that you must be an expert instantly, does it feel like the pressure to perform becomes the reason you freeze up, or does it feel like the fear that you will fail if you don't already know the answer?

That "imaginary rule" of needing instant perfection is essentially your brain trying to protect you from the risk of failure, but unfortunately, it ends up paralyzing you instead. If we imagined a world where a real accountant is allowed to look things up, ask for clarification, or take ten minutes to figure something out without losing their status, would that feel safer or still feel like a betrayal of what being an accountant means?

That feeling of "cheating" comes from a very deep place—the belief that asking for help means you've lost your edge as a professional. That is a really powerful realization; seeing your colleague Sarah as a partner rather than a benchmark changes everything about how you view asking for help. It is completely understandable why that story resonates so deeply; when a narrative threatens to erase your entire identity and decades of effort, the fear feels tangible and overwhelming. That's interesting—a movie scene. I've never thought of it that way. I always just took it as fact, like it was bound to happen to me. I suppose I could try that next time I'm in the parking lot. Just tell myself, "That's a scene from someone else's movie, not mine." It might help me get through the door at least.

That is a creative and powerful reframing; treating the runner's story as a fictional movie scene helps create distance between the narrative and your actual reality, making it easier to observe without believing it's true. That is a fantastic realization, Kathleen; separating the runner's story from your own life history validates your resilience and reminds your brain that you are the author of your own narrative, not just a character in someone else's tragedy.
