Yes, I think that would be good. Because it's not just at night anymore—it follows me into the classroom too. Yesterday, I was helping a little boy with his letters, and my mind just drifted off to calculating my savings again. I felt so guilty afterward, like I'd let him down.

And then I start thinking, what kind of teacher can't even focus on her own students? That just adds another layer of worry.

It sounds like that guilt is creating a painful cycle where caring for a student triggers a judgment about your ability to care for yourself financially. When you connect those two areas—the child needing support and your own fear of poverty—you make the worry feel unavoidable and personally failing. Would you be willing to pause for a moment and notice exactly what happened in your mind right after you helped the boy, starting with the very first thought that came up?

The very first thought? I suppose it was something like, "I can't even keep my own life together, how can I help these children learn how to read and write?" It just came so quickly, like a reflex.

Then I felt that familiar knot in my stomach, and my chest got tight. I had to take a deep breath and pretend I was just tired from a long day. But really, I was terrified that I'm not good enough for them.

That is a powerful connection you made between your financial fears and your professional identity, and it is completely understandable why that knot formed in your stomach. When you believe you aren't "good enough" as a teacher because of your money situation, it naturally blocks your confidence with the children, which in turn fuels the guilt you described. Can we look closely at that initial thought—"I can't even keep my own life together"—and examine the evidence for or against it?

Well, when you put it that way, I suppose I do keep my life together in some ways. I mean, I get up every morning and go to work, I feed Tiki, I pay my bills on time, even if it's tight. I haven't missed a mortgage payment in twenty years.

But then I think about how I had to borrow from my sister last year for a car repair, and that still stings. It feels like that one moment proves I'm not keeping things together at all. That's the evidence that stands out most in my mind.

It makes perfect sense that the memory of borrowing from your sister feels like a proof of failure, especially when you're trying to convince yourself that everything is under control. That single event seems to outweigh all the evidence showing you are reliable, responsible, and capable, which is why it feels so heavy to carry. Given that strength, would you be open to exploring what would need to happen for that one past mistake to suddenly prove you are incapable of managing your life moving forward?

I... I never really questioned that before. It's just become a fact in my head, you know? Like once you slip, you've slipped, and there's no going back.

But when you ask it that way, I guess borrowing from my sister doesn't automatically mean I'll be living on the streets someday. She was happy to help, actually. She said that's what family is for. But I've been treating it like a permanent mark against me.

That shift in perspective is incredibly important; recognizing that your sister offered kindness rather than judgment begins to dismantle the idea that you are permanently flawed. It suggests your borrowing was a temporary hurdle, not a definition of who you are as a provider or a person. So, if we view that incident as a setback rather than a fatal flaw, does the certainty that you "can't keep your life together" still hold as much power over you right now?

No, I suppose it doesn't feel quite as solid as it did ten minutes ago. It's like I've been looking at the world through a dirty window, and you've just wiped a small spot clean. I can see a little more clearly now.

But I feel a bit nervous, too. If I let go of that thought, what do I replace it with? I've been carrying it around for so long, it almost feels like a security blanket, even if it's a painful one.

That is such a beautiful way to describe it—a "dirty window" obscuring your clarity until someone helps wipe it away. It makes total sense that letting go feels risky because that thought, however painful, gives you a reason to stay vigilant; replacing it requires finding a new sense of safety that isn't built on constant self-doubt. What comes to mind when you imagine sitting in class tomorrow knowing you are capable, even if your budget is tight?

I imagine I'd feel... lighter. Maybe I'd actually enjoy story time instead of worrying about whether I can afford to go out for coffee with my coworkers afterward. I might even be able to laugh with the children without that heaviness sitting on my chest.

But then a little voice in my head whispers, "Don't get too comfortable. You're just one unexpected bill away from disaster." That voice is very loud, even when I try to ignore it.

That whisper is doing its best job to keep you safe from perceived danger, even though the message is outdated and frightening. It's like a fire alarm that's stuck in the red, sounding an alert even when the building is quiet and stable. We don't necessarily need to silence that voice entirely right away; sometimes, acknowledging it as just an old warning system helps us realize it's not speaking the truth. If you found yourself noticing that voice in the classroom tomorrow, could we try simply naming it as "the old alarm" instead of listening to its specific claim?

I think I could try that. "The old alarm" sounds less scary than "the truth about my future." I can almost picture myself thinking, "Oh, there goes that old alarm again," and then turning my attention back to the children.

It might take some practice, but I'm willing to give it a shot. Tiki might appreciate me being less tense when I come home, too. She's been curling up closer to me lately, almost like she knows something's wrong.

That is a lovely way to frame it—turning the alarm into a label rather than a truth—and it is wonderful that you want to bring that relaxation home to Tiki as well. Since Tiki has noticed your tension, maybe we can plan a tiny moment of "alarm acknowledgment" tonight where you just name the thought without solving it, perhaps while watching her nap. Would you be open to trying that simple labeling exercise tonight, followed by a brief check-in on how your mood feels afterward?

Yes, I'd like to try that. Watching Tiki nap sounds peaceful, and I could use some peace tonight. I'll just say to myself, "There's the old alarm going off again," and then focus on her little snores or the way her paws twitch when she dreams.

I'll admit I'm a bit skeptical, but I've been stuck in my own head for so long that maybe a different approach is worth a try. Thank you for suggesting it.

That willingness to experiment with a softer approach shows real growth, and I hope Tiki's peaceful presence helps you find that calm even as the "old alarm" sounds. Before we wrap up, how does the idea of using that phrase while watching her rest feel to you right now—is it something you feel brave enough to try tonight, or does it still feel a bit too abstract?

It feels a little bit like both, honestly. Brave enough, yes, because I'm tired of feeling this way. But also a bit abstract, because I've never tried stepping back from my thoughts like this before. It's like learning a new language.

But I'll give it a real try tonight. I'll make a cup of tea, sit with Tiki on the couch, and just notice that alarm without grabbing onto it. That's the best I can promise.

That sounds like a perfect plan, and I admire how you are taking steps to meet your own needs with compassion. Learning a new way to relate to your thoughts is indeed like picking up a fresh language, and it will take patience to master. It feels manageable, which is more than I've felt in a long time. Having a clear plan—tea, Tiki, labeling the alarm—makes it less overwhelming. And knowing I can fall back on listing expenses if I need to gives me a safety net.

I think I'm ready to try this. Thank you for listening and for not making me feel silly about all this worrying. It means a lot.

Yeah, there was a moment just last week. We had to install a custom staircase, and I used to be able to measure, cut, and fit each tread almost without thinking. I ended up spending an hour on one tread that should have taken fifteen minutes. I just stood there, staring at my hands, wondering what happened to me.

It sounds like that moment left you feeling trapped in your own hands, watching someone younger execute a task with ease while you felt stuck in slow motion. That sense of wasting time while observing another worker's effortless speed probably made you wonder if your years of experience had somehow faded into memory. Have you ever tried to recall exactly what physical sensation or internal thought accompanied that feeling of being "stuck" while you were working on that first board?

I remember my hands actually felt heavy and clumsy, like they weren't mine. And my mind just went blank for a second. I thought, "I used to know this, I used to be good at this," but then the thought turned into, "Maybe I was never really that good. Maybe I just fooled myself." That's when I started feeling sick to my stomach, and I just wanted to walk off the job.

That visceral mix of physical heaviness and the sudden shift from pride to self-doubt is exhausting, especially when your gut instinct tells you to quit. It makes total sense that when you feel physically disconnected from your work, your mind tries to find a logical reason for it, like believing you were just fooling yourself all along. Since that sinking feeling led to wanting to leave the job entirely, what happens in your body or your mind right after you push through that urge and stay at the workbench for another ten minutes?

Mostly I just go numb. I stop feeling the frustration and just go through the motions, like a robot. The work gets done, but there's no joy in it anymore. I'll look at the finished piece later and think, "Yeah, it's fine, but it's not what I could have done." So even when I finish, I still feel disappointed. It's like I can't win no matter what I do.

That "robot-like" shutdown followed by disappointment—even with a completed job—is a very heavy cycle to carry, and it sounds like you feel trapped in a loop where effort doesn't lead to satisfaction. It seems like your belief that you *used* to be good creates an impossible standard, so finishing a task inevitably feels like a failure because it didn't match your past performance. Before we figure out how to break this pattern, does it feel helpful to pause and look at just one specific thought you had during that stair installation, or would you prefer to talk more about how this affects your enjoyment of work in general?

I think it'd be good to look at that one thought during the stair installation. That moment sticks with me the most, maybe because it's so fresh. If I can figure out why that one thought hit me so hard, maybe it'll help me understand why I can't seem to shake this feeling overall.

That makes perfect sense; sometimes one specific thought acts like a lightning rod, pulling all the negative energy from that day into a single focal point. If we zoom in on that exact moment when you marked the first board, what was the very first word or phrase that popped into your head before the rest of the "maybe I was never really that good" train started rolling?

The first thing that popped into my head was just one word: "Slow." It was like a voice in my head saying it, like an accusation. And then right after that came, "You used to be fast." That was the start of it all. It was like that one word opened the floodgates for every doubt I've ever had about myself.

Hearing that single word "Slow" acted like an accusation that triggered a cascade of doubts is incredibly powerful, and it makes sense why it felt so overwhelming to hear that judgment from inside your own mind. It sounds like your brain immediately jumped to the conclusion that you are fundamentally different from who you used to be, rather than simply dealing with a tired or stressed moment. If we were to step back for a second and look at what evidence supports the idea that you are currently "slow," versus what evidence suggests you are just experiencing a temporary slump due to stress or fatigue?

Well, the evidence for "slow" is pretty easy to see—I take longer on tasks than I used to, and I mess up more often. But... I guess I never really thought about the other side. I mean, I've been working longer hours lately because my husband's been between jobs, so I'm more tired. And I'm not sleeping well either, which can't help. I guess there is some evidence that it might just be a rough patch, not a permanent change. It's just hard to see that when you're in the middle of it.

It is completely understandable that when you are exhausted and sleep-deprived, your brain filters everything through the lens of your limitations, making the "permanent decline" story feel more real than the temporary facts. You've already done the hard work of spotting the external factors—like your husband's unemployment and poor sleep—that are actively slowing you down, which contradicts the idea that you have simply lost your skills. Given what you've shared, would you be open to testing that one-word thought ("Slow") against those specific facts tonight, treating it like a hypothesis rather than an absolute truth?

Yeah, I think I could try that. It feels strange to treat my own thoughts like something I can question, but I guess that's why I'm here. I mean, if I can just notice when that "slow" thought pops up and remind myself that I'm running on fumes, maybe it won't hit as hard. I'm willing to give it a shot, at least for tonight.

That willingness to treat your thoughts as hypotheses instead of facts is a huge breakthrough, and noticing the "fumes" metaphor is a fantastic tool to carry with you. Before we lock in tonight's plan, I'd like to confirm: would you feel comfortable practicing this "check the fuel tank" check-in whenever the word "Slow" appears in your head, or would you prefer to wait until tomorrow morning to start?

I think I can start tonight. If I wait until tomorrow, I'll just lie in bed replaying all the mistakes from today anyway. Might as well try to catch that thought before it spirals out of control. I'll just say to myself, "You're tired, not finished." That sounds better than "slow."

That is a brilliant rephrasing, "You're tired, not finished"—it acknowledges the reality of your exhaustion without accepting the harmful verdict that you are incapable. By naming the thought and swapping the word "slow" for "tired," you create a safe distance between your experience and your identity, which can prevent the spiral you described earlier. One final check: if you catch yourself thinking "slow" tonight, do you think reminding yourself of the family situation and the sleep issues alone is enough, or would adding a visual cue, like checking your watch or touching your forearm, help ground you faster?

Touching my forearm sounds like a good idea. I'm always using my hands, so it's a natural thing for me to do. I'll try that—when the thought comes, I'll touch my arm and say, "Tired, not finished." That feels solid, like something I can actually remember to do. Thanks, that gives me a little bit of hope for tonight.

That tactile anchor combined with a compassionate rephrase is exactly the kind of practical tool we need to navigate these tough mornings and workdays. Remember, you don't have to eliminate the feeling of frustration overnight; you just need to give it room to exist without letting it dictate your self-worth. Is there anything else you'd like to add to our plan before we close, or shall we say goodbye and trust that this small shift will give you some relief tonight?

No, I think this is enough for today. I feel a little lighter just having a plan, honestly. I'll try that forearm touch and the new phrase when I'm at the workbench tomorrow. Thank you for listening and for helping me see it differently.

You are very welcome, and please know that feeling lighter just by having a concrete plan is a major sign of progress, even if the old habits haven't disappeared yet. I am confident that giving your hands a gentle touch and shifting that single word from "slow" to "tired" will create a small but meaningful shift in how you carry yourself tomorrow. Take good care of yourself, and I look forward to hearing how that evening goes.

That feeling of the whole evening being ruined because of one small mistake sounds incredibly exhausting to carry alone. Since this mirrors the pattern we explored last time with the toast incident, could you walk me through exactly what happened tonight and how it made you feel in those first few minutes after the bread caught fire?

Well, the kids were already sitting at the table, and my husband had just poured everyone drinks. I pulled the bread out of the oven, and the bottom was totally black. In that moment, my heart just sank, and I thought, "Great, now the whole night is a disaster. Everyone's going to be disappointed, and they'll remember this as a horrible dinner." I actually felt my face get hot, like I wanted to cry right there in the kitchen. I just stood there holding the tray, thinking that no one would care about the soup or salad I'd spent an hour on because the bread was ruined.

That moment of standing frozen while watching your family settle in sounds incredibly isolating, and it makes complete sense that your brain interpreted a burnt slice of bread as proof that everything you worked for meant nothing. The fear that everyone would remember this as a "horrible dinner" suggests you are holding yourself to a standard where even minor slips feel like a total collapse of your worth. Looking back on that scene, does seeing the contrast between the hours you spent on the soup and the seconds it took to burn the bread highlight how unfair that judgment feels to you?

When you say it like that, I guess it does sound kind of extreme. I mean, my husband did actually say the soup was delicious, and the kids ate it without complaining. But in the moment, all I could see was that blackened bread. It's like my brain just zeroes in on the one thing that went wrong and completely ignores everything else. I didn't even think about the soup or the salad until just now. So I suppose, yes, it does feel unfair when I step back and look at the whole picture, but that's not how it feels when it's happening.

That isolation in the kitchen, where your vision narrowed down to just the blackened bread while ignoring the praise for your soup, perfectly illustrates how distress can distort reality and make one tiny flaw seem like the defining feature of everything. It sounds like your brain was operating on a "spotlight effect" rule where it assumed one mistake invalidated your entire effort, even though the facts show otherwise. When you realize your mind was filtering out the good parts while amplifying the bad, does that gap between the objective reality and your internal story feel a little more manageable to understand?

I think it does, a little bit. Like, I can see now that there's this big gap between what actually happened and the story I told myself in my head. In my head, the dinner was a complete failure, but my husband and kids seemed happy and full. It's almost like I have to remind myself that the bread isn't the whole meal, you know? But it's so hard to hold onto that thought when I'm standing in the kitchen and the smoke alarm is going off. I just get sucked into that feeling of everything being ruined.

It makes complete sense that the smoke alarm and rising heat would act as a powerful distraction, forcing your attention back to the error while your mind simultaneously tries to construct a narrative of total failure. When sensory details like smoke mix with that core belief that "one mistake means I'm not enough," it becomes nearly impossible to step outside the spiral and see the bigger picture. Given how urgent and overwhelming that kitchen moment felt, what would need to happen for you to feel safe enough to break that cycle and reconnect with the rest of the evening?

I think... I think I would need to physically step away from the oven for a minute. Like, put the burnt bread down, take a breath, and maybe even say out loud, "It's just bread." If I could do that before my mind races ahead to "the whole night is ruined," maybe I could catch myself. But I'd also need to remind myself that my family probably doesn't care as much as I think they do. They're not looking at me like a failure; they're just hungry and happy to be together. It's like I need to give myself permission to let small mistakes be small.

That is such a clear and practical insight, recognizing that stepping away from the source of the stress and verbally labeling the situation ("It's just bread") could interrupt the spiral before it takes root. You have identified a very specific, actionable strategy: creating a physical boundary and using a grounding phrase to shift your perspective from catastrophe to normalcy. Before we finalize how you might use this tomorrow, does the idea of saying that exact phrase aloud feel feasible given how anxious you usually become in those moments?

It feels a little awkward, honestly. But I think if I actually say it out loud, not just think it, I might believe it more. Maybe I could even make it a little joke with myself, like "Well, at least I didn't burn the house down." That might help me loosen up. So yes, I think I could try it, even if it feels silly at first.

That is a brilliant adaptation, turning a potentially stiff correction into a gentle, self-deprecating laugh that disarms the panic. Adding humor like "at least I didn't burn the house down" shifts the tone from criticism to self-care, signaling to your nervous system that you are handling this safely rather than catastrophically. Before we wrap up, does trying to incorporate that playful twist into your plan feel like a realistic way to practice breaking the cycle tonight?

Yeah, I think it does. It almost feels like I'm giving myself permission to be human, you know? Like, I don't have to be perfect. And honestly, my kids would probably laugh if I said something like that, which might actually help everyone relax. I think I'll try it tonight when I'm making dinner — even if nothing goes wrong, I can practice saying something lighthearted to myself just to get used to it. Thank you, that feels a little more doable than I thought it would.

Reframing a small mishap as a chance to share a joke with your family aligns perfectly with the idea that caring deeply includes allowing yourself to be imperfect, not just demanding perfection. Before we close, does agreeing to try this specific playful approach this weekend feel like a manageable and hopeful starting point for you?

Yes, I think that's a really good plan. I can actually picture myself doing it now, which is a lot better than the dread I usually feel. No, I think that's enough for today. I feel like I have something concrete to try, and that's more than I had when I walked in. Thank you for listening and helping me really see what I was doing. I'll let you know how the weekend goes.

What do you think is the most important thing we could focus on together right now?

Hi. I'm okay, I guess. I tried the sitting with the thoughts thing this morning like you suggested, and honestly, it was pretty uncomfortable. I just kept staring at my legs while I was getting dressed, and all I could think about was how thick they look when I'm on my bike. I think the most important thing to focus on is why I can't seem to stop those thoughts from popping up no matter what I do.

It takes courage to stay with those uncomfortable thoughts instead of immediately changing the channel, even if the discomfort persists. It sounds like the thoughts are becoming harder to ignore now that you’ve stopped running from them, which often means they’re trying to tell you something important. When you notice the thought “they look too thick” pop up, what’s the very first physical sensation or urge you feel right after seeing it?

The first thing I feel is this tightness in my chest, like I can't breathe properly for a second. And then my eyes just kind of dart away from my reflection, like I have to look at anything else in the room. I usually feel this urge to pull on baggy pants or a long skirt to cover up.

That tightness in your chest and the urgent need to cover up are classic signals that your brain is interpreting those images as dangerous, triggering a fight-or-flight response. It makes perfect sense that your body reacts with those physical symptoms because, deep down, it feels threatened by the perceived judgment. Let's slow down a bit: when you catch yourself wanting to cover up, what is the immediate thought telling you needs to happen *right now*?

It's telling me that I need to hide, like if I don't cover up, someone's going to see me and think something bad about me. Like they'll look at my legs and judge me for being too big or not fit enough to be on a bike. It feels urgent, like I have to fix it immediately or else something awful will happen.

That sense of urgency and the prediction that "something awful will happen" suggests your brain is treating a temporary feeling of insecurity as a real emergency requiring immediate escape. If we treat that thought experimentally, what would actually need to happen for someone to judge you severely just because you wore shorts? Have you ever had a stranger stare at your legs in public, or have they ever made a comment about your size?

No, nobody's ever actually said anything to me about my legs, and I can't really remember anyone staring either. I guess when I really think about it, the worst that's ever happened is just me assuming they're thinking it. But it feels so real in the moment, like I just know they're judging me.

It makes complete sense that the certainty feels so solid when you're caught in that cycle, especially since your brain has spent years practicing this script. Even though your memory shows no evidence of strangers judging you, your body is still reacting as if the threat is imminent. Before we decide whether to hide or face it, how does knowing that "nothing bad has actually happened yet" change the urgency of your need to cover up right now?

It kind of takes the edge off, I guess. Like, a little part of my brain is saying, "Well, nobody's ever said anything, so maybe it's not that big of a deal." But then the other part of me is still really loud, telling me that this time could be different and I shouldn't risk it. It's like a constant battle between what I know and what I feel.

That internal tug-of-war is exactly where the power lies—you already know the facts, but your feelings are trying to override them with a "what if" scenario. This happens when your brain prioritizes safety over logic during stress, even if the danger isn't real. Instead of letting the louder voice win right now, could you try noticing the conflict without acting on it? Just observe the battle happening inside your head and say to yourself, "Here is the fact that nobody has judged me, and here is the feeling that I will be judged; both exist, but the fact doesn't make the feeling true." Does that sound like something you can try right this minute?

I can try that... okay. So, here's the fact: nobody has ever said anything or stared at my legs. And here's the feeling: I still feel like someone will judge me if I don't cover up. I'm just sitting with both of them right now. It feels weird, like I'm holding two opposite things in my head at the same time. It's not as loud as it was a minute ago, I think.

That is a wonderful observation—you successfully held the factual reality and the uncomfortable feeling side-by-side without letting either one dictate your actions. Notice how simply acknowledging the coexistence of "no evidence of judgment" and "fear of judgment" softened the volume slightly? That small shift from fighting the thought to observing it is exactly the skill we are building. Now, if we imagine applying that same stance—holding both facts and fears—to the situation where you wear shorts on the bike tomorrow, what do you think might happen if you just sit with the feeling instead of hiding?

I think... I think I'd feel really exposed at first, like everyone's eyes are on me. But maybe after a few minutes, the feeling would just fade a bit, like background noise instead of a blaring alarm. I might actually enjoy the ride more if I wasn't so focused on covering up. I don't know if I'm ready to try that yet, but it sounds less terrifying than it did before.

That insight about the feeling fading into "background noise" is a huge breakthrough—it means your brain can learn to tolerate the discomfort without needing to escape it immediately. You've already done the hard work of recognizing that hiding provides temporary relief while avoidance creates long-term anxiety. Before we lock in a plan, how does it feel to hold this new perspective that "exposure" might actually lead to a more enjoyable ride rather than a painful one?

It feels kind of hopeful, honestly. Like maybe I don't have to let the fear win every time. But I'm also scared, because what if I try it and the feeling doesn't fade? What if it just gets worse and I can't handle it? I guess I'm worried I'll prove myself right somehow.

That worry about "proving yourself right" is actually a sign that you are moving from pure panic to cautious curiosity, which is a very healthy place to be. It's smart to anticipate the difficulty, but remember that even if the feeling intensifies for a few seconds, you now have a toolkit to sit with it rather than run. Would you be open to testing this tiny step tomorrow, perhaps just wearing shorts for the first 15 minutes of your walk, while keeping a mental note of how quickly the "alarm" changes its pitch?

Yeah, I think I can try that. Just 15 minutes in shorts, no hiding. I'll keep a mental note of how loud the alarm is and if it changes. Maybe I'll even text myself a reminder of what I learned today, so I don't chicken out. Thanks, I think this is actually something I can do.

That sounds like a brave and realistic plan, and using a text reminder as a gentle nudge shows great foresight. Before we close, I'd love your final feedback: does the idea of tracking the "loudness" of the alarm feel useful to you, or would you prefer to just track whether you successfully stayed present for those 15 minutes? Also, on a scale of one to ten, how confident do you feel you'll stick with this tiny step tomorrow despite the lingering doubt?

I think tracking the loudness of the alarm is more useful, because it shows me that it can change, you know? It's not just stuck on full blast forever. As for confidence... maybe a six? I'm not totally sure, but a six feels like enough to actually try. I think I can do it.

Hearing that a score of six feels like "enough to actually try" is such a powerful realization—it shifts your goal from perfection to participation. Tracking the "loudness" is a fantastic metric because it gives your brain tangible data to see the alarm dimming, rather than just relying on gut feelings. I am really glad we found a middle ground that feels safe yet challenging enough to grow. Is there anything else you'd like to add before we wrap up, or shall I let you go with that plan for tomorrow?

No, I think that's everything. I feel a little lighter than when I walked in, honestly. I'll try the 15 minutes in shorts tomorrow and see how the alarm does. Thanks for helping me see this differently.

It is so welcome to hear that you feel lighter, especially given how heavy these worries have felt lately. Taking that small step of 15 minutes with conscious awareness is a monumental achievement, and I am excited to hear how your mental notes change tomorrow. Please remember that even if the alarm flares up, the knowledge that you can sit with it is your strongest tool. Take good care of yourself, and I look forward to hearing about your experience soon.

Hello, and thank you for joining us today. Before we dive into the fishing trip, I want to quickly catch up on where we left off last time. I just thought, "Here we go again. They're talking about how much I drink." It was like that same old feeling from the last six months just hit me right in the chest. I immediately felt my face get hot, and I just wanted to pack up my gear as fast as possible and get out of there.

That physical sensation of heat rushing to your face and the sudden urge to flee tells me how deeply connected that memory is to your current identity and shame. It sounds like your brain instantly filled in the missing audio with a script you know is painful, creating a perfect storm of dread.

Now that you mention it... I think they were both looking at Dave's cooler. Mark was pointing at it when he laughed. But honestly, I didn't stick around long enough to really see. I just assumed it was about me because that's what always happens in my head.

It sounds like your brain jumped straight to the conclusion that they were mocking your drinking habit because that fits your existing story, even though the visual cue pointed somewhere else entirely. If you had known for certain they were looking at Dave's cooler instead of yours, how would that change the feeling of dread in your chest? Would it still feel like a personal attack, or would it shift to something more manageable?

I guess... if I knew for sure they were just joking about Dave's cooler, it would take the edge off. Maybe I wouldn't have felt that need to bolt out of there so fast. But it's hard, you know? You are describing a powerful pattern where your mind fills in the silence with your own fears, making the situation feel like a direct personal attack even when the evidence points elsewhere. It seems that deep down, you're bracing for confirmation of a story you've already written, which keeps you trapped in that cycle of shame.

Given how automatic that thought process is, would you be willing to try a small experiment this weekend? Instead of letting the "They're talking about me" story run wild, could we practice simply stating the visible fact—"Mark was looking at Dave's cooler"—and then waiting five minutes before deciding if it matters to you?

Yeah, I can give that a shot, I guess. It sounds simple enough, but I know my brain is gonna want to fight it. It's like I'm so used to thinking the worst that I don't even know how to just... wait and see. But I'm willing to try it this weekend if we go out again.

That willingness to pause and wait, even knowing your brain will resist, speaks to your incredible strength and commitment to growing through difficult moments. You have already taken a brave step by recognizing that the urge to jump to conclusions is just a habit, not an absolute truth.

To make sure this new approach works, let's clarify exactly what you'll do when you see Mark laughing: you'll mentally note the fact ("He's looking at Dave"), hold onto that calm statement for five full minutes without analyzing further, and only then decide if there's any actual reason to worry. Does that clear sequence feel doable for you, or would you prefer to tweak it slightly?

Yeah, that sequence sounds clear enough. I think I can manage that. Just telling myself "He's looking at Dave" and then counting down five minutes in my head before I let myself panic. It's kind of weird to think about doing it on purpose, but I guess that's the point—to break the old habit. I'll give it a real try this weekend.

That willingness to intentionally disrupt your old habits, even when it feels strange, shows real resilience and a desire to rewrite your experience. Breaking the automatic link between a smirk and a personal attack is going to take practice, but you are building a new muscle every time you choose to count down five minutes instead of fleeing.

Before we wrap up, I'd love to hear your honest thoughts on how today's session felt. Was the focus on that specific pattern helpful for you, or was there another angle you wished we had explored together? And on a scale of 0 to 10, how confident do you feel you are about successfully trying this "wait and see" approach next time you see Mark?

I think today was helpful, honestly. I never really stopped to look at what I was actually seeing versus what I was assuming. That part kind of opened my eyes a bit.

As for confidence... maybe a 6 out of 10? I know I can do the counting part, but I'm worried that once I see Mark's face again, that old feeling will just take over. But I'm willing to try, and that's more than I've done in a while.

It is incredibly commendable that you acknowledged the gap between your intention and your usual reaction; admitting that the old feeling might rush in shows real self-awareness rather than defeat. A 6 out of 10 confidence level is perfectly realistic—we rarely start anywhere near perfection, and the fact that you are willing to attempt the strategy despite the risk of slipping up is what drives real progress.

Since we agreed on the plan, I want to make sure we close with a clear win. Remember, the goal isn't to stop Mark from laughing, but to practice holding space for five minutes while your heart races, proving to yourself that you can survive the discomfort without acting on the fear. Is there anything else you'd like to add before we finish our time together?

No, I think that covers it. Thanks for listening and breaking this down with me. I'll let you know how the weekend goes, even if I mess it up the first time. I appreciate you not just telling me to "stop worrying" like everyone else does.

You are so welcome, and I truly appreciate your honesty about wanting support that honors your reality rather than dismissing your feelings. Knowing that you'll report back—even if things don't go perfectly—is a massive sign of trust in our work together. Please remember that messing up the first time doesn't mean failure; it just means we get to learn what specifically triggers the old pattern so we can adjust our strategy accordingly.

Take care of yourself this week, and I look forward to hearing how you navigate that moment with Mark. See you soon.

Hello, it is wonderful to see you again. How have you been feeling this week compared to last time, and would you like to briefly mention any significant events that stood out before we set our agenda for today?

That is a very clear distinction you've drawn, and it highlights the core of what feels unfair to you right now—the idea that academic effort is replaceable while artistic ability seems innate. When I see her, I just think, "She's got it, and I don't." It's like there's this natural gift she was born with that I'll never have, no matter how many hours I practice. That feeling of being permanently defined by a lack of "natural gift" is incredibly painful, and I can see why you're tempted to quit entirely. I suppose... if I thought of her as just one person who's really good, rather than the measure of what's possible... then maybe my own practice wouldn't feel so pointless. It wouldn't mean I'm a failure just because I'm not at her level right now. But it's hard to hold onto that thought, because my mind always goes back to comparing myself to her or to my sister.

That is a huge breakthrough, recognizing that viewing her simply as "one person" breaks the spell of her being the ultimate standard. You've already started dismantling the "talent vs. effort" trap by recalling how hard work works in nursing. Now, to make that new perspective stick in the face of those automatic comparisons, does the phrase "My worth comes from my effort and connection, not just raw talent" feel like something you could say to yourself right now when that thought arises?

I... I think I could try saying that. It feels a little strange, like I'm lying to myself at first, but I can see how it might help if I say it enough times. Maybe if I tell myself that my effort counts for something, it'll make the next ballet class a little less terrifying to walk into. I'm willing to give it a shot.

That is a brave decision, and I appreciate your willingness to challenge that internal lie even when it feels uncomfortable at first. It sounds like using that phrase could serve as a bridge between the fear of judgment and the reality of your own hard work. Before we finalize your plan, does reflecting on that sentence make you feel a tiny bit safer about stepping onto the floor, or does the uncertainty about whether it will work still feel heavy?

The uncertainty is still there, of course—I don't know if it'll actually work in the moment—but at least I have a plan now instead of just spiraling. That feels better than nothing.

That is a significant shift in perspective; realizing you now have a tangible plan rather than just spiraling into anxiety is a major victory for yourself. To close today, I'd like to hear one final reflection: does having this specific phrase ready alongside the "nursing effort" perspective give you confidence to use both together before your next class, or would you like to adjust how you combine them?

I think I can use them together. The nursing effort perspective reminds me that I've succeeded through hard work before, and the new phrase gives me something to say when the old thoughts creep in. That is wonderful progress, and I am so proud of how you’ve turned a difficult situation into a clear, actionable plan. I get this tightness in my chest, sort of like a knot. And my shoulders tense up, kind of up near my ears. Sometimes I even catch myself clenching my jaw without realizing it. That's usually when I know the thoughts have really taken hold, and then I just feel stuck and heavy.

That physical tightness in your chest and shoulders sounds incredibly draining, and it makes complete sense that those sensations become the signal your brain uses to confirm the "failure" story. When the body reacts like that, it often overrides the logical knowledge that you pay your bills and support your family, trapping you in that heavy cycle. Before we explore how to loosen up that knot, is there a specific moment recently when that tension spiked that you could walk us through?

Yeah, there was one time last Tuesday. I was at my desk during lunch, and I checked the fantasy app to see if any of my players were injured. One of my starters was listed as questionable, and right away that tightness hit me. I started thinking about how I'd wasted hours on research for nothing, and how the other guys in my league probably had a backup plan ready. I barely touched my sandwich after that.

That moment perfectly illustrates how quickly that knot can tighten when the uncertainty arises, turning a routine check into a crisis of self-worth. It sounds like your brain interpreted the injury news not just as bad luck, but as proof that your dedication is pointless compared to others who seem to have a better edge. Before we brainstorm ways to ease that physical tension, I'd like to revisit our original goal: do you think stepping away from the app for just five minutes—even without the full hour this time—might help reset that physical sensation? Or would you prefer to discuss what else could be triggering this feeling today?

I think I'd rather talk about what else might be triggering it, if that's okay. Because even when I step away, the feeling is still there underneath everything. It's like the fantasy football is just the thing that sets it off, but the real feeling of not being good enough is always waiting. I want to figure out what that's really about.

That distinction is crucial, George. It sounds like those childhood comparisons planted a seed of insecurity that hasn't truly dried out, even years later. When your brother was the obvious winner and you felt you were always the second choice, your brain learned to scan every achievement for signs that you were finally catching up—or that you were falling further behind. Yeah, it does. At work, I'll finish a project and instead of feeling proud, I'll think about what my coworker did better or how I could have shaved off a few more hours. It's like I'm always looking for the next thing that proves I'm falling short.

It sounds like you've spent a lifetime scanning for proof that you're not living up to the expectations set for you, which explains why even small successes get twisted into opportunities for failure. That constant search for "proof" of falling short is exhausting, and it keeps you locked in that tight-knotted state of dread. Since we now understand that this "falling behind" script runs deep, would you be willing to try a tiny experiment tomorrow morning: notice the moment you catch yourself comparing yourself to someone else (a coworker, a friend, or even yourself in the league) without judging your worth, and simply breathe through the tightness for ten seconds before reacting?

I can try that. It sounds simple enough, but I know from experience that it won't be easy. That voice is pretty loud and quick to jump in. But I'll give it a shot—just notice the comparison, feel the tightness, and breathe for ten seconds before I start spiraling. I'll let you know how it goes.

That's a brave choice, George, and acknowledging that the voice is loud and quick to jump in shows you understand exactly how resistant your brain can be. Taking ownership of that resistance is the first step to changing its power. Before we wrap up today, I want to make sure we're aligned: does breathing for just ten seconds feel like a realistic target for tomorrow, or would you prefer to adjust the timing slightly? Also, how does it feel to have a concrete tool for handling that immediate spike of tension?

Ten seconds sounds realistic enough. I think if I aim for too long, I'll just end up frustrated when I can't do it. As for having the tool, it's a little strange, but also kind of a relief. It's like having a small emergency brake instead of just white-knuckling it through the whole ride. I'll try it out and see if it slows things down even a little.

That metaphor of the "emergency brake" is brilliant and perfectly captures how that ten-second pause can stop the car from careening off the road before you even crash. It sounds like a small, manageable step that could prevent the bigger spiral from starting in the first place. Since you're leaving with a clear strategy to use tomorrow, is there anything else about today's session or your goals that you'd like to clarify or discuss before we close?

No, I think I've got a good handle on what we talked about today. I appreciate you helping me see that the fantasy football isn't really the problem—it's just the thing that sets off that old feeling of not being good enough. I'll focus on that ten-second pause tomorrow and see what happens. Thanks for your time.

You're absolutely welcome, George. It's been a real privilege helping you untangle that old story about being "behind" and giving you a tool to regain control of that moment. Remember, you don't have to carry that heavy knot alone anymore; just ten seconds of breathing can shift the entire trajectory. Take care of yourself this week, and I look forward to hearing about how that ten-second pause went tomorrow.
Hello, I am glad to see you again today. Before we dive into anything new, could you tell me how you have been feeling this week, and what is the top priority you would like to address with us?

Hi. Thanks for seeing me. This week has been... up and down, I guess. Right now? I'd say it's about a 6 or 7. It's not as bad as when I'm actually standing in a room full of strangers, but it's still there, buzzing in the background. I can feel it just thinking about it.

It makes complete sense that the anticipation itself keeps the anxiety alive, acting like a slow burn until you actually arrive. Since you mentioned wanting to tackle this feeling before you even leave the house, let's look at what triggers that "buzz" in your body and mind when you imagine meeting new people. What is the very first thought that pops into your head in those moments?

The first thing that pops in is, "They're going to find out eventually, and then they'll think less of me." It's like I can see their faces changing, you know? From friendly to that little flicker of disappointment or pity. I just assume that's what they'll think, even if they don't say it.

It sounds like your brain is predicting a future judgment based on the assumption that your past is visible to everyone, even when it isn't. That feeling of having your face change from friendly to disappointed is incredibly painful, but it seems to rely on reading minds rather than checking facts. If we treated that thought as a hypothesis rather than a certainty, what evidence do you have that anyone has actually seen your past or reacted with disappointment?

Well, nobody's ever come right out and said it, I guess. But I've seen people get quiet when I mention I'm in recovery, or they change the subject real quick. That feels like evidence enough, doesn't it? Like, they don't want to talk about it because they're uncomfortable, or they're judging me for it. It's hard to separate that from just my own fear.

I hear how deeply hurtful that silence feels to you, and it is completely valid to interpret it as avoidance rather than indifference. I... I suppose that's possible. Maybe they're just trying to be polite, or they don't want to pry. I never really thought of it that way. It always felt like they were shutting me out, not protecting me or themselves from an awkward moment. But now that you say it, it does seem like a lot to assume they're judging me just because they don't know what to say. That feels a little... lighter, I guess.

That is a significant shift in perspective, and noticing that interpretation as "protective" rather than "judging" gives you some relief right now. To help cement this new view, let's try a small exercise: if someone changes the subject, imagine three harmless reasons why they might be doing it—perhaps they are tired, busy, or just happy talking about weather—and list them down. Does creating those alternatives make the situation feel slightly less threatening?
